rin · data-oriented design · build an ECS

rin-dod

Build an archetype entity component system from nothing, in fifteen chapters you read, compile and step through: from an entity as a number to a game running on it.

Start with 1.1, an entity is a number

Data-oriented design in rin, in two courses and a dojo:

  1. Build an ECS. Start here. Fifteen chapters that build an archetype entity component system from nothing, in the order of its name: entities, then components, then systems. It ends with a game running on it. Each chapter is a program that compiles on its own, the output it must print, and a guide that builds it step by step.
  2. Advanced: layout and SIMD. Seven lessons, for after. They cover what a loop fetches from memory, aliasing and noalias, what the compiler vectorizes and how to check it in the assembly, and which layout suits which access pattern.
  3. The dojo. The thirteen building blocks an ECS is made of, taken out on their own: a playground to watch each one work and break, and a kata to write it yourself, timed, against a harness, until your hands know it.

There is no renderer, no window and no library: only data, and the loops that stream it.

Read each chapter's guide first. It explains the new idea and builds its code step by step, and every sample in it is copied from the chapter's program. Then open the program: it holds everything built so far, with the chapter's new code near the end, so any chapter can be opened in a debugger and stepped through as a whole ECS. Run it and read the output against the code. Each guide ends with exercises, most of them "break this on purpose and watch what happens".

Each chapter's file starts from the previous chapter's, so diffing two neighbours shows exactly what a chapter changed:

git diff --no-index ecs/src/2.components/2.5.typed_access/typed_access.rin ecs/src/2.components/2.6.add_remove/add_remove.rin

The ECS is called kayan, after the C sketch it grew out of.

Build and run

Needs the rin compiler with noalias (rin 5413d4e or later; rin.exe from rin-windows-x64, through RIN_HOME or PATH), CMake, Ninja, clang-cl and the Windows SDK.

rin build
build\cmake\ids.exe

Every chapter and lesson is its own program, named after its file. Or compile one by hand: rin writes C, and any C compiler does the rest, with rin's folder and its std on the include path:

rin compile ecs/src/2.components/2.4.archetypes/archetypes.rin -o archetypes.c
clang -std=c11 -g -I <rin> -I <rin>/std archetypes.c -o archetypes

python tools/check.py builds every program with clang and warnings as errors, runs it, and compares what it prints with its .expected file. --sanitize adds AddressSanitizer and UBSan, --bless rewrites the expected files after a deliberate change, and a word filters the programs. tools/check_snippets.py checks that every sample in the ECS guides is in its program:

python tools/check.py ecs
python tools/check.py kayan --sanitize
python tools/check_snippets.py

The checker also works on Linux. There it relaxes -Wformat only: rin's printfmt and std print write %llu for u64, which is unsigned long on 64-bit Linux.

Reading it in a browser

Open website/index.html. It has every chapter's and lesson's guide, its source with line numbers, and the output it must print, with an index on the left. It is generated from the files in this repository, so after changing a program or a guide run python tools/site.py to bring it up to date.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.1

An entity is a number

ecs/src/1.entities/1.1.ids/ids.rin

An ECS has three parts: Entities, Components and Systems. This chapter builds all three in the simplest way that works, about a hundred lines, so you can see the whole shape before any of it gets clever. The chapters after this one keep the shape and fix its costs, one at a time.

The idea

A game is full of things: a turret, drones, bullets. An ECS splits each thing into three parts:

  • An entity names the thing. It is just a number. It has no data and no behaviour of its own.
  • Components are the thing's data: a position, a velocity, health. Each component is plain data, a small struct or a number.
  • Systems are the behaviour: loops that run over every entity that has the components they need. Movement runs over everything with a position and a velocity.

A turret is entity 0 with a position and health. A drone is entity 1 with a position, a velocity and health. Nothing says "turret" or "drone" anywhere; what a thing is comes from which components it has.

Step 1: the entity

kayan_entity: struct = {
    index: u32;
}

An entity is a number, so why the struct? Because a bare u32 can be mixed up with any other u32. A proc that takes a kayan_entity cannot be handed a count or a row index by mistake, and the struct costs nothing at run time: it compiles to the same 4 bytes. It also gives the number room to grow, and in 1.3 it does.

Step 2: the world

Where do components live? The simplest answer: one array per component, with one slot for every possible entity, indexed by the entity's number. Beside each array, a flag per entity saying whether it has that component.

kayan_world: struct = {
    count: u32;
    positions: [8]vec2;
    has_position: [8]b32;
    velocities: [8]vec2;
    has_velocity: [8]b32;
    healths: [8]f32;
    has_health: [8]b32;
}

Look at the shape. This is lesson 1's struct of arrays: every position together, every velocity together. An entity's data is spread across the arrays, all at the same index. Entity 1's position is positions[1] and its health is healths[1].

Step 3: spawning

A new entity is the next number:

kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> kayan_entity = {
    if (w*.count == 8) {
        printfmt("the world is full\n");
        exit(1);
    }
    e: kayan_entity = { .index = w*.count };
    w*.count += 1;
    return e;
}

It has no components yet: every flag for its number is still false.

Step 4: giving it components

Giving an entity a component is writing the value at its number and raising the flag:

set_position: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, p: vec2) -> void = {
    w*.positions[e.index] = p;
    w*.has_position[e.index] = true;
}

set_velocity and set_health are the same, one per component. Writing one proc per component type is tedious, and Part 2 replaces all of them with a single generic kayan_set<T>. For now, plain is better: you can see exactly which bytes get written.

Building a drone is spawning a number and attaching data to it:

    drone_a: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w&);
    set_position(w&, drone_a, { .x = 10.0, .y = 0.0 });
    set_velocity(w&, drone_a, { .x = -1.0, .y = 0.5 });
    set_health(w&, drone_a, 100.0);

Step 5: a system

A system is a loop. Movement runs over everything with a position and a velocity:

movement_system: proc(w: *kayan_world, dt: f32) -> u32 = {
    moved: u32 = 0;
    for (i: u32 = 0; i < w*.count; i += 1) {
        if (w*.has_position[i] && w*.has_velocity[i]) {
            w*.positions[i].x += w*.velocities[i].x * dt;
            w*.positions[i].y += w*.velocities[i].y * dt;
            moved += 1;
        }
    }
    return moved;
}

It doesn't know about turrets, drones or bullets. It knows about positions and velocities, and anything that has both moves, including bullets that didn't exist when the system was written. That's the ECS idea in one proc: behaviour attaches to data, not to types of thing.

Run it

spawned turret 0, drones 1 and 2, bullet 3
    entity 0  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1  position (10.00,  0.00)  velocity (-1.00,  0.50)  health 100
    entity 2  position ( 0.00, 10.00)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100
    entity 3  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity ( 4.00,  4.00)  health -
step 1: the movement system looked at 4 entities and moved 3
step 2: the movement system looked at 4 entities and moved 3
...
every component array has room for 8; 4 entities exist
    positions hold 4 values, velocities 3, healths 3

The turret has no velocity, so movement skips it. The bullet has no health, and nothing cares.

What this costs

It works, and every later chapter keeps this shape: entities are numbers, components are arrays of plain data, systems are loops. But look at the last two lines of the output and at the loop:

  1. Every array is as long as the most entities the world can hold. Velocity has room for 8 and holds 3. A game with 10,000 entities and 50 component types would have 50 arrays of 10,000, mostly empty.
  2. Every system visits every entity and checks flags to skip the ones that don't apply. Movement looked at 4 and moved 3. With 10,000 entities of which 50 move, it would look at 10,000 to move 50.
  3. Nothing can be destroyed. There's no despawn, and numbers only go up.

The next chapter fixes 3. Chapter 1.4 packs the data so systems stop skipping, and Part 2 fixes 1 and 2 for good with tables.

Try

  1. Give the turret a velocity and run it. Nothing else changes: the turret moves because it now has the data movement wants.
  2. Add a lifetime: [8]f32 component with its flags, and an aging_system that counts it down. How many places did you have to touch?
  3. Spawn a ninth entity. Read the error, then think about what a game would need instead of a fixed 8.

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.2

Despawning, and reusing numbers

ecs/src/1.entities/1.2.despawn/despawn.rin

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, on its own, to watch and to practise.

Games destroy things constantly: a bullet hits, a drone dies, an effect fades. 1.1 could only add. This chapter adds kayan_despawn, and with it the first real problem in ECS design: what happens to an entity's number when the entity is gone?

Step 1: a free list

If despawned numbers were never reused, a game firing one bullet a frame would use up 8 numbers in 8 frames and 4 billion in a couple of years of play. More to the point, every array would keep growing. So despawned numbers go on a free list, and spawning takes from it first:

kayan_world: struct = {
    count: u32;
    alive: [8]b32;
    free: [8]u32;
    free_count: u32;

count is now how many numbers have ever been handed out, not how many entities exist; the numbers on the free list are the gaps. alive says which numbers are in use.

Step 2: spawning reuses

kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> kayan_entity = {
    e: kayan_entity = {};
    if (w*.free_count > 0) {
        w*.free_count -= 1;
        e.index = w*.free[w*.free_count];
    } else {
        if (w*.count == 8) {
            printfmt("the world is full\n");
            exit(1);
        }
        e.index = w*.count;
        w*.count += 1;
    }
    w*.alive[e.index] = true;
    return e;
}

The free list is a stack: the last number freed is the first reused.

Step 3: despawning

kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {
    w*.alive[e.index] = false;
    w*.has_position[e.index] = false;
    w*.has_velocity[e.index] = false;
    w*.has_health[e.index] = false;
    w*.free[w*.free_count] = e.index;
    w*.free_count += 1;
}

Despawning lowers every flag, so the entity's old components can't leak into whatever reuses the number. The values stay in the arrays, but with the flags down nobody reads them. Systems need no change: a despawned entity has no flags, so movement skips it without knowing anything about despawning.

Step 4: the bug

Now the problem. Things in a game refer to other things: a turret aims at a drone, a missile chases a target, a health bar follows a unit. With entities as numbers, a reference is a number:

    target: kayan_entity = drone_a;

The program then destroys the drone, and the turret fires. The bullet is a new entity, and it takes the first free number, the drone's:

the turret targets entity 1, a drone
...
entity 1 is destroyed and despawned
    entity 1  (free)
the turret fires: the bullet is entity 1
...
the turret aims at entity 1, at (2.00, 2.00), moving (4.00, 4.00)
    that is the turret's own bullet, not the drone: the number was reused

Nothing told the turret its target died, and nothing could: references can be anywhere, in any number of places. The number in target is still a valid number, it just names a different entity now. No crash, no error, just a turret shooting at its own bullet. In a real game this is the bug where a homing missile turns around mid-flight, or a health bar jumps to another unit.

Run it

the turret targets entity 1, a drone
    entity 0  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1  position (10.00,  0.00)  velocity (-1.00,  0.50)  health 100
    entity 2  position ( 0.00, 10.00)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100
entity 1 is destroyed and despawned
    entity 0  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1  (free)
    entity 2  position ( 0.00, 10.00)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100
the turret fires: the bullet is entity 1
...

Why not just...

  • ...never reuse numbers? The arrays would grow forever, and every system would walk an ever-longer list of dead numbers.
  • ...find and clear every reference on despawn? You'd need to know where every reference lives. That's exactly what an ECS is trying to avoid: things refer to each other loosely, by number.
  • **...check alive[target.index]?** It says true: the number is alive. It's alive as a different entity, and nothing can tell the two apart.

The next chapter tells them apart with one extra number per entity.

Try

  1. Despawn the bullet too, then spawn two more entities. Which numbers do they get, and in what order? Why?
  2. Comment out the lines that lower the flags in kayan_despawn and run it. What does the new bullet have that it shouldn't?
  3. Despawn drone_a twice. What does the free list look like after? Spawn twice more and see why that is a problem.

Here an entity can be despawned, and its number goes on a free5// list, so the next spawn takes it instead of growing the world. Without that,6// a game that fires a bullet a frame would run out of numbers in seconds.7//8// Reuse has a cost, and this program walks straight into it. Something that9// kept an entity's number, the turret's target, still holds it after the10// entity is gone. When the number is handed to a new entity, the old11// reference silently names the new one. 1.3 fixes that.12 13import "std/print.rin"14 15vec2: struct = {16    x: f32;17    y: f32;18}19 20kayan_entity: struct = {21    index: u32;22}23 24// `alive` says which numbers are in use. `free` holds the numbers of despawned25// entities, `free_count` of them, ready to be handed out again.26kayan_world: struct = {27    count: u32;28    alive: [8]b32;29    free: [8]u32;30    free_count: u32;31    positions: [8]vec2;32    has_position: [8]b32;33    velocities: [8]vec2;34    has_velocity: [8]b32;35    healths: [8]f32;36    has_health: [8]b32;37}38 39// A free number is reused before a new one is made. A reused number must start40// with no components: whatever the last entity at this number had was cleared41// when it was despawned.42kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> kayan_entity = {43    e: kayan_entity = {};44    if (w*.free_count > 0) {45        w*.free_count -= 1;46        e.index = w*.free[w*.free_count];47    } else {48        if (w*.count == 8) {49            printfmt("the world is full\n");50            exit(1);51        }52        e.index = w*.count;53        w*.count += 1;54    }55    w*.alive[e.index] = true;56    return e;57}58 59// The entity's components are dropped by lowering their flags, and its number60// goes on the free list. Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.3

Generations

ecs/src/1.entities/1.3.generations/generations.rin

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, on its own, to watch and to practise.

1.2 ended with a turret aiming at its own bullet. The number it remembered was reused, and nothing could tell the old entity from the new one. The fix is small and used by nearly every ECS: count each number's lives.

The idea

Give each number a generation. Entity 1 in its first life is 1:1. When it's despawned, number 1's generation goes up to 2, so the next entity to reuse it is 1:2. A reference carries both numbers:

kayan_entity: struct = {
    index: u32;
    generation: u32;
}

A reference with a generation is called a handle. The turret's target is the handle 1:1. After the drone dies and the bullet becomes 1:2, the target still says 1:1, and 1:1 != 1:2. One comparison catches the bug.

Step 1: the world keeps generations

kayan_world: struct = {
    count: u32;
    generations: [8]u32;
    free: [8]u32;
    free_count: u32;

generations[i] is the life number i is in now, or the life it'll be in next if i is free. 1.2's alive array is gone, because the generations already say it:

kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {
    return e.index < w*.count && w*.generations[e.index] == e.generation;
}

A handle is alive when its generation is the one its number is in now.

Step 2: despawn bumps the generation

kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    w*.has_position[e.index] = false;
    w*.has_velocity[e.index] = false;
    w*.has_health[e.index] = false;
    w*.generations[e.index] += 1;
    w*.free[w*.free_count] = e.index;
    w*.free_count += 1;
    return kayan_status.ok;
}

The generation goes up at despawn, not at the next spawn. So a free number already holds a generation that no handle has been given yet, and no handle can match it. That's why there's no separate alive flag: "free" and "every existing handle is stale" are the same fact.

Despawning a dead handle now returns dead and changes nothing. In 1.2, despawning twice put the same number on the free list twice, and two later entities would have shared it.

Step 3: a status you can't ignore

kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {
    ok,
    dead,
}

enum[must_use] makes ignoring the result a compile error. When you mean to ignore it, you say so with _ = kayan_despawn(...). The program does that where it knows the handle is alive.

Step 4: generations start at 1

        e.index = w*.count;
        w*.count += 1;
        w*.generations[e.index] = 1;

A brand-new number starts at generation 1, never 0. So the zeroed handle, 0:0, can never be alive, and {} is a free "no entity" value. A turret with nothing to aim at holds {}, and checking it needs no special case.

Step 5: every access checks

get_position: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *vec2 = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || !w*.has_position[e.index]) {
        return null;
    }
    return w*.positions[e.index]&;
}

Reading through a handle checks it first. A dead handle gives null instead of whatever data now sits at the number. The turret checks its target every time it aims, and picks a new one when the old one is gone.

Run it

the turret aims at 1:1, at (10.00, 0.00)
drone 1:1 is destroyed and despawned
the turret fires: the bullet is 1:2, the same number in its next life
    entity 0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  velocity -                health 500
    entity 1:2  position ( 2.00,  2.00)  velocity ( 4.00,  4.00)  health -
    entity 2:1  position ( 0.25,  9.50)  velocity ( 0.50, -1.00)  health 100
the turret's target 1:1 is dead; it picks 2:1 instead
the turret aims at 2:1, at (0.25, 9.50)
despawning 1:1 again: dead
the zeroed handle 0:0 is alive: no

The same moment that ended 1.2, and this time the handle knows.

Notes

  • Cost: a handle is 8 bytes instead of 4, and checking one is one load and one compare. Cheap enough to do on every access.
  • Wrapping: a u32 generation wraps after 4 billion reuses of the same number. A stale handle would have to survive that long to be fooled. Some ECSs use fewer bits for the generation, packing index and generation into one u32 or u64. The idea is the same.
  • What it doesn't fix: the arrays are still as long as the most entities, and systems still skip holes. That's next.

Try

  1. Keep a copy of the bullet's handle, despawn the bullet, spawn something new, and check the old handle with kayan_alive.
  2. Remove _ = from one of the kayan_despawn calls and compile. Read the error.
  3. Make kayan_alive compare only the index. Which line of the output goes wrong first?

Build an ECS · part 1, entities · 1.4

The entity index

ecs/src/1.entities/1.4.entity_index/entity_index.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 3. the slot map, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Handles fixed identity. Two costs from 1.1 remain: every array is as long as the most entities, and every system walks all of it, skipping holes. This chapter packs the data: live entities in rows 0 to count - 1, no holes, so a system is a straight loop over the rows. That's the stream lesson 1 measured as the fast case.

Packing has a consequence that the rest of the course is built around: an entity's data no longer sits at its number, and it moves.

To keep this chapter about the index, every entity is the same kind of thing: a particle with a position and a velocity. Part 2 brings back different kinds, each packed in a table of its own.

Step 1: two halves

kayan_slot: struct = {
    generation: u32;
    row: u32;
}
kayan_world: struct = {
    slot_count: u32;
    slots: [8]kayan_slot;
    free: [8]u32;
    free_count: u32;

    count: u32;
    entities: [8]kayan_entity;
    positions: [8]vec2;
    velocities: [8]vec2;
}

The world now has two halves:

  • The slots, indexed by the entity's number. A number never moves, so this is where a handle looks first. A slot holds the generation from 1.3, and now also the row the entity's data is in.
  • The rows, packed. count of them, each with its components side by side in the arrays, and entities[row] saying which entity owns the row.

The two point at each other: slot to row, row to entity. That two-way link is called the entity index.

Step 2: spawning appends a row

    row: u32 = w*.count;
    w*.count += 1;
    w*.entities[row] = e;
    w*.positions[row] = p;
    w*.velocities[row] = v;
    w*.slots[e.index].row = row;
    return e;

The number comes from the free list or the end, exactly as in 1.3. The data goes in the next row, which is always the end of the packed rows. The slot records where.

Step 3: despawning swap-removes

To keep the rows packed, a hole can't be left behind. The last row moves into it, called swap-remove:

kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    row: u32 = w*.slots[e.index].row;
    last: u32 = w*.count - 1;
    if (row != last) {
        moved: kayan_entity = w*.entities[last];
        w*.entities[row] = moved;
        w*.positions[row] = w*.positions[last];
        w*.velocities[row] = w*.velocities[last];
        w*.slots[moved.index].row = row;
    }
    w*.count -= 1;
    w*.slots[e.index].generation += 1;
    w*.free[w*.free_count] = e.index;
    w*.free_count += 1;
    return kayan_status.ok;
}

The line that matters is this one:

        w*.slots[moved.index].row = row;

The entity that owned the last row now lives somewhere else, and its slot must say so. entities[last] is how we know whose slot to fix: without that column, a moved row would be anonymous. Forget the line and that entity's handle still finds a row, just the wrong one, and nothing crashes.

Swap-remove costs one row copy, however many rows there are. Removing by shifting everything after the hole down would keep the order, but cost a copy of every later row. ECSs don't promise order, so they take the cheap one.

Step 4: reading through the index

get_position: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *vec2 = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return null;
    }
    return w*.positions[w*.slots[e.index].row]&;
}

Handle to slot to row. That's one extra lookup compared with 1.3, and it's the price of packing. Systems don't pay it, because they don't go through handles:

movement_system: proc(w: *kayan_world, dt: f32) -> void = {
    for (row: u32 = 0; row < w*.count; row += 1) {
        w*.positions[row].x += w*.velocities[row].x * dt;
        w*.positions[row].y += w*.velocities[row].y * dt;
    }
}

No flags, no holes, no handles. Every row is a live particle. This is the loop the rest of the course works to keep.

Step 5: checking the invariant

Rows move all the time, and one missed slot update corrupts the world silently. So the world can check itself:

kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> u32 = {
    problems: u32 = 0;
    for (row: u32 = 0; row < w*.count; row += 1) {
        e: kayan_entity = w*.entities[row];
        if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
            printfmt("kayan_verify: row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", row, e.index, e.generation);
            problems += 1;
        } else if (w*.slots[e.index].row != row) {
            printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in row {}, its slot says row {}\n",
                e.index, e.generation, row, w*.slots[e.index].row);
            problems += 1;
        }
    }
    live: u32 = w*.slot_count - w*.free_count;
    if (live != w*.count) {
        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows, {} live entities\n", w*.count, live);
        problems += 1;
    }
    return problems;
}

The invariant: every row belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that row, and there are as many rows as live entities. Every structural change in this course has to keep it true. When something goes wrong later, run kayan_verify first.

Run it

spawned 5 particles
    row 0  0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)
    row 1  1:1  position ( 1.00,  0.00)
    ...
    row 4  4:1  position ( 4.00,  0.00)
    slots:  0 -> row 0  1 -> row 1  2 -> row 2  3 -> row 3  4 -> row 4
despawn 1:1, in row 1: the last row moves into the hole
    row 0  0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)
    row 1  4:1  position ( 4.00,  0.00)
    row 2  2:1  position ( 2.00,  0.00)
    row 3  3:1  position ( 3.00,  0.00)
    slots:  0 -> row 0  1 free  2 -> row 2  3 -> row 3  4 -> row 1
despawn 4:1, which the last despawn moved: its handle still finds it
...
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Follow 4:1: it starts in row 4, moves to row 1 when 1:1 is removed, and its handle still finds it there because its slot was updated.

Part 1 in one picture

handle 4:1 ──> slots[4] { generation 1, row 1 } ──> rows[1] { owner 4:1, position, velocity }
  • Handles never change: they're what the rest of the game keeps.
  • Slots never move: one per number, holding the generation and the row.
  • Rows move all the time, and stay packed so systems can stream them.

Part 2 keeps exactly this, and generalizes the one kind of row into tables, one per combination of components.

Try

  1. Delete the line w*.slots[moved.index].row = row;, run it, and read what kayan_verify reports. Then look at what get_position returns for the moved entity.
  2. Despawn every particle, then spawn three. Which numbers and rows do they get?
  3. Add a kayan_get_velocity and use it to stop one particle by handle.
  4. Write a print_rows that prints rows in handle order instead of row order. What does it have to do?

Two things keep track:11//12//   * each row records which entity owns it, `entities[row]`;13//   * each number has a slot recording its generation and its current row.14//15// A handle finds its data through its slot. When a row moves, the moved16// entity's slot is updated. That one line is the invariant everything else in17// this course relies on, and `kayan_verify` checks it.18//19// To keep the chapter about the index, every entity here is the same kind of20// thing: a particle with a position and a velocity. Part 2 brings back21// different kinds, each packed in a table of its own.22 23import "std/print.rin"24 25vec2: struct = {26    x: f32;27    y: f32;28}29 30kayan_entity: struct = {31    index: u32;32    generation: u32;33}34 35kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {36    ok,37    dead,38}39 40// Where a number's entity is: its generation, and the row its data is in.41kayan_slot: struct = {42    generation: u32;43    row: u32;44}45 46// Two halves. The slots, indexed by the entity's number, which never moves. The47// rows, packed, indexed by row, which moves: `count` of them, each with its48// owner and its components side by side.49kayan_world: struct = {50    slot_count: u32;51    slots: [8]kayan_slot;52    free: [8]u32;53    free_count: u32;54 55    count: u32;56    entities: [8]kayan_entity;57    positions: [8]vec2;58    velocities: [8]vec2;59}60 61kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {62    return e.index < w*.slot_count && w*.slots[e.index].generation == e.generation;63}64 65// A number, as in 1.3, and the next row at the end of the packed rows.66kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, p: vec2, v: vec2) -> kayan_entity = {67    e: kayan_entity = {};68    if (w*.free_count > 0) {69        w*.free_count -= 1;70        e.index = w*.free[w*.free_count];71    } else {72        if (w*.slot_count == 8) {73            printfmt("the world is full\n");74            exit(1);75        }76        e.index = w*.slot_count;77        w*.slot_count += 1;78        w*.slots[e.index].generation = 1;79    }80    e.generation = w*.slots[e.index].generation;81 82    row: u32 = w*.count;83    w*.count += 1;84    w*.entities[row] = e;85    w*.positions[row] = p;86    w*.velocities[row] = v;87    w*.slots[e.index].row = row;88    return e;89}90 91// Swap-remove: the last row moves into the hole, so the rows stay packed. The92// entity that owned the last row now lives at `row`, and its slot must say so.93kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {94    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {95        return kayan_status.dead;96    }97    row: u32 = w*.slots[e.index].row;98    last: u32 = w*.count - 1;99    if (row != last) {100        moved: kayan_entity = w*.entities[last];101        w*.entities[row] = moved;102        w*.positions[row] = w*.positions[last];103        w*.velocities[row] = w*.velocities[last];104        w*.slots[moved.index].row = row;105    }106    w*.count -= 1;107    w*.slots[e.index].generation += 1;108    w*.free[w*.free_count] = e.index;109    w*.free_count += 1;110    return kayan_status.ok;111}112 113// Handle, then slot, then row: the data is wherever the row is now.114get_position: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *vec2 = {115    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {116        return null;117    }118    return w*.positions[w*.slots[e.index].row]&;119}120 121// No flags and no holes: every row is a live particle. Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.1

Components and signatures

ecs/src/2.components/2.1.components/components.rin

In the dojo: 6. bitsets, on its own, to watch and to practise.

Part 1 hard-coded its components: a positions array, a velocities array, a flag for each. Adding a component meant editing the world, kayan_spawn, kayan_despawn and every printer. Part 2 builds a world that works for components it has never heard of. This chapter lays the ground with four ideas:

  1. A component is a plain struct.
  2. Each component type has an id, a small number fixed at compile time.
  3. The world keeps a registry: per id, the component's size, alignment and name, which is all it needs to store bytes it doesn't understand.
  4. A set of components is a signature: one bit per id in a u64.

There are no entities in this chapter. 2.3 puts the two halves together.

Step 1: components are plain structs

position: struct = { at: vec2; }
velocity: struct = { per_second: vec2; }
health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; }
damage: struct = { amount: f32; }
lifetime: struct = { seconds: f32; }
burning: struct = { per_second: f32; }
turret: struct = { cooldown: f32; timer: f32; }

No procs, no pointers to other entities, no idea that a world exists. That's deliberate. Behaviour belongs to systems, and data that knows nothing can be copied, moved and stored as raw bytes, which the world is about to do.

Why position { at: vec2 } rather than using vec2 directly? Because a component's type is how the world tells components apart. Position and velocity are both two floats, but they're different things, and making them different types is what lets you ask for one and not the other.

Step 2: an id per component type

component: enum = {
    position,
    velocity,
    health,
    damage,
    lifetime,
    burning,
    turret,
}

The enum gives each component a number. Then one line per type connects the type to its number:

component_of: proc<position>() -> component = { return component.position; }
component_of: proc<velocity>() -> component = { return component.velocity; }

Each line is a specialization of the generic proc component_of<T> for one type. component_of<health>() is resolved by the compiler to component.health. Nothing is looked up at run time; the id is a constant in the generated code.

Step 3: the world speaks ids, never types

The world can't be generic over component types. Which combinations exist is only known while the game runs (the "untyped core" from our earlier discussion). So the world works in ids and bits, and a small typed layer translates:

kayan_bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {
    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);
}

// The typed layer: from a type to the id and bit the world works in.
kayan_id_of: proc<T>() -> u32 = {
    return cast(component_of<T>(), u32);
}

kayan_mask_of: proc<T>() -> u64 = {
    return kayan_bit(kayan_id_of<T>());
}

Game code says kayan_mask_of<velocity>(), and the world only ever sees 2, a bit.

Step 4: the registry

To store a component as bytes, the world needs three facts about it: how many bytes, what alignment, and a name for printing. rin's compiler already wrote all three down. position<> is the reflect record for position, data the compiler puts into the program. So the registry is an array of pointers to reflect records, indexed by id:

kayan_world: struct = {
    infos: [64]*const reflect;
    component_count: u32;
}
kayan_register: proc(w: *kayan_world, id: u32, info: *const reflect) -> void = {
    if (id >= 64) {
        printfmt("kayan: component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold\n", id);
        exit(1);
    }
    w*.infos[id] = info;
    if (id + 1 > w*.component_count) {
        w*.component_count = id + 1;
    }
}
register_components: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {
    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);
    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);

Each line names the type twice, once for the id and once for the record. A generic kayan_register_type<T> that took T<>& would be nicer, but rin doesn't yet allow T<> on a generic parameter, so registration names each type.

Step 5: signatures

A set of components is a u64 with a bit set per component in the set. What a thing is is a signature:

    drone: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>();

Every question you'd ask about sets is a bit operation:

kayan_contains: proc(signature: u64, wanted: u64) -> b32 = {
    return (signature & wanted) == wanted;
}

"Does this drone have what movement wants?" is kayan_contains(drone, moves), one AND and one compare. Adding a component is |, and removing one is & ~:

    put_out: u64 = burning_drone & ~kayan_mask_of<burning>();

64 bits means at most 64 component types per world, which is plenty for learning and for most games. Larger ECSs use wider bitsets or sorted id lists; the idea is the same.

Run it

the registry: 7 components
    id  name       size  align
     0  position      8      4
     1  velocity      8      4
     2  health        8      4
     3  damage        4      4
     4  lifetime      4      4
     5  burning       4      4
     6  turret        8      4
signatures, one bit per component, highest id first:
    drone          0000111  {position velocity health}
    bullet         0011011  {position velocity damage lifetime}
    turret         1000001  {position turret}
    burning drone  0100111  {position velocity health burning}
movement wants {position velocity}:
    drone yes, bullet yes, turret no, burning drone yes
a burning drone with burning removed is a drone again: yes

Read the bits as a table: each column is a component, each row a kind of thing. That table is the next three chapters. Each distinct row will become a table of its own.

Try

  1. Add a shield: struct = { points: f32; } component. What do you have to touch? (Three lines.) Print a "shielded drone" signature.
  2. Print kayan_contains(moves, drone) (arguments swapped). Why is the answer different?
  3. Reorder the component enum. Which outputs change, and which don't?

"1" : "0");116    }117}118 119// Does a set contain every component of another? One AND and one compare.120kayan_contains: proc(signature: u64, wanted: u64) -> b32 = {121    return (signature & wanted) == wanted;122}123 124// `position<>` is the compiler's reflect record for position: its name, size125// and alignment, written into the program as data. Registering hands the world126// that record under position's id.127register_components: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {128    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);129    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);130    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<health>(), health<>&);131    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<damage>(), damage<>&);132    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<lifetime>(), lifetime<>&);133    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<burning>(), burning<>&);134    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<turret>(), turret<>&);135}136 137main: proc() -> i32 = {138    w: kayan_world = {};139    register_components(w&);140 141    printfmt("the registry: {} components\n", w.component_count);142    printfmt("    id  name       size  align\n");143    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w.component_count; id += 1) {144        info: *const reflect = w.infos[id];145        printf("    %2u  %-9s  %4u  %5u\n", id, info*.name, cast(info*.size, u32), cast(info*.align, u32));146    }147 148    // What a thing is, written as the set of its components.149    drone: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>();150    bullet: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<damage>()151        | kayan_mask_of<lifetime>();152    gun: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<turret>();153    burning_drone: u64 = drone | kayan_mask_of<burning>();154 155    printfmt("signatures, one bit per component, highest id first:\n");156    printf("    drone          "); Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.2

Columns

ecs/src/2.components/2.2.columns/columns.rin

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, 8. index, not pointer, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

1.4 kept components in typed arrays: positions: [8]vec2. A world that works for any component can't, because it doesn't know the types. It knows, from the registry, each component's size and alignment, and that's enough.

A column is one component's array, kept as bytes. Row r is the size bytes starting at r * size. Everything a table does with its data is a byte operation on columns: grow, copy one row over another, zero a new row. None of it depends on the type. The type comes back only at the edge, where game code reads a column as []T.

This chapter builds the column and exercises it by hand. 2.3 puts columns in a table.

Step 1: what a column is

kayan_column: struct = {
    data: ^u8;
    size: u64;
    align: u64;
}

Bytes, plus how many bytes make a row, plus the alignment to allocate with. No count and no capacity: every column of a table has the same number of rows, so the table keeps those once (2.3).

A column for a component is made from its reflect record:

kayan_column_init: proc(info: *const reflect) -> kayan_column = {
    c: kayan_column = {};
    c.size = info*.size;
    c.align = info*.align;
    return c;
}

Step 2: rows are byte offsets

kayan_column_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> *u8 = {
    return c*.data[row * c*.size]&;
}

That's the whole addressing scheme: row * size. With it, copying and zeroing rows is memcpy and memset:

kayan_column_copy_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, to: u64, from: u64) -> void = {
    memcpy(kayan_column_row(c, to), kayan_column_row(c, from), c*.size);
}

kayan_column_zero_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> void = {
    memset(kayan_column_row(c, row), 0, c*.size);
}

kayan_column_copy_row is swap-remove's copy from 1.4, for any component.

Step 3: growing

kayan_column_grow: proc(arena: *memops_arena, c: *kayan_column, count: u64, capacity: u64) -> void = {
    data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(arena, c*.size * capacity, c*.align), ^u8);
    if (count > 0) {
        memcpy(data, c*.data, c*.size * count);
    }
    c*.data = data;
}

A new block for capacity rows, with the rows in use copied over. The old block stays in the arena, unused: an arena frees everything at once, never one allocation. Doubling the capacity each time keeps the waste to at most the size of what's in use, and the copies to a few per table over a whole game.

This is also why pointers into a column go stale: after a grow, the data is somewhere else. 2.5 shows it happening.

Step 4: the typed view

kayan_column_slice: proc<T>(c: *kayan_column, count: u64) -> []T = {
    if (c*.size != sizeof(T)) {
        printfmt("kayan: a column of {}-byte rows read as a {}-byte type\n", c*.size, sizeof(T));
        exit(1);
    }
    raw: ^T = cast(c*.data, ^T);
    return raw[0..count];
}

This is the untyped/typed split in one proc. Below it, bytes. Above it, a []T that game code indexes like any slice, bounds checked in Debug. The size check catches the one mistake the byte level can't: reading a column as the wrong type.

Writing goes through the typed view too:

        ps: []position = kayan_column_slice<position>(positions&, count);
        hs: []health = kayan_column_slice<health>(healths&, count);
        ps[row] = { .at = { .x = cast(i, f32), .y = 1.0 } };
        hs[row] = { .points = 50.0 + 10.0 * cast(i, f32), .max = 100.0 };

(Writing kayan_column_slice<position>(...)[row] = ... in one line would be nicer. rin doesn't allow indexing a call's result directly yet, because the bounds check would evaluate the call twice. Hence the locals.)

Step 5: rows stay rows across columns

The program keeps two columns side by side, positions and healths, and moves them together:

    last: u64 = count - 1;
    kayan_column_copy_row(positions&, 1, last);
    kayan_column_copy_row(healths&, 1, last);
    count -= 1;

Same operation, each column using its own row size. Row 1 is still one entity's data across both columns. That's a table in all but name.

Run it

a position column has 8-byte rows, a health column 8-byte rows
    grew to room for 2 rows
    grew to room for 4 rows
    grew to room for 8 rows
five rows, written through the typed view:
    row 0  position ( 0.00,  1.00)  health  50 / 100
    row 1  position ( 1.00,  1.00)  health  60 / 100
...
row 1's health as the column stores it, bytes: 00 00 70 42 00 00 c8 42
    that is 60.0 and 100.0 as little-endian f32s; the column never knew
swap-removed row 1: row 4 moved into it, in both columns

The byte line is the point of the chapter. 00 00 70 42 is 60.0 as an f32, and the column stored it without knowing it was a float, or a health, or anything at all.

Try

  1. Read the health column as []damage (4-byte rows) and run it. Read the message.
  2. Start the capacity at 1 instead of 2. How many grows does it take to fit 5 rows? What if it grew by 1 each time instead of doubling?
  3. Print the bytes of a position row. Which bytes are x and which are y?

It knows, from5// the registry, each component's size and alignment, and that is enough. A6// column is an array of a component kept as bytes: row `r` is the `size` bytes7// at `r * size`.8//9// Everything a table needs to do with its data is a byte operation on columns:10// grow, copy a row over another (swap-remove), zero a new row. None of it11// depends on the type. The type comes back at the edge, where game code reads12// the column as `[]T`, and that typed view checks the size matches.13//14// This chapter builds the column and exercises it on its own, with the count15// and capacity kept beside it by hand. 2.3 puts columns in a table.16 17import "std/print.rin"18import "std/memops.rin"19 20vec2: struct = {21    x: f32;22    y: f32;23}24 25position: struct = { at: vec2; }26health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; }27 28component: enum = {29    position,30    health,31}32 33component_of: proc<position>() -> component = { return component.position; }34component_of: proc<health>() -> component = { return component.health; }35 36// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------37// The column: bytes, and how many of them make one row38// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------39 40// A column does not know its count or capacity. The old block stays in the arena: an arena frees everything at once,64// never one allocation, and this course accepts the waste.65kayan_column_grow: proc(arena: *memops_arena, c: *kayan_column, count: u64, capacity: u64) -> void = {66    data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(arena, c*.size * capacity, c*.align), ^u8);67    if (count > 0) {68        memcpy(data, c*.data, c*.size * count);69    }70    c*.data = data;71}72 73kayan_column_copy_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, to: u64, from: u64) -> void = {74    memcpy(kayan_column_row(c, to), kayan_column_row(c, from), c*.size);75}76 77kayan_column_zero_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> void = {78    memset(kayan_column_row(c, row), 0, c*.size);79}80 81// The typed view: the column's first `count` rows as `[]T`. Reading a column82// as the wrong type would reinterpret its bytes, so the size is checked: the83// one mistake the byte level cannot catch is caught here, at the edge.84kayan_column_slice: proc<T>(c: *kayan_column, count: u64) -> []T = {85    if (c*.size != sizeof(T)) {86        printfmt("kayan: a column of {}-byte rows read as a {}-byte type\n", c*.size, sizeof(T));87        exit(1);88    }89    raw: ^T = cast(c*.data, ^T);90    return raw[0..count];91}92 93// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------94// Using it95// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------96 97print_bytes: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> void = {98    bytes: *u8 = kayan_column_row(c, row);99    raw: ^u8 = cast(bytes, ^u8);100    for (i: u64 = 0; Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.3

A table

ecs/src/2.components/2.3.tables/tables.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 4. a type-erased column, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The two halves meet. Part 1 built the entity index: handles, slots, packed rows, swap-remove. 2.1 and 2.2 built the component side: ids, a registry, columns of bytes. A table is 1.4's packed rows with the typed arrays replaced by columns, one per component in its signature:

table {position velocity health}
  entities  [ 0:1 | 3:1 | 2:1 | ... ]     who owns each row
  columns   position [ ... ]  velocity [ ... ]  health [ ... ]
  count, capacity                         shared by every column

Row r is entity entities[r], and its components are row r of every column. This world still has a single table, so every entity has the same components; 2.4 gives each combination its own.

Step 1: the table

kayan_table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    entities: ^kayan_entity;
    columns: [64]kayan_column;
}
  • signature says which components the table has.
  • columns[id] is in use when the signature has bit id. The rest stay zeroed. 64 slots indexed by id means finding a column is an index, never a search. kayan in C looked columns up by name in a hash map, which is the thing this replaces.
  • count and capacity belong to the table, shared by every column and by entities, so they can't disagree.

A table is made from a signature and the registry:

kayan_table_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_table = {
    t: kayan_table = {};
    t.signature = signature;
    for (id: u32 = 0; id < 64; id += 1) {
        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {
            if (id >= w*.component_count || w*.infos[id] == null) {
                printfmt("kayan: signature {} uses component {}, which was never registered\n", signature, id);
                exit(1);
            }
            t.columns[id] = kayan_column_init(w*.infos[id]);
        }
    }
    return t;
}

The signature is the column list. In your C kayan, the signature and the columns were written separately and could disagree (archetype D had position columns its signature didn't mention). Here one is made from the other.

Step 2: rows, for every column at once

Adding a row grows every column together when the table is full, then zeroes the new row in each:

kayan_table_add_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {
    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {
        kayan_table_grow(w, t);
    }
    row: u64 = t*.count;
    t*.count += 1;
    t*.entities[row] = e;
    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {
        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {
            kayan_column_zero_row(t*.columns[id]&, row);
        }
    }
    return row;
}

Removing a row is 1.4's swap-remove, for every column:

kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, row: u64) -> void = {
    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;
    if (row != last) {
        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {
            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {
                kayan_column_copy_row(t*.columns[id]&, row, last);
            }
        }
        moved: kayan_entity = t*.entities[last];
        t*.entities[row] = moved;
        vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(moved.index, u64))*.row = cast(row, u32);
    }
    t*.count = last;
}

Compare it with 1.4's kayan_despawn: the same moves and the same slot fix, but over columns of bytes instead of named arrays. This proc works for any table that will ever exist.

Step 3: the typed view of a table

kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table) -> []T = {
    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();
    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {
        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);
        exit(1);
    }
    return kayan_column_slice<T>(t*.columns[id]&, t*.count);
}

kayan_slice<position>(t) is the table's position column as a []position, cut to the rows in use. Systems will live on this in Part 3: get the slices, loop over rows.

Step 4: the world

kayan_world: struct = {
    arena: *memops_arena;
    infos: [64]*const reflect;
    component_count: u32;
    slots: vec<kayan_slot>;
    free: vec<u32>;
    live: u64;
    table: kayan_table;
}

The registry from 2.1, the slots and free list from Part 1 (as vecs now, so the 8-entity limit is gone), and one table. Spawning is Part 1's spawn with the row coming from the table:

    e.generation = slot*.generation;
    slot*.row = cast(kayan_table_add_row(w, w*.table&, e), u32);
    w*.live += 1;
    return e;

and despawning is Part 1's despawn calling kayan_table_remove_row.

Step 5: writing a new entity's data

There's no typed get or set yet (that's 2.5), so the program finds the row and writes through the column slices:

        row: u64 = kayan_row(w&, drones[i]);
        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(w.table&);
        vs: []velocity = kayan_slice<velocity>(w.table&);
        hs: []health = kayan_slice<health>(w.table&);
        ps[row] = { .at = { .x = 10.0 * cast(i, f32), .y = 0.0 } };

Run it

spawned 6 drones into one table; it grew from 4 rows to 8
    6 rows, room for 8
    row 0  0:1  position ( 0.00,  0.00)  health 100
...
despawn 0:1 and 3:1
    4 rows, room for 8
    row 0  5:1  position (50.00,  0.00)  health 100
    row 1  1:1  position (10.00,  0.00)  health 100
    row 2  2:1  position (20.00,  0.00)  health 100
    row 3  4:1  position (40.00,  0.00)  health 100
spawn 3:2: a reused number, the next row, zeroed except what we set
...
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Row 0 went to 5:1 (the last row moved into the hole), then row 3 went to 4:1 the same way. Every column moved together, and the slots followed.

Try

  1. Remove velocity from the table's signature and run it. Which line fails, and why is failing there the right behaviour?
  2. Make kayan_table_grow start at 1 row. Count the grows for 6 drones.
  3. Delete the slot fix in kayan_table_remove_row and run kayan_verify.

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.4

Many tables: archetypes

ecs/src/2.components/2.4.archetypes/archetypes.rin

In the dojo: 3. the slot map, 8. index, not pointer, 9. interning, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

2.3's world had one table, so every entity had the same components. Real games mix: a turret has a position and a turret component, a drone has a position, velocity and health, a bullet has a position, velocity, damage and lifetime. Each combination gets a table of its own. Every row of a table has every component in its signature, so there are no holes and no flags. A table for one combination is called an archetype.

table 0 {position turret}                   0:1
table 1 {position velocity health}          1:1 2:1 3:1
table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime} 4:1 5:1

Nobody declares the archetypes. The first time something spawns with a new combination, the world makes its table and remembers it by signature, so the next spawn finds it.

Step 1: slots say which table

kayan_slot: struct = {
    generation: u32;
    table: u32;
    row: u32;
}

Handle to slot to (table, row). That's the whole entity index from here on.

Step 2: the world keeps every table

kayan_world: struct = {
    arena: *memops_arena;
    infos: [64]*const reflect;
    component_count: u32;
    tables: vec<kayan_table>;
    by_signature: hashmap<u64, u32>;
    slots: vec<kayan_slot>;
    free: vec<u32>;
    live: u64;
}

tables holds them all, and by_signature maps a signature to its table's index. Tables are referred to by index, never by pointer. Making a new table can grow the tables vec and move every table in memory, and an index survives that. A pointer is good until the next table is made:

kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world, index: u32) -> *kayan_table = {
    return vec<kayan_table>at(w*.tables&, cast(index, u64));
}

Step 3: where archetypes come from

kayan_table_for: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> u32 = {
    found: *u32 = hashmap<u64, u32>get(w*.by_signature&, signature);
    if (found != null) {
        return found*;
    }
    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables.length, u32);
    _ = vec<kayan_table>append(w*.arena, w*.tables&, kayan_table_init(w, signature));
    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>put(w*.arena, w*.by_signature&, signature, index);
    return index;
}

Found, or made. A game has tens of archetypes, maybe a few hundred, so a linear search would do too. The hashmap costs two lines with rin's std, and 2.6 makes the lookup rare anyway.

Step 4: spawning takes a signature

kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {

and puts the new entity in that signature's table:

    table_index: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, signature);
    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, table_index);
    slot*.table = table_index;
    slot*.row = cast(kayan_table_add_row(w, t, e), u32);

Note the order: the table's pointer is taken after kayan_table_for, because finding the table can make one and move the rest. Getting this order wrong is the classic archetype-ECS bug. It works until the first new archetype appears mid-game.

Despawning finds the table through the slot:

    kayan_table_remove_row(w, kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table), cast(slot*.row, u64));

Step 5: the invariant, over every table

kayan_verify now walks every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to the live count. Same invariant, one more field.

Step 6: one column, many tables

The end of the program reads every position in the world:

    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {
        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w&, ti);
        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);

The position column of each table, in turn. Positions are no longer one array; they're one array per archetype that has them. This is exactly what a query does in Part 3: visit the tables that have the right components, and stream their columns.

Run it

spawned the turret: the world made table 0 for it
spawned 3 drones: the first made a table, the others found it
spawned 2 bullets
6 entities in 3 tables:

    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1
despawn drone 1:1: a swap-remove inside its own table
    table 0 {position turret}: 0:1
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 3:1 2:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1
every position, table by table:
...
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Try

  1. Spawn a "drone with damage" (position, velocity, health, damage). How many tables now?
  2. Spawn 100 entities with 100 different signatures (use the bits of a counter). What does that do to a system that visits tables? This is called archetype fragmentation.
  3. Take the table pointer before kayan_table_for in kayan_spawn, then spawn something with a new signature and print the tables. Where did the row go? Nothing crashes, and the sanitizers stay quiet too: the old tables are still valid arena memory, which is what makes this bug so quiet.

id < 64; id += 1) {182        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {183            if (id >= w*.component_count || w*.infos[id] == null) {184                printfmt("kayan: signature {} uses component {}, which was never registered\n", signature, id);185                exit(1);186            }187            t.columns[id] = kayan_column_init(w*.infos[id]);188        }189    }190    return t;191}192 193// Double the room in `entities` and in every column at once.194kayan_table_grow: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table) -> void = {195    capacity: u64 = t*.capacity == 0 ? 4 : t*.capacity * 2;196    entities: ^kayan_entity = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(w*.arena,197        sizeof(kayan_entity) * capacity, alignof(kayan_entity)), ^kayan_entity);198    if (t*.count > 0) {199        memcpy(entities, t*.entities, sizeof(kayan_entity) * t*.count);200    }201    t*.entities = entities;202    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {203        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {204            kayan_column_grow(w*.arena, t*.columns[id]&, t*.count, capacity);205        }206    }207    t*.capacity = capacity;208}209 210// A new row at the end, owned by `e`, with every component zeroed.211kayan_table_add_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {212    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {213        kayan_table_grow(w, t);214    }215    row: u64 = t*.count;216    t*.count += 1;217    t*.entities[row] = e;218    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {219        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {220            kayan_column_zero_row(t*.columns[id]&, row);221        }222    }223    return row;224}225 226// 1.4's swap-remove, for every column: the last row is copied over `row`, and227// the slot of the entity that owned the last row is told where it went.228kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, row: u64) -> void = {229    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;230    if (row != last) {231        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {232            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {233                kayan_column_copy_row(t*.columns[id]&, row, last);234            }235        }236        moved: kayan_entity = t*.entities[last];237        t*.entities[row] = moved;238        vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(moved.index, u64))*.row = cast(row, u32);239    }240    t*.count = last;241}242 243// The typed view of one of the table's columns: T's rows, all of them in use.244// Asking for a component the table does not have is a bug, so it stops.245kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table) -> []T = {246    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();247    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {248        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);249        exit(1);250    }251    return kayan_column_slice<T>(t*.columns[id]&, t*.count);252}253 254// A pointer to a table is good until the next table is made.255kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world, index: u32) -> *kayan_table = {256    return vec<kayan_table>at(w*.tables&, cast(index, u64));257}258 259// The table for a signature: found if it exists, made if it does not. This is260// where archetypes come from.261kayan_table_for: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> u32 = {262    found: *u32 = hashmap<u64, u32>get(w*.by_signature&, signature);263    if (found != null) {264        return found*;265    }266    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables.length, u32);267    _ = vec<kayan_table>append(w*.arena, w*.tables&, kayan_table_init(w, signature));268    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>put(w*.arena, w*.by_signature&, signature, index);269    return index;270}271 272// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------273// The world274// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------275 276kayan_world_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, arena: *memops_arena) -> void = {277    w* = {};278    w*.arena = arena;279}280 281kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {282    if (cast(e.index, u64) >= w*.slots.length) {283        return false;284    }285    return vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation == e.generation;286}287 288// A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the table289// for that signature.290kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {291    e: kayan_entity = {};292    if (!vec<u32>is_empty(w*.free&)) {293        e.index = vec<u32>pop(w*.free&);294    } else {295        e.index = cast(w*.slots.length, u32);296        _ = vec<kayan_slot>append(w*.arena, w*.slots&, { .generation = 1 });297    }298    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));299    e.generation = slot*.generation;300    // kayan_table_for can make a table and move the others, so the table's301    // pointer is taken after it.302    table_index: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, signature);303    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, table_index);304    slot*.table = table_index;305    slot*.row = cast(kayan_table_add_row(w, t, e), u32);306    w*.live += 1;307    return e;308}309 310kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {311    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {312        return kayan_status.dead;313    }314    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));315    kayan_table_remove_row(w, kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table), cast(slot*.row, u64));316    slot*.generation += 1;317    _ = vec<u32>append(w*.arena, w*.free&, e.index);318    w*.live -= 1;319    return kayan_status.ok;320}321 322// The table and row a live entity is in. Typed get and set arrive in 2.5;323// until then, game code finds the table and row and indexes the columns.324kayan_table_of: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *kayan_table = {325    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table);326}327 328kayan_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {329    return cast(vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.row, u64);330}331 332// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose333// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to334// the live count.335kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> u64 = {336    problems: u64 = 0;337    rows: u64 = 0;338    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {339        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));340        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {341            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];342            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {343                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);344                problems += 1;345                continue;346            }347            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));348            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {349                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",350                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);351                problems += 1;352            }353        }354        rows += t*.count;355    }356    if (rows != w*.live) {357        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);358        problems += 1;359    }360    return problems;361}362 363kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {364    printf("{");365    first: b32 = true;366    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {367        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {368            printf(first ? "%s" : " %s", w*.infos[id]*.name);369            first = false;370        }371    }372    printf("}");373}374 375kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {376    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {377        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));378        printf("    table %u ", cast(ti, u32));379        kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);380        printf(":");381        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {382            printf(" %u:%u", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation);383        }384        printf("\n");385    }386}387 388// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------389// The program390// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------391 392// Until 2.5's typed get, writing a component is: find the entity's table and393// row, take the typed view of the column, write the row.394place: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, x: f32, y: f32) -> void = {395    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(kayan_table_of(w, e));396    ps[kayan_row(w, e)] = { .at = { .x = x, .y = y } };397}398 399main: proc() -> i32 = {400    arena: memops_arena = {};401    memops_arena_initialize(arena&);402    w: kayan_world = {};403    kayan_world_init(w&, arena&);404    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);405    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);406    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<health>(), health<>&);407    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<damage>(), damage<>&);408    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<lifetime>(), lifetime<>&);409    kayan_register(w&, kayan_id_of<turret>(), turret<>&);410 411    // What each kind of thing is, as a set of components.412    gun: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<turret>();413    drone: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>();414    bullet: u64 = kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<damage>()415        | kayan_mask_of<lifetime>();416 417    t0: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w&, gun);418    place(w&, t0, 0.0, 0.0);419    printfmt("spawned the turret: the world made table {} for it\n", w.tables.length - 1);420 421    drones: [3]kayan_entity = {};422    for (i: u32 = 0; i < 3; i += 1) {423        drones[i] = kayan_spawn(w&, drone);424        place(w&, drones[i], 10.0 * cast(i + 1, f32), 5.0);425    }426    printfmt("spawned 3 drones: the first made a table, the others found it\n");427 428    b0: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w&, bullet);429    b1: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w&, bullet);430    place(w&, b0, 0.0, 1.0);431    place(w&, b1, 1.0, 0.0);432    printfmt("spawned 2 bullets\n");433    printfmt("{} entities in {} tables:\n", w.live, w.tables.length);434    kayan_print_tables(w&);435 436    printfmt("despawn drone {}:{}: a swap-remove inside its own table\n", drones[0].index, drones[0].generation);437    _ = kayan_despawn(w&, drones[0]);438    kayan_print_tables(w&);439 440    // The positions of everything, table by table: the same column, in each441    // table that has it.442    printfmt("every position, table by table:\n");443    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {444        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w&, ti);445        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);446        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {447            printf("    table %u row %u  %u:%u at (%5.2f, %5.2f)\n", ti, cast(row, u32),448                t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation,449                cast(ps[row].at.x, f64), cast(ps[row].at.y, f64));450        }451    }452    printfmt("kayan_verify: {} problems\n", kayan_verify(w&));453    return 0;454}

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.5

Typed access

ecs/src/2.components/2.5.typed_access/typed_access.rin

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, 8. index, not pointer, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world stores any component in any combination, as bytes. Game code should never see the bytes. This chapter adds the typed layer on top:

kayan_get<position>(w, e)          -> *position, or null
kayan_has<velocity>(w, e)          -> b32
kayan_set<health>(w, e, value)     -> ok, dead, or missing

Each is a few lines that turn the type into an id, find the entity's table and row through its slot, and hand the row back as a T. The byte-level core underneath doesn't change at all. This is the split we talked about: C-style byte fiddling below, type-safe generic procs on top, each written once.

Step 1: get

kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *T = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return null;
    }
    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));
    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);
    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {
        return null;
    }
    rows: []T = kayan_slice<T>(t);
    return rows[cast(slot*.row, u64)]&;
}

Handle, slot, table, row, typed view. It's the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. Two ways to get null: the handle is dead, or the entity has no T. The caller checks once and then has a real pointer.

Step 2: has and set

kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {
    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;
}

kayan_has doesn't touch the row at all. An entity's components are its table's signature, one AND away.

kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    p: *T = kayan_get<T>(w, e);
    if (p == null) {
        return kayan_status.missing;
    }
    p* = value;
    return kayan_status.ok;
}

kayan_set writes a component the entity already has. Giving it a component it doesn't have changes which table it belongs in, and that's 2.6. So the status gains a third value:

kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {
    ok,
    dead,
    missing,
}

Step 3: building things

With kayan_set, game code builds entities with small procs. Engines call these prefabs or archetype constructors:

spawn_drone: proc(w: *kayan_world, x: f32, y: f32) -> kayan_entity = {
    e: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w, kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>());
    _ = kayan_set<position>(w, e, { .at = { .x = x, .y = y } });
    _ = kayan_set<velocity>(w, e, { .per_second = { .x = -1.0, .y = 0.0 } });
    _ = kayan_set<health>(w, e, { .points = 100.0, .max = 100.0 });
    return e;
}

The _ = says "I know this returns a status and I'm ignoring it on purpose". Here that's safe: the entity was just spawned with exactly these components.

Reading and changing is kayan_get:

    h: *health = kayan_get<health>(w&, a);
    h*.points -= 25.0;

Step 4: keep handles, borrow pointers

The pointer kayan_get returns points into a column. 2.2 showed what columns do when their table fills up: they move. So a pointer is good until the next structural change: a spawn, a despawn, or (from 2.6) an add or remove. The program proves it:

    kept: *health = kayan_get<health>(w&, a);
    for (i: u32 = 0; i < 8; i += 1) {
        _ = spawn_drone(w&, 40.0 + cast(i, f32), 0.0);
    }
    kept*.points = 1.0;
kept a pointer to 0:1's health, spawned 8 drones (the table grew), wrote 1 through it:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 75
    the write went to the column's old block; the handle still finds the real one

The health is still 75. The write landed in the column's old block, which the arena still owns, so nothing crashes and no sanitizer complains. It's just lost. Hence the rule every ECS has in some form:

Keep handles. Borrow pointers: get, use, forget.

Run it

two drones and a bullet, built with kayan_set:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 100
    1:1 at (30.00, -5.00), health 100
drone 0:1 is hit through kayan_get<health>:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 75
the bullet has a velocity: yes; a health: no
kayan_get<health> on the bullet is null: yes
kayan_set<health> on the bullet: missing
despawned 1:1; kayan_set<health> on it now: dead
    1:1 is not a live drone
...
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Try

  1. Write spawn_turret and spawn_bullet-style procs for your own kinds of thing.
  2. Move the kept pointer's kayan_get to after the spawning loop. Now the write sticks. Why?
  3. Make kayan_set add the component when it's missing, instead of returning missing. What would it need from 2.6?

Count and capacity are the table's, shared by its columns and by126// `entities`, so they can never disagree.127kayan_table: struct = {128    signature: u64;129    count: u64;130    capacity: u64;131    entities: ^kayan_entity;132    columns: [64]kayan_column;133}134 135// The world: the registry, the slots and free list, and every table, with a136// map from signature to table index so finding one is a lookup, not a search.137// Tables are referred to by index, never by pointer: making a table can grow138// `tables` and move all of them, and an index survives that.139kayan_world: struct = {140    arena: *memops_arena;141    infos: [64]*const reflect;142    component_count: u32;143    tables: vec<kayan_table>;144    by_signature: hashmap<u64, u32>;145    slots: vec<kayan_slot>;146    free: vec<u32>;147    live: u64;148}149 150kayan_bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {151    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);152}153 154kayan_id_of: proc<T>() -> u32 = {155    return cast(component_of<T>(), u32);156}157 158kayan_mask_of: proc<T>() -> u64 = {159    return kayan_bit(kayan_id_of<T>());160}161 162kayan_register: proc(w: *kayan_world, id: u32, info: *const reflect) -> void = {163    if (id >= 64) {164        printfmt("kayan: component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold\n", id);165        exit(1);166    }167    w*.infos[id] = info;168    if (id + 1 > w*.component_count) {169        w*.component_count = id + 1;170    }171}172 173kayan_table_has: proc(t: *kayan_table, id: u32) -> b32 = {174    return (t*.signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0;175}176 177// A table for a signature: one empty column per component in it, sized from178// the registry. Every component in the signature must be registered.179kayan_table_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_table = {180    t: kayan_table = {};181    t.signature = signature;182    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {220        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {221            kayan_column_zero_row(t*.columns[id]&, row);222        }223    }224    return row;225}226 227// 1.4's swap-remove, for every column: the last row is copied over `row`, and228// the slot of the entity that owned the last row is told where it went.229kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, row: u64) -> void = {230    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;231    if (row != last) {232        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {233            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {234                kayan_column_copy_row(t*.columns[id]&, row, last);235            }236        }237        moved: kayan_entity = t*.entities[last];238        t*.entities[row] = moved;239        vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(moved.index, u64))*.row = cast(row, u32);240    }241    t*.count = last;242}243 244// The typed view of one of the table's columns: T's rows, all of them in use.245// Asking for a component the table does not have is a bug, so it stops.246kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table) -> []T = {247    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();248    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {249        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);250        exit(1);251    }252    return kayan_column_slice<T>(t*.columns[id]&, t*.count);253}254 255// A pointer to a table is good until the next table is made.256kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world, index: u32) -> *kayan_table = {257    return vec<kayan_table>at(w*.tables&, cast(index, u64));258}259 260// The table for a signature: found if it exists, made if it does not. null) {265        return found*;266    }267    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables.length, u32);268    _ = vec<kayan_table>append(w*.arena, w*.tables&, kayan_table_init(w, signature));269    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>put(w*.arena, w*.by_signature&, signature, index);270    return index;271}272 273// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------274// The world275// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------276 277kayan_world_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, arena: *memops_arena) -> void = {278    w* = {};279    w*.arena = one.324kayan_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {325    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {326        return 0;327    }328    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, ---------------------------------------------------------------------------334 335// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. The pointer is337// good until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.338kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *T = {339    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {340        return null;341    }342    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));343    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);344    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {345        return null;346    }347    rows: []T = kayan_slice<T>(t);348    return rows[cast(slot*.row, u64)]&;349}350 351kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {352    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;353}354 355// Write e's T.
