Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.6

Adding and removing components

ecs/src/2.components/2.6.add_remove/add_remove.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 10. memoized edges, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

A drone catches fire: it gains a burning component. The fire goes out: it loses it. Changing what an entity is, while the game runs, is the thing your C kayan couldn't do, because its archetypes were structs fixed at compile time. In an archetype ECS a table holds exactly one combination, so a drone that gains a component no longer belongs in its table. It moves:

  1. find the table for its signature plus (or minus) the component;
  2. add a row there, and copy every component the two tables share;
  3. swap-remove its old row, fixing whoever moves into the hole;
  4. point its slot at the new table and row.

Its handle doesn't change. Everything else about it is where it was, one table over.

Step 1: the move

kayan_move: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {
    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));
    from_index: u32 = slot*.table;
    if (from_index == to_index) {
        return;
    }
    from: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);
    to: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);
    from_row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);
    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(w, to, e);
    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {
        if (kayan_table_has(from, id) && kayan_table_has(to, id)) {
            memcpy(kayan_column_row(to*.columns[id]&, to_row),
                kayan_column_row(from*.columns[id]&, from_row), from*.columns[id].size);
        }
    }
    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);
    slot*.table = to_index;
    slot*.row = cast(to_row, u32);
}

Every piece is something you've already built: kayan_table_add_row (2.3), a byte copy per shared column (2.2), kayan_table_remove_row with its slot fix (1.4). Components only the new table has start zeroed (add_row zeroes them). Components only the old table has disappear with the old row.

A move costs one row copy in and one row copy out. That's cheap, but not free, and it's why components that flip on and off every frame are sometimes better as a field (a bool on_fire inside health) than as a component.

Step 2: add and remove, typed

kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {
        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;
        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));
    }
    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);
}

If the entity already has a T, adding is just setting. Otherwise it moves to the table with T, then sets it. kayan_remove<T> is the mirror image: missing if it has no T, otherwise a move to the table without T.

Step 3: the archetype graph

Which table is "the table with T"? Its signature is the old one plus T's bit, so it could be looked up in by_signature every time. But a game toggling components does that constantly, always between the same few tables. So each table remembers its neighbours:

kayan_table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    entities: ^kayan_entity;
    columns: [64]kayan_column;
    add_edges: [64]u32;
    remove_edges: [64]u32;
}

add_edges[id] is where this table's entities go when they gain component id. remove_edges[id] is where they go when they lose it. Each is stored as index + 1, so the zero a new table starts with means "not known yet", with no initialization pass.

kayan_table_with: proc(w: *kayan_world, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {
    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id];
    if (edge != 0) {
        w*.edge_hits += 1;
        return edge - 1;
    }
    w*.lookups += 1;
    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature | kayan_bit(id));
    // kayan_table_for can move the tables, so both pointers are taken after it.
    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id] = to + 1;
    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.remove_edges[id] = from + 1;
    return to;
}

The first move from {position velocity health} with burning looks the table up (and makes it). It then writes the answer on both tables: an add edge one way and a remove edge back. After that, catching fire and putting it out both follow edges. The tables and their edges form a graph, the archetype graph, and flecs is built around it.

Run it

4 drones:
    table 0 {position velocity health}: 0:1 1:1 2:1 3:1
frame 1
    0:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
    table 0 {position velocity health}: 3:1 1:1
    table 1 {position velocity health burning}: 0:1 2:1
frame 2
    0:1 is put out: ok
    1:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
...
frame 3
    1:1 is put out: ok
    2:1 is put out: ok
    3:1 is put out: missing
    3:1 catches fire: ok
...
2:1 moved tables twice and kept its data: at (30.00, 0.00), health 100
moves that looked up a table by signature: 1; that followed an edge: 6
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Watch row order shuffle as entities move: 3:1 jumps to row 0 of table 0 when 0:1 leaves. Order is never promised, and swap-remove is why. And one lookup for seven moves: that's the graph working.

Try

  1. Add a stunned component and a second edge: stun a burning drone. How many tables exist now, and which edges were written?
  2. Print every table's known edges after frame 3.
  3. Make kayan_add<burning> on a drone that's already burning add to the rate instead of replacing it. Where does that logic belong: in kayan or in the game?

i < 4; i += 1) {564        d[i] = spawn_drone(w&, 10.0 * cast(i + 1, f32), 0.0);565    }566    printfmt("4 drones:\n");567    kayan_print_tables(w&);568 569    printfmt("frame 1\n");570    ignite(w&, d[0]);571    ignite(w&, d[2]);572    kayan_print_tables(w&);573 574    printfmt("frame 2\n");575    put_out(w&, d[0]);576    ignite(w&, d[1]);577    ignite(w&, d[2]);578    kayan_print_tables(w&);579 580    printfmt("frame 3\n");581    put_out(w&, d[1]);582    put_out(w&, d[2]);583    put_out(w&, d[3]);584    ignite(w&, d[3]);585    kayan_print_tables(w&);586 587    p: *position = kayan_get<position>(w&, d[2]);588    printf("%u:%u moved tables twice and kept its data: at (%.2f, %.2f), health %.0f\n", d[2].index, d[2].generation,589        cast(p*.at.x, f64), cast(p*.at.y, f64), cast(kayan_get<health>(w&, d[2])*.points, f64));590    printfmt("moves that looked up a table by signature: {}; that followed an edge: {}\n", w.lookups, w.edge_hits);591    printfmt("kayan_verify: {} problems\n", kayan_verify(w&));592    return 0;593}

Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.7

Inspecting the world

ecs/src/2.components/2.7.inspecting/inspecting.rin

In the dojo: 11. a reflection walk, on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world can store, copy and move any component, but it can't show you one. When something goes wrong at frame 3,000, you want to see an entity: every component it has, every field, with names. In C that means writing a printer per component and keeping each in step with its struct. In rin, the compiler already wrote down everything a printer needs. Each component's reflect record lists its fields with their names, types and byte offsets. The world registered those records back in 2.1 to learn component sizes. Here they pay off a second time.

kayan_inspect(w, e)       every component of e, field by field
kayan_print_layout(w)     every table, its columns, and their memory

Neither names a single component type. Add a component tomorrow and both print it.

Step 1: a component as bytes

Tools work from reflect records, not types, so they need the byte view:

kayan_get_bytes: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> []u8 = {
    none: []u8 = {};
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || id >= w*.component_count) {
        return none;
    }
    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));
    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);
    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {
        return none;
    }
    c: *kayan_column = t*.columns[id]&;
    row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);
    all: []u8 = c*.data[0..t*.count * c*.size];
    return all[row * c*.size..(row + 1) * c*.size];
}

It's kayan_get<T>'s path, stopping one step early: the row's bytes as a slice, sized by the column. Game code uses the typed layer; tools use this.

Step 2: walking fields

kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {
    fields: ^const reflect_field = reflect_fields(type);
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {
        f: *const reflect_field = fields[i]&;
        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {
            continue;
        }
        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];
        kayan_indent(depth);
        printf("%s:", f*.name);
        info: *const reflect = f*.info;
        if (info != null && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {
            printf("\n");
            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);
        } else {
            printf(" ");
            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);
            printf("\n");
        }
    }
}

For each field the record says, cut its bytes out of the component by offset and size. A struct field (at: vec2 inside position) has a record of its own, so the printer recurses into it. A builtin field (f32, u32) is printed by its type's name.

Because each field's bytes are cut with a bounds-checked slice, a record that disagreed with the data would stop a Debug build instead of printing garbage.

Step 3: hiding bookkeeping

Fields can carry tags with @:

turret: struct = { cooldown: f32; timer: f32 @ "hidden"; }

The inspector skips anything tagged "hidden". The component decides what a tool shows; the tool doesn't need to know the component.

Step 4: an entity, and the layout

kayan_inspect walks the entity's signature and prints each component with kayan_print_fields. kayan_print_layout walks every table and prints each column's row size and bytes used out of bytes allocated, which shows where memory goes.

Run it

0:1 {position turret}
    position
        at:
            x: 0.00
            y: 0.00
    turret
        cooldown: 0.50
...
2:1 {position velocity health burning}
...
    health
        points: 60.00
        max: 100.00
    burning
        per_second: 10.00
...
1:1 (dead)
table 1 {position velocity health}: 0 rows, room for 4
    position   8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use
    velocity   8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use
    health     8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use

The turret's timer isn't printed. Table 1 is empty but keeps its capacity: drone 1:1 was its only remaining row after 2:1 caught fire and moved out, and then 1:1 was despawned. Tables never shrink in this course. A real engine might trim empty ones between levels.

Part 2 in one picture

handle 2:1 ──> slots[2] { generation 1, table 2, row 0 }
                                         │
table 2 {position velocity health burning}
  entities  [ 2:1 ]
  position  [ (30, -5) ]     velocity [ (-1, 0) ]     health [ 60/100 ]     burning [ 10 ]
  add_edges / remove_edges ──> neighbouring tables in the archetype graph

The storage half of the ECS is done: identity (Part 1), and any component, in any combination, changing at run time (Part 2). Part 3 is the behaviour: queries to find tables, and systems to run over them.

Try

  1. Add a field to health and run it. Nothing in the inspector changes.
  2. Tag health.max as hidden.
  3. Write kayan_set_f32_by_name(w, e, "health", "points", 10.0) with the reflect records: find the component by name, the field by name, check it's an f32, write it. That's the core of an editor or a console.

Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.1

Queries

ecs/src/3.systems/3.1.queries/queries.rin

In the dojo: 6. bitsets, 12. a watermark, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Part 2 finished the storage. Everything from here on is behaviour, and in an ECS behaviour lives in systems: code that runs over every entity with some set of components. "Every entity with a position and a velocity" isn't in one place. It's spread over every table whose signature has both bits. So a system's first job is finding those tables, and the thing that finds them is a query:

all {position velocity}, none {}   ->   tables 1, 2, 3

A query matches tables, not entities. A game has a handful of tables and rarely makes new ones, so the matching is done once and kept. Each frame, a system walks the kept list, and inside each table streams the columns.

Step 1: the query

kayan_query: struct = {
    all: u64;
    none: u64;
    tables: vec<u32>;
    checked: u64;
}
  • all: a table must have every one of these components.
  • none: and none of these. "Drones that aren't burning" is all {health}, none {burning}.
  • tables: the matching tables, by index. Indices, as always, because pointers to tables go stale.
  • checked: how many of the world's tables the query has looked at.

Matching is two ANDs on the signature:

kayan_matches: proc(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {
    return (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0;
}

Step 2: keeping it up to date

Tables are only ever added, always at the end of w.tables, and never removed. So a query that has checked the first checked tables only needs to look at the ones after that:

kayan_query_update: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {
    for (ti: u64 = q*.checked; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {
        if (kayan_matches(kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32))*.signature, q*.all, q*.none)) {
            _ = vec<u32>append(w*.arena, q*.tables&, cast(ti, u32));
        }
    }
    q*.checked = w*.tables.length;
}

The first update checks every table. After that, a frame with no new tables costs one comparison. A new table is checked once, by each query, the next time each is updated. flecs does the same thing in reverse: when a table is made, it tells the queries.

Step 3: walking a query

This is the shape of every system:

    kayan_query_update(w&, movers&);
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < movers.tables.length; i += 1) {
        t: *kayan_table = kayan_query_table(w&, movers&, i);
        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);
        vs: []velocity = kayan_slice<velocity>(t);
        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {
            ps[row].at.x += vs[row].per_second.x * 0.5;
            ps[row].at.y += vs[row].per_second.y * 0.5;
        }
    }

Two loops. The outer one is over tables, a few iterations. The inner one is over rows: two dense arrays, read and written in order. That's lesson 1's move_soa. The query's job is to hand you the arrays; what you do with them is the same data-oriented loop as always.

The drones and the bullet are in different tables, and the loop doesn't care. The turret isn't matched (no velocity), and the loop never sees it, not even to skip it.

Run it

movers: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 2, entities: 4
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1
targets: all {position health}, none {burning}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
on_fire: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 0, entities: 0

Then drone 2:1 catches fire, which makes table 3, after the queries were made:

2:1 catches fire, and the world makes table 3 for it
the queries have checked 3 tables; updating them checks the new one only
movers: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 4
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1
    table 3 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
targets: all {position health}, none {burning}; tables: 1, entities: 2
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
on_fire: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 3 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1

movers picked up the new table, targets refused it (none {burning}), and on_fire got its first. Nobody re-scanned the old tables.

Last, the bullet is despawned. Its table is now empty, and stays in movers. Walking an empty table costs one look at count.

Why this is fast

A query's cost doesn't depend on how many entities there are. It depends on how many tables match, and that number is small and stable. 10,000 drones in one table is one table to visit. That's the payoff of grouping entities by signature back in 2.4: the "which entities have X and Y?" question gets answered per table, once, instead of per entity, every frame.

The flip side is archetype fragmentation (2.4's Try): if every entity had a unique signature, every query would match thousands of one-row tables.

Try

  1. Write a query for "everything with a position that isn't a turret" and print it.
  2. Make 100 drones and walk movers. How many times does the outer loop run?
  3. Add any: u64 to the query: at least one of these components. Where in kayan_matches does it go?

"%s" : " %s", w*.infos[id]*.name);519            first = false;520        }521    }522    printf("}");523}524 525kayan_print_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, ti: u32) -> void = {526    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);527    printf("    table %u ", ti);528    kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);529    printf(":");530    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {531        printf(" %u:%u", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation);532    }533    printf("\n");534}535 536kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {537    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {538        kayan_print_table(w, ti);539    }540}541 542// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------543// The inspector: reflect records, no component types544// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------545 546kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {547    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {548        printf("    ");549    }550}551 552// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name.553kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {554    if (strcmp(type_name, "f32") == 0) {555        printf("%.2f", cast(cast(at[0]&, *const f32)*, f64));556    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "u32") == 0) {557        printf("%u", cast(at[0]&, *const u32)*);558    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "i32") == 0) {559        printf("%d", cast(at[0]&, *const i32)*);560    } else {561        printf("<%s>", type_name);562    }563}564 565// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented566// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and567// size, both from the reflect record.568kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {569    fields: ^const reflect_field = reflect_fields(type);570    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {571        f: *const reflect_field = fields[i]&;572        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {573            continue;574        }575        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];576        kayan_indent(depth);577        printf("%s:", f*.name);578        info: *const reflect = f*.info;579        if (info != null && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {580            printf("\n");581            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);582        } else {583            printf(" ");584            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);585            printf("\n");586        }587    }588}589 590kayan_inspect: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {591    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {592        printfmt("{}:{} (dead)\n", e.index, e.generation);593        return;594    }595    printf("%u:%u ", e.index, e.generation);596    signature: u64 = kayan_signature(w, e);597    kayan_print_signature(w, signature);598    printf("\n");599    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {600        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {601            info: *const reflect = w*.infos[id];602            printf("    %s\n", info*.name);603            bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);604            kayan_print_fields(info, bytes, 2);605        }606    }607}608 609// Every table: rows in use out of room, and per column its row size and its610// bytes in use out of bytes allocated.     table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}:
    table 3 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.2

Systems

ecs/src/3.systems/3.2.systems/systems.rin

In the dojo: 13. a dispatch table, on its own, to watch and to practise.

3.1's movement loop had the shape of every system: bring a query up to date, then for each of its tables take the columns as slices and loop over the rows. This chapter names that shape and splits it in two:

  • the kernel: a plain loop over plain slices. It knows nothing about tables, entities or worlds. This is lessons 1 to 7: noalias, streaming, vectorization.
  • the system: a query, plus a small proc kayan calls on each table the query matches. It takes the table's columns and calls the kernel.

A frame runs the systems in order, each over all of its tables. The order is the schedule, and it's written down once, as data.

Step 1: the kernels

integrate: proc(ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void = {
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < ps.length; i += 1) {
        ps[i].at.x += vs[i].per_second.x * dt;
        ps[i].at.y += vs[i].per_second.y * dt;
    }
}

That's the whole thing, and it's the code you'd want to write if there were no ECS at all. Kernels are where you profile, read assembly and reach for SIMD (the lessons). Everything else in this course exists to hand them the right slices. burn and age look the same.

Step 2: what a system gets

kayan_iter: struct = {
    world: *kayan_world;
    table: *kayan_table;
    dt: f32;
}

kayan_system_proc: alias = *proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void;

One struct instead of three parameters. It's the same idea as flecs' ecs_iter_t, and it has two practical reasons. Adding to it later (3.3 adds a field) changes no system's signature. And a system that uses only the table still uses its one parameter. rin compiles to C with -Wextra -Werror, and an unused parameter is an error there.

The system itself is the adapter:

move_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {
    integrate(kayan_slice<position>(it*.table), kayan_slice<velocity>(it*.table), it*.dt);
}

Columns out, kernel in. No loop here: the kernel has it.

Step 3: a system is data

kayan_system: struct = {
    name: ^const char;
    query: kayan_query;
    run: kayan_system_proc;
    tables: u64;
    rows: u64;
}

A name, a query, a proc pointer. tables and rows count the work, for the output. The schedule is an array of these:

    systems: [3]kayan_system = {};
    systems[0] = kayan_system_init("burn", kayan_mask_of<health>() | kayan_mask_of<burning>(), 0, burn_system);
    systems[1] = kayan_system_init("age", kayan_mask_of<lifetime>(), 0, age_system);
    systems[2] = kayan_system_init("move", kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>(), 0, move_system);

Step 4: a frame

kayan_progress: proc(w: *kayan_world, systems: []kayan_system, dt: f32) -> void = {
    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems.length; s += 1) {
        sys: *kayan_system = systems[s]&;
        kayan_query_update(w, sys*.query&);
        for (i: u64 = 0; i < sys*.query.tables.length; i += 1) {
            it: kayan_iter = {};
            it.world = w;
            it.table = kayan_query_table(w, sys*.query&, i);
            it.dt = dt;
            if (it.table*.count > 0) {
                sys*.tables += 1;
                sys*.rows += it.table*.count;
                sys*.run(it&);
            }
        }
    }
}

kayan_progress is flecs' name for the same thing. For each system in order, for each of its tables, one call. The game loop becomes:

    for (frame: u32 = 1; frame <= 8; frame += 1) {
        kayan_progress(w&, systems, dt);

Order is data flow

Systems run one after another, never interleaved, and each sees everything the earlier ones wrote this frame. So the order is a statement about data: a system that reads what another writes runs after it. Move before collide means bullets hit where they are now, not where they were. Damage before death means a drone dies in the frame its health hits zero, not the next. 3.4's schedule has nine systems, and each position in it is one of these decisions.

Bigger engines go further. Each system declares what it reads and writes, and the scheduler uses that to run systems that don't conflict at the same time, on other threads. Underneath, the order is still a list like this one.

Run it

the schedule, run in this order every frame:
burn: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 2 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
age: all {lifetime}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 3 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
move: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 6
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
    table 3 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
...
after frame 8, 2.00 seconds:
    0:1 at ( 0.00,  0.00)
    1:1 at (18.00,  4.00)  health 100
    3:1 at (26.00, -4.00)  health 100
    2:1 at (22.00,  0.00)  health 84, burning
    4:1 at (17.00,  0.00)  lifetime -1.50
    5:1 at (17.00,  4.00)  lifetime -1.00
    6:1 at (17.00, -4.00)  lifetime -0.50

8 frames, one call per table per frame:
    burn called  8 times, over  8 rows
    age  called  8 times, over 24 rows
    move called 24 times, over 48 rows
3 bullets are out of time and still in the world

move made 24 calls in 8 frames, three tables a frame, and each call is one tight loop. Call overhead is per table, never per entity.

And the last line is the cliffhanger. Each bullet's lifetime ran out, and nothing removed it, because a system in this chapter changes values, never structure. Despawning from inside a system looks like a one-line fix. It isn't, and 3.3 shows why.

Try

  1. Swap burn and move in the schedule. Does anything change? Now think of a pair where it would.
  2. Add a heal system for drones that aren't burning (all {health}, none {burning}).
  3. Build in Release and find integrate in the assembly. Is it vectorized? (Lesson 1 shows how to look.)

It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does444// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.445kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {446    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {447        return kayan_status.dead;448    }449    p: *T = kayan_get<T>(w, e);450    if (p == null) {451        return kayan_status.missing;452    }453    p* = value;454    return kayan_status.ok;455}456 457// Give e a T. If it already has one, this is kayan_set; if not, it moves to458// the table with T and then sets it.459kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {460    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {461        return kayan_status.dead;462    }463    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {464        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;465        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));466    }467    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);468}469 470// Take e's T away, moving it to the table without T.471kayan_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {472    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {473        return kayan_status.dead;474    }475    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {476        return kayan_status.missing;477    }478    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;479    kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_without(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));480    return kayan_status.ok;481}482 483// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose484// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to485// the live count.486kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> u64 = {487    problems: u64 = 0;488    rows: u64 = 0;489    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {490        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));491        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {492            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];493            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {494                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);495                problems += 1;496                continue;497            }498            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));499            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {500                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",501                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);502                problems += 1;503            }504        }505        rows += t*.count;506    }507    if (rows != w*.live) {508        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);509        problems += 1;510    }511    return problems;512}513 514kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {515    printf("{");516    first: b32 = true;517    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {518        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {519            printf(first ? "%s" : " %s", w*.infos[id]*.name);520            first = false;521        }522    }523    printf("}");524}525 526kayan_print_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, ti: u32) -> void = {527    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);528    printf("    table %u ", ti);529    kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);530    printf(":");531    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {532        printf(" %u:%u", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation);533    }534    printf("\n");535}536 537kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {538    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {539        kayan_print_table(w, ti);540    }541}542 543// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------544// The inspector: reflect records, no component types545// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------546 547kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {548    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {549        printf("    ");550    }551}552 553// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name.554kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {555    if (strcmp(type_name, "f32") == 0) {556        printf("%.2f", cast(cast(at[0]&, *const f32)*, f64));557    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "u32") == 0) {558        printf("%u", cast(at[0]&, *const u32)*);559    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "i32") == 0) {560        printf("%d", cast(at[0]&, *const i32)*);561    } else {562        printf("<%s>", type_name);563    }564}565 566// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented567// under their field. Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.3

Commands

ecs/src/3.systems/3.3.commands/commands.rin

In the dojo: 5. a command buffer, 7. an arena, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

3.2's systems change values, never structure, so bullets whose time ran out stay in the world. The obvious fix is to despawn them from inside the system. It's wrong, and seeing exactly why is most of this chapter.

Step 1: the bug

expire_now_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {
    t: *kayan_table = it*.table;
    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(t);
    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {
        if (ls[row].seconds <= 0.0) {
            _ = kayan_despawn(it*.world, t*.entities[row]);
        }
    }
}

Four bullets, three of them out of time:

1. an expire system that despawns as it goes
    lifetimes:  0:1 0.00  1:1 1.00  2:1 0.00  3:1 0.00
after one frame:
    lifetimes:  3:1 0.00  1:1 1.00
kayan_verify: 0 problems. The world is fine; the loop missed one.

Row by row:

row 0: 0:1 is out of time. Despawn: the last row, 3:1, moves into row 0.
row 1: 1:1 has time left.
row 2: 2:1 is out of time. Despawn: it's the last row, so nothing moves.
row 3: the table has 2 rows now. Stop.

3:1 moved into row 0, which the loop had already passed, so it was never looked at. The world is perfectly consistent (kayan_verify agrees). The loop is what's wrong: a despawn swap-removes from the table the loop is walking.

Walking backwards fixes this case (lesson 2 does it), because the row that moves in has already been looked at. But it doesn't fix the general problem:

  • Adding or removing a component moves the entity to another table. If the query matches that table too and visits it later, the entity is processed twice.
  • If that table is new, making it can grow w.tables and move every table. The t the loop is holding then points at the old copy, which the arena still owns, so nothing crashes and every write after that is lost. This is 2.4's bug, from inside a loop.
  • One system's despawn can land in a table another system is halfway through, if a system despawns entities it found through a second query.

Step 2: record now, apply later

So a system doesn't change structure. It records a command saying what should change, and the world applies every command after the frame's last system:

during the frame   values change; tables, rows and pointers do not
after the frame    spawns, despawns, adds and removes, in order
kayan_command_kind: enum = {
    spawn,
    despawn,
    add,
    remove,
}

kayan_command: struct = {
    kind: kayan_command_kind;
    entity: kayan_entity;
    spawn: u32;
    id: u32;
    signature: u64;
    value: []u8;
}

A command names the entity, and for an add or remove the component id. An add carries its value as bytes. The bytes, and the list of commands, live in a frame arena the world owns:

    frame: memops_arena;
    commands: vec<kayan_command>;

After the commands are applied, memops_arena_clear drops all of them at once, whatever they were.

Step 3: recording

The typed procs a system calls copy the value into the frame arena and append a command:

kayan_defer_value: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, value: T) -> []u8 = {
    data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push(w*.frame&, sizeof(T), alignof(T)), ^u8);
    memcpy(data, value&, sizeof(T));
    return data[0..sizeof(T)];
}
kayan_defer_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> void = {
    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),
        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(w, value) });
}

The fixed expire system is the broken one with one word changed:

expire_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {
    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(it*.table);
    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);
    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {
        if (ls[row].seconds <= 0.0) {
            kayan_defer_despawn(it*.world, es[row]);
        }
    }
}

Now the table doesn't change while the loop runs, so the loop can take the entities as a slice up front, like any other column.

Step 4: applying, by id

Commands hold bytes and ids, not types. So applying an add needs 2.6's add by id:

kayan_add_id: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32, value: []const u8) -> kayan_status = {

It's the same move-then-write as before, with the write a memcpy of the value's bytes into the row. Once that exists, the typed kayan_add<T> from 2.6 shrinks to a one-line wrapper. That's the pattern from the start of the course: byte fiddling written once, a type-safe generic layer on top.

kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {
    bytes: ^const u8 = cast(value&, ^const u8);
    return kayan_add_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>(), bytes[0..sizeof(T)]);
}

kayan_flush walks the list in order and applies each command. It's called at the end of kayan_progress:

    kayan_flush(w);
}

Step 5: commands that arrive too late

By the time a command is applied, its entity may be gone. The usual case is two systems both asking to despawn the same thing. Applying in order handles that for free: the first despawn works, and the second finds a dead handle. Part 1's generations make that check one comparison:

        if (status == kayan_status.ok) {
            w*.applied += 1;
        } else {
            w*.skipped += 1;
        }

Step 6: spawning from a system

A turret firing is a spawn in the middle of a frame. The new entity doesn't exist until the commands are applied, so there's no handle to give its components to. kayan_defer_spawn returns a pending spawn instead: the spawn command's place in the list. Components are given to that:

            shot: kayan_pending = kayan_defer_spawn(it*.world, bullet_signature());
            kayan_pending_set<position>(it*.world, shot, ps[row]);
            kayan_pending_set<velocity>(it*.world, shot, { .per_second = { .x = 8.0, .y = 0.0 } });
            kayan_pending_set<damage>(it*.world, shot, { .amount = 25.0 });
            kayan_pending_set<lifetime>(it*.world, shot, { .seconds = 2.0 });

When the flush reaches the spawn, it makes the entity and writes the handle into the command. The adds after it look the handle up there. The bullet is spawned with its full signature, so the adds land in the table it's already in: no moves. And it doesn't move until the next frame, because no system ran over it this one.

Step 7: a system with two queries

A bullet that reaches a target damages it. The hit system walks the bullets (its own query) and, for each, the targets (a second query). It reaches the second query through a new field, ctx, which kayan passes through untouched:

    targets: *kayan_query = cast(it*.ctx, *kayan_query);

The damage is a value, so it's written now. The bullet's despawn is structure, so it's recorded. Walking a second query in the middle of a frame is safe because of commands: no table is made or moved until the frame is over.

Run it

2. an expire system that records despawns
    lifetimes:  0:1 0.00  1:1 1.00  2:1 0.00  3:1 0.00
    despawn 0:1
    despawn 2:1
    despawn 3:1
after one frame:
    lifetimes:  1:1 1.00

All three. Then the turret, with two targets 0.25 apart in its line of fire and a third out of it:

3. a turret, two targets in its line of fire, one out of it
frame 1
    spawn {position velocity damage lifetime} -> 4:1
frame 2
frame 3
    spawn {position velocity damage lifetime} -> 5:1
frame 4
    despawn 4:1
    despawn 4:1: skipped, dead
frame 5

...
health: 1:1 50, 2:1 50, 3:1 100
commands applied: 17, skipped: 2

In frame 4, bullet 4:1 is close enough to both targets. Both lose 25, and both hits record a despawn. The first applies; the second finds 4:1 already dead and is skipped. In frame 5 the next bullet gets number 4 back with generation 2: Part 1, working.

17 commands, for three bullets and two despawns: each spawn is five, the spawn and its four components.

Try

  1. In expire_now_system, loop to ls.length instead of t*.count. Now all three get despawned. Work out why. (Hint: what's in the rows past the end of the table?) Is that loop correct?
  2. Write a system that adds burning directly (not deferred) to every target it walks. Count how many times it visits each entity.
  3. Flush after each system instead of after the frame. What does that change about what later systems see? (flecs calls these sync points.)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------489// The typed layer490// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------491 492// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed493// view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. The pointer is494// good until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.495kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *T = {496    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {497        return null;498    }499    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));500    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);501    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {502        return null;503    }504    rows: []T = kayan_slice<T>(t);505    return rows[cast(slot*.row, u64)]&;506}507 508kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {509    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;510}511 512// Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does513// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.514kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {515    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {516        return kayan_status.dead;517    }518    p: *T = kayan_get<T>(w, e);519    if (p == null) {520        return kayan_status.missing;521    }522    p* = value;523    return kayan_status.ok;524}525 526// Give e a T, or take its T away: the byte procs, with the type turned into an527// id and the value into its bytes.528kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {529    bytes: ^const u8 = cast(value&, ^const u8);530    return kayan_add_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>(), bytes[0..sizeof(T)]);531}532 533kayan_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {534    return kayan_remove_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>());535}536 537// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose538// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to539// the live count.540kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> u64 = {541    problems: u64 = 0;542    rows: u64 = 0;543    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {544        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));545        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {546            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];547            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {548                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);549                problems += 1;550                continue;551            }552            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));553            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {554                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",555                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);556                problems += 1;557            }558        }559        rows += t*.count;560    }561    if (rows != w*.live) {562        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);563        problems += 1;564    }565    return problems;566}567 568kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {569    printf("{");570    first: b32 = true;571    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {572        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {573            printf(first ? "%s" : " %s", w*.infos[id]*.name);574            first = false;575        }576    }577    printf("}");578}579 580kayan_print_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, ti: u32) -> void = {581    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);582    printf("    table %u ", ti);583    kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);584    printf(":");585    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {586        printf(" %u:%u", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation);587    }588    printf("\n");589}590 591kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {592    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {593        kayan_print_table(w, ti);594    }595}596 597// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------598// The inspector: reflect records, no component types599// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------600 601kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {602    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {603        printf("    ");604    }605}606 607// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name.608kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {609    if (strcmp(type_name, "f32") == 0) {610        printf("%.2f", cast(cast(at[0]&, *const f32)*, f64));611    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "u32") == 0) {612        printf("%u", cast(at[0]&, *const u32)*);613    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "i32") == 0) {614        printf("%d", cast(at[0]&, *const i32)*);615    } else {616        printf("<%s>", type_name);617    }618}619 620// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented621// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and622// size, both from the reflect record.623kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {624    fields: ^const reflect_field = reflect_fields(type);625    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {626        f: *const reflect_field = fields[i]&;627        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {628            continue;629        }630        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];631        kayan_indent(depth);632        printf("%s:", f*.name);633        info: *const reflect = f*.info;634        if (info != null && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {635            printf("\n");636            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);637        } else {638            printf(" ");639            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);640            printf("\n");641        }642    }643}644 645kayan_inspect: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {646    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {647        printfmt("{}:{} (dead)\n", e.index, e.generation);648        return;649    }650    printf("%u:%u ", e.index, e.generation);651    signature: u64 = kayan_signature(w, e);652    kayan_print_signature(w, signature);653    printf("\n");654    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {655        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {656            info: *const reflect = w*.infos[id];657            printf("    %s\n", info*.name);658            bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);659            kayan_print_fields(info, bytes, 2);660        }661    }662}663 664// Every table: rows in use out of room, and per column its row size and its665// bytes in use out of bytes allocated. The memory a table holds and does not666// use is the cost of doubling on growth.667kayan_print_layout: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {668    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {669        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);670        printf("table %u ", ti);671        kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);672        printf(": %u rows, room for %u\n", cast(t*.count, u32), cast(t*.capacity, u32));673        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {674            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {675                size: u64 = t*.columns[id].size;676                printf("    %-9s %2u bytes a row, %4u of %4u bytes in use\n", w*.infos[id]*.name, cast(size, u32),677                    cast(size * t*.count, u32), cast(size * t*.capacity, u32));678            }679        }680    }681}682 683// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------684// Queries685// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------686 687// The tables a system runs over: every table whose signature has all of `all`688// and none of `none`, kept by index. Tables are only ever added, at the end of689// w.tables, so the query remembers how many it has checked and, brought up to690// date, looks at the new ones only.691kayan_query: struct = {692    all: u64;693    none: u64;694    tables: vec<u32>;695    checked: u64;696}697 698kayan_query_init: proc(all: u64, none: u64) -> kayan_query = {699    q: kayan_query = {};700    q.all = all;701    q.none = none;702    return q;703}704 705kayan_matches: proc(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {706    return (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0;707}708 709// Check the tables made since the query last looked. With none new, this is710// one comparison, so call it before every walk.711kayan_query_update: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {712    for (ti: u64 = q*.checked; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {713        if (kayan_matches(kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32))*.signature, q*.all, q*.none)) {714            _ = vec<u32>append(w*.arena, q*.tables&, cast(ti, u32));715        }716    }717    q*.checked = w*.tables.length;718}719 720// The query's i-th table. Like any table pointer, good until a table is made.721kayan_query_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query, i: u64) -> *kayan_table = {722    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables&, i)*);723}724 725// How many entities the query matches: the rows of its tables.726kayan_query_count: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> u64 = {727    kayan_query_update(w, q);728    n: u64 = 0;729    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables.length; i += 1) {730        n += kayan_query_table(w, q, i)*.count;731    }732    return n;733}734 735kayan_print_query: proc(w: *kayan_world, name: ^const char, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {736    kayan_query_update(w, q);737    printf("%s: all ", name);738    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.all);739    printf(", none ");740    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.none);741    printfmt("; tables: {}, entities: {}\n", q*.tables.length, kayan_query_count(w, q));742    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables.length; i += 1) {743        kayan_print_table(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables&, i)*);744    }745}746 747// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------748// Commands749// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------750 751// A spawn that has been recorded and not applied. There is no entity yet, so752// this is the spawn command's place in the list; give it components with753// kayan_pending_set.754kayan_pending: struct = {755    command: u32;756}757 758kayan_defer: proc(w: *kayan_world, c: kayan_command) -> u32 = {759    index: u32 = cast(w*.commands.length, u32);760    _ = vec<kayan_command>append(w*.frame&, w*.commands&, c);761    return index;762}763 764// A copy of `value`, as bytes, in the frame arena.765kayan_defer_value: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, value: T) -> []u8 = {766    data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push(w*.frame&, sizeof(T), alignof(T)), ^u8);767    memcpy(data, value&, sizeof(T));768    return data[0..sizeof(T)];769}770 771kayan_defer_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_pending = {772    p: kayan_pending = {};773    p.command = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.spawn, .signature = signature });774    return p;775}776 777kayan_pending_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, p: kayan_pending, value: T) -> void = {778    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .spawn = p.command + 1, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),779        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(w, value) });780}781 782kayan_defer_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {783    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.despawn, .entity = e });784}785 786kayan_defer_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> void = {787    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),788        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(w, value) });789}790 791kayan_defer_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {792    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.remove, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>() });793}794 795// One applied command. The components given to a new entity are part of its796// spawn line, so they are not printed on their own.797kayan_print_command: proc(w: *kayan_world, c: *kayan_command, status: kayan_status) -> void = {798    if (c*.spawn != 0 && status == kayan_status.ok) {799        return;800    }801    printfmt("    {} ", c*.kind);802    if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {803        kayan_print_signature(w, c*.signature);804        printf(" -> ");805    } else if (c*.kind != kayan_command_kind.despawn) {806        printf("%s, ", w*.infos[c*.id]*.name);807    }808    printf("%u:%u", c*.entity.index, c*.entity.generation);809    if (status != kayan_status.ok) {810        printfmt(": skipped, {}", status);811    }812    printf("\n");813}814 815// Apply the frame's commands in the order they were recorded, then let them816// all go at once. A command for an entity that died after it was recorded817// (despawned by an earlier command, most likely) does nothing, and is counted.818kayan_flush: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {819    for (i: u64 = 0; i < w*.commands.length; i += 1) {820        c: *kayan_command = vec<kayan_command>at(w*.commands&, i);821        if (c*.spawn != 0) {822            c*.entity = vec<kayan_command>at(w*.commands&, cast(c*.spawn - 1, u64))*.entity;823        }824        status: kayan_status = kayan_status.ok;825        if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {826            c*.entity = kayan_spawn(w, c*.signature);827        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.despawn) {828            status = kayan_despawn(w, c*.entity);829        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.add) {830            status = kayan_add_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id, c*.value);831        } else {832            status = kayan_remove_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id);833        }834        if (status == kayan_status.ok) {835            w*.applied += 1;836        } else {837            w*.skipped += 1;838        }839        if (w*.trace) {840            kayan_print_command(w, c, status);841        }842    }843    w*.commands = {};844    memops_arena_clear(w*.frame&);845}846 847// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------848// Systems849// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------850 851// What a system gets for each table it runs on: the world, the table, and the852// frame's time step. One struct rather than three parameters, so that adding853// to it later changes no system's signature.854kayan_iter: struct = {855    world: *kayan_world;856    table: *kayan_table;857    dt: f32;858    ctx: *void;859}860 861kayan_system_proc: alias = *proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void;862 863// A system: a name, the query that finds its tables, and the proc run on each864// of those tables that has rows. `tables` and `rows` count what it has run865// over. `ctx` is handed to the proc as is: whatever the system needs beyond866// its own tables, such as another query, or the game's state.867kayan_system: struct = {868    name: ^const char;869    query: kayan_query;870    run: kayan_system_proc;871    ctx: *void;872    tables: u64;873    rows: u64;874}875 876kayan_system_init: proc(name: ^const char, all: u64, none: u64, run: kayan_system_proc, ctx: *void) -> kayan_system = {877    s: kayan_system = {};878    s.name = name;879    s.query = kayan_query_init(all, none);880    s.run = run;881    s.ctx = ctx;882    return s;883}884 885// One frame: every system in order, each over every table it matches that has886// rows, then the commands they recorded. A system sees every value the887// systems before it wrote this frame, and no structural change until the888// next.889kayan_progress: proc(w: *kayan_world, systems: []kayan_system, dt: f32) -> void = {890    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems.length; s += 1) {891        sys: *kayan_system = systems[s]&;892        kayan_query_update(w, sys*.query&);893        for (i: u64 = 0; i < sys*.query.tables.length; i += 1) {894            it: kayan_iter = {};895            it.world = w;896            it.table = kayan_query_table(w, sys*.query&, i);897            it.dt = dt;898            it.ctx = sys*.ctx;899            if (it.table*.count > 0) {900                sys*.tables += 1;901                sys*.rows += it.table*.count;902                sys*.run(it&);903            }904        }905    }906    kayan_flush(w);907}908 909kayan_print_schedule: proc(w: *kayan_world, systems: []kayan_system) -> void = {910    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems.length; s += 1) {911        kayan_print_query(w, systems[s].name, systems[s].query&);912    }913}914 915// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------916// The program917// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------918 919bullet_signature: proc() -> u64 = {920    return kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<damage>() | kayan_mask_of<lifetime>();921}922 923spawn_bullet: proc(w: *kayan_world, x: f32, seconds: f32) -> kayan_entity = {924    e: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w, bullet_signature());925    _ = kayan_set<position>(w, e, { .at = { .x = x, .y = 0.0 } });926    _ = kayan_set<velocity>(w, e, { .per_second = { .x = 8.0, .y = 0.0 } });927    _ = kayan_set<damage>(w, e, { .amount = 25.0 });928    _ = kayan_set<lifetime>(w, e, { .seconds = seconds });929    return e;930}931 932spawn_target: proc(w: *kayan_world, x: f32, y: f32) -> kayan_entity = {933    e: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(w, kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<health>());934    _ = kayan_set<position>(w, e, { .at = { .x = x, .y = y } });935    _ = kayan_set<health>(w, e, { .points = 100.0, .max = 100.0 });936    return e;937}938 939// The wrong way: despawn as the loop goes. Row `row` is swap-removed, the last940// row moves into it, and the loop moves on to row + 1.941expire_now_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {942    t: *kayan_table = it*.table;943    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(t);944    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {945        if (ls[row].seconds <= 0.0) {946            _ = kayan_despawn(it*.world, t*.entities[row]);947        }948    }949}950 951// The right way: record the despawn. The table does not change until the952// frame is over, so every row is looked at once.953expire_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {954    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(it*.table);955    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);956    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {957        if (ls[row].seconds <= 0.0) {958            kayan_defer_despawn(it*.world, es[row]);959        }960    }961}962 963age_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {964    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(it*.table);965    for (row: u64 = 0; row < ls.length; row += 1) {966        ls[row].seconds -= it*.dt;967    }968}969 970move_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {971    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);972    vs: []velocity = kayan_slice<velocity>(it*.table);973    for (row: u64 = 0; row < ps.length; row += 1) {974        ps[row].at.x += vs[row].per_second.x * it*.dt;975        ps[row].at.y += vs[row].per_second.y * it*.dt;976    }977}978 979// A turret whose timer is up spawns a bullet where it stands. The bullet does980// not exist until the frame ends, so it first moves next frame.981turret_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {982    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);983    ts: []turret = kayan_slice<turret>(it*.table);984    for (row: u64 = 0; row < ts.length; row += 1) {985        if (ts[row].timer <= 0.0) {986            shot: kayan_pending = kayan_defer_spawn(it*.world, bullet_signature());987            kayan_pending_set<position>(it*.world, shot, ps[row]);988            kayan_pending_set<velocity>(it*.world, shot, { .per_second = { .x = 8.0, .y = 0.0 } });989            kayan_pending_set<damage>(it*.world, shot, { .amount = 25.0 });990            kayan_pending_set<lifetime>(it*.world, shot, { .seconds = 2.0 });991            ts[row].timer += ts[row].cooldown;992        }993        ts[row].timer -= it*.dt;994    }995}996 997// A bullet within half a unit of a target hits it. The damage is a value, so998// it is written now; the bullet's despawn is structure, so it is recorded. The999// targets are another query, which the system gets through its ctx. During a1000// frame no table is made or moved, so walking a second query is safe.1001hit_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1002    w: *kayan_world = it*.world;1003    targets: *kayan_query = cast(it*.ctx, *kayan_query);1004    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);1005    ds: []damage = kayan_slice<damage>(it*.table);1006    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1007    kayan_query_update(w, targets);1008    for (b: u64 = 0; b < es.length; b += 1) {1009        for (i: u64 = 0; i < targets*.tables.length; i += 1) {1010            t: *kayan_table = kayan_query_table(w, targets, i);1011            tps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);1012            ths: []health = kayan_slice<health>(t);1013            for (row: u64 = 0; row < tps.length; row += 1) {1014                dx: f32 = tps[row].at.x - ps[b].at.x;1015                dy: f32 = tps[row].at.y - ps[b].at.y;1016                if (dx * dx + dy * dy < 0.25) {1017                    ths[row].points -= ds[b].amount;1018                    kayan_defer_despawn(w, es[b]);1019                }1020            }1021        }1022    }1023}1024 1025make_world: proc(w: *kayan_world, arena: *memops_arena) -> void = {1026    kayan_world_init(w, arena);1027    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);1028    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);1029    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<health>(), health<>&);1030    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<damage>(), damage<>&);1031    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<lifetime>(), lifetime<>&);1032    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<turret>(), turret<>&);1033    kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<burning>(), burning<>&);1034}1035 1036// Four bullets, three of them out of time.1037four_bullets: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {1038    _ = spawn_bullet(w, 1.0, 0.0);1039    _ = spawn_bullet(w, 2.0, 1.0);1040    _ = spawn_bullet(w, 3.0, 0.0);1041    _ = spawn_bullet(w, 4.0, 0.0);1042}1043 1044print_lifetimes: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {1045    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, kayan_table_for(w, bullet_signature()));1046    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(t);1047    printf("    lifetimes:");1048    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {1049        printf("  %u:%u %.2f", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation, cast(ls[row].seconds, f64));1050    }1051    printf("\n");1052}1053 1054main: proc() -> i32 = {1055    arena: memops_arena = {};1056    memops_arena_initialize(arena&);1057    lifetime_only: u64 = kayan_mask_of<lifetime>();1058 1059    printfmt("1. an expire system that despawns as it goes\n");1060    a: kayan_world = {};1061    make_world(a&, arena&);1062    four_bullets(a&);1063    print_lifetimes(a&);1064    wrong: [1]kayan_system = {};1065    wrong[0] = kayan_system_init("expire", lifetime_only, 0, expire_now_system, null);1066    kayan_progress(a&, wrong, 0.25);1067    printfmt("after one frame:\n");1068    print_lifetimes(a&);1069    printfmt("kayan_verify: {} problems. Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.4

A game

ecs/src/3.systems/3.4.game/game.rin

In the dojo: this chapter puts the building blocks together; the dojo has each one on its own, to watch and to practise.

Everything together. Three lanes, a turret at the left end of each, and drones coming from the right in waves:

  • a turret fires down its lane while there's a drone in it;
  • a bullet that reaches a drone damages it;
  • a drone below half health catches fire;
  • a drone with no health left is destroyed;
  • a drone that gets to the left end has reached the base.

The top of the file is kayan, exactly as 3.3 left it. The game is the bottom: components, kernels, systems, a schedule and a level script. Every rule of the game is a system over a query. Every structural change a system makes is a command.

The pieces

The components are the same seven from 2.1. A drone is a signature:

drone_signature: proc() -> u64 = {
    return kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>();
}

A burning drone is that plus burning, which puts it in another table. There is no drone type anywhere in the program. A drone is whatever lives in a table with these columns.

What the systems share (the drones query, the clock, the score) is one struct, handed to the systems that need it through ctx:

game: struct = {
    drones: kayan_query;
    time: f32;
    fired: u32;
    hits: u32;
    fires: u32;
    kills: u32;
    breaches: u32;
    came: u32;
}

The schedule

    systems: [9]kayan_system = {};
    systems[0] = kayan_system_init("turret", shooting, 0, turret_system, g&);
    systems[1] = kayan_system_init("age", kayan_mask_of<lifetime>(), 0, age_system, null);
    systems[2] = kayan_system_init("expire", kayan_mask_of<lifetime>(), 0, expire_system, null);
    systems[3] = kayan_system_init("move", movers, 0, move_system, null);
    systems[4] = kayan_system_init("hit", bullets, 0, hit_system, g&);
    systems[5] = kayan_system_init("ignite", kayan_mask_of<health>(), kayan_mask_of<burning>(), ignite_system, g&);
    systems[6] = kayan_system_init("burn", kayan_mask_of<health>() | kayan_mask_of<burning>(), 0, burn_system, null);
    systems[7] = kayan_system_init("die", kayan_mask_of<health>(), 0, die_system, g&);
    systems[8] = kayan_system_init("breach", kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<health>(), 0, breach_system, g&);

Read it as the frame, top to bottom. Each line's position is a data-flow decision (3.2):

  • move before hit: bullets hit where they are, not where they were.
  • hit before ignite, burn and die: a drone takes damage, catches fire and is destroyed in the same frame its health drops.
  • die before breach: only a drone that survived the frame can reach the base. breach also checks health > 0 itself, because both run in the same frame and die's despawn hasn't been applied yet.
  • ignite has none {burning}: a drone catches fire once. The add is a command, so next frame it's in the burning table and the query no longer matches it.

The rules

Each one is a few lines. The ones that only change values call kernels:

burn_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {
    burn(kayan_slice<health>(it*.table), kayan_slice<burning>(it*.table), it*.dt);
}

The ones that change structure record commands:

        if (hs[row].points < 0.5 * hs[row].max && hs[row].points > 0.0) {
            kayan_defer_add<burning>(it*.world, es[row], { .per_second = 10.0 });
            g*.fires += 1;
        }

The turret is the most involved. It asks the drones query whether anything is ahead of it in its lane, then spawns a bullet with a pending spawn (3.3):

        if (ts[row].timer <= 0.0 && drone_ahead(it*.world, g, ps[row].at.x, ps[row].at.y)) {

hit is 3.3's hit system, with one extra thought about speed. A bullet moves a unit a frame and a fast drone a quarter, so they close by at most 1.25 a frame. A hit window of ±0.75 is 1.5 wide, so no bullet can pass through a drone between two frames:

                if (dx * dx < 0.5625 && dy * dy < 0.25) {

The level

The waves aren't a system. They're the level script, and it runs between frames, in the game loop, where spawning directly is safe:

    for (frame: u32 = 0; frame < frames; frame += 1) {
        g.time = cast(frame, f32) * dt;
        if (frame % 32 == 0 && frame / 32 < 8) {
            send_wave(w&, g&, frame / 32);
        }
        kayan_progress(w&, systems, dt);
        problems += kayan_verify(w&);

kayan_verify runs after every frame: 512 checks of Part 1's invariant over the whole world.

Drawing by table

The picture of the lanes walks a query of everything with a position. What an entity is drawn as comes from its table's signature, decided once per table, not per entity:

glyph_of: proc(signature: u64) -> i32 = {
    if ((signature & kayan_mask_of<turret>()) != 0) {
        return 'T';
    }
    if ((signature & kayan_mask_of<burning>()) != 0) {
        return '*';
    }
    if ((signature & kayan_mask_of<health>()) != 0) {
        return 'd';
    }
    return '-';
}

In an OOP engine this would be a virtual draw() per object. Here it's a property of a table, and the inner loop is a plain loop over positions.

Exact on purpose

Every speed and time step is a power of two: dt is 1/16, drones move 2 or 4 units a second, bullets 16, fire burns 10 a second (0.625 a frame). So every position, health and timer is exactly representable, and no rounding ever happens. That's why a Debug build, a Release build, gcc, clang and a CPU that fuses multiply-adds all print the same game. Real games give that up for nicer numbers. Rounding differences usually don't matter, but they do the day you want a replay or a lockstep network game.

The last three drones burn down one unit short of the base. There's one more hit than bullets: once, a bullet reached two drones in the same frame. That's also the one skipped command, its second despawn.

What you built

Part 1  entities       handles, generations, slots, swap-remove, kayan_verify
Part 2  components     ids, columns, tables, archetypes, typed access,
                       moving between tables, the archetype graph, reflection
Part 3  systems        queries, kernels and schedules, commands, a game

That's a working archetype ECS, about 650 lines of kayan without comments. It's the design flecs is built on (tables, the archetype graph, cached queries, command buffers), and Bevy and Unity DOTS are close cousins, minus their years of features.

Things worth adding next, roughly in order of how much they teach:

  • Relationships: child_of(parent) as a component, flecs' big idea.
  • Change detection: a per-column version number, so a system can skip tables nothing wrote to.
  • Parallel systems: systems that don't write what others read can run at the same time. The schedule already holds what you need to decide that.
  • Removing empty tables, and the queries' table lists with them.
  • Serialization: the reflect records already describe every byte; write the tables out and read them back.

Try

  1. Add a fourth lane. What changes? (Only the level: lanes, the picture.)
  2. Make bullets pierce: they don't despawn on a hit, but each drone can only be hit by a bullet once. Where does "once" live? (A component on the bullet? On the drone?)
  3. Add a shield component that absorbs the next hit, then removes itself. Which systems change?
  4. Print kayan_inspect of a drone the frame it catches fire.
