id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {245        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {246            kayan_column_grow(w*.arena, t*.columns[id]&, t*.count, capacity);247        }248    }249    t*.capacity = capacity;250}251 252// A new row at the end, owned by `e`, with every component zeroed.253kayan_table_add_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {254    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {255        kayan_table_grow(w, t);256    }257    row: u64 = t*.count;258    t*.count += 1;259    t*.entities[row] = e;260    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {261        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {262            kayan_column_zero_row(t*.columns[id]&, row);263        }264    }265    return row;266}267 268// 1.4's swap-remove, for every column: the last row is copied over `row`, and269// the slot of the entity that owned the last row is told where it went.270kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world, t: *kayan_table, row: u64) -> void = {271    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;272    if (row != last) {273        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {274            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {275                kayan_column_copy_row(t*.columns[id]&, row, last);276            }277        }278        moved: kayan_entity = t*.entities[last];279        t*.entities[row] = moved;280        vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(moved.index, u64))*.row = cast(row, u32);281    }282    t*.count = last;283}284 285// The typed view of one of the table's columns: T's rows, all of them in use.286// Asking for a component the table does not have is a bug, so it stops.287kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table) -> []T = {288    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();289    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {290        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);291        exit(1);292    }293    return kayan_column_slice<T>(t*.columns[id]&, t*.count);294}295 296// Who owns each of the table's rows.297kayan_entities: proc(t: *kayan_table) -> []kayan_entity = {298    return t*.entities[0..t*.count];299}300 301// A pointer to a table is good until the next table is made.302kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world, index: u32) -> *kayan_table = {303    return vec<kayan_table>at(w*.tables&, cast(index, u64));304}305 306// The table for a signature: found if it exists, made if it does not. This is307// where archetypes come from.308kayan_table_for: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> u32 = {309    found: *u32 = hashmap<u64, u32>get(w*.by_signature&, signature);310    if (found != null) {311        return found*;312    }313    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables.length, u32);314    _ = vec<kayan_table>append(w*.arena, w*.tables&, kayan_table_init(w, signature));315    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>put(w*.arena, w*.by_signature&, signature, index);316    return index;317}318 319// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------320// The world321// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------322 323kayan_world_init: proc(w: *kayan_world, arena: *memops_arena) -> void = {324    w* = {};325    w*.arena = arena;326    // A frame's commands are small: 256 MB of address space is plenty.327    memops_arena_initialize(w*.frame&, 0x10000000);328}329 330kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {331    if (cast(e.index, u64) >= w*.slots.length) {332        return false;333    }334    return vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation == e.generation;335}336 337// A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the table338// for that signature.339kayan_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {340    e: kayan_entity = {};341    if (!vec<u32>is_empty(w*.free&)) {342        e.index = vec<u32>pop(w*.free&);343    } else {344        e.index = cast(w*.slots.length, u32);345        _ = vec<kayan_slot>append(w*.arena, w*.slots&, { .generation = 1 });346    }347    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));348    e.generation = slot*.generation;349    // kayan_table_for can make a table and move the others, so the table's350    // pointer is taken after it.351    table_index: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, signature);352    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, table_index);353    slot*.table = table_index;354    slot*.row = cast(kayan_table_add_row(w, t, e), u32);355    w*.live += 1;356    return e;357}358 359kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {360    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {361        return kayan_status.dead;362    }363    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));364    kayan_table_remove_row(w, kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table), cast(slot*.row, u64));365    slot*.generation += 1;366    _ = vec<u32>append(w*.arena, w*.free&, e.index);367    w*.live -= 1;368    return kayan_status.ok;369}370 371// The components a live entity has: its table's signature. 0 for a dead one.372kayan_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {373    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {374        return 0;375    }376    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table)*.signature;377}378 379// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------380// Moving between tables381// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------382 383// The table an entity of table `from` moves to when it gains component `id`.384// The first time, it is found by signature, which can make the table; the385// answer is written on both tables, as from's add edge and the destination's386// remove edge, so neither direction is looked up again.387kayan_table_with: proc(w: *kayan_world, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {388    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id];389    if (edge != 0) {390        return edge - 1;391    }392    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature | kayan_bit(id));393    // kayan_table_for can move the tables, so both pointers are taken after it.394    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id] = to + 1;395    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.remove_edges[id] = from + 1;396    return to;397}398 399// The same for losing component `id`.400kayan_table_without: proc(w: *kayan_world, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {401    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.remove_edges[id];402    if (edge != 0) {403        return edge - 1;404    }405    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature & ~kayan_bit(id));406    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.remove_edges[id] = to + 1;407    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.add_edges[id] = from + 1;408    return to;409}410 411// Move a live entity to table `to_index`. Components both tables have are412// copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;413// components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.414kayan_move: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {415    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));416    from_index: u32 = slot*.table;417    if (from_index == to_index) {418        return;419    }420    from: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);421    to: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);422    from_row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);423    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(w, to, e);424    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {425        if (kayan_table_has(from, id) && kayan_table_has(to, id)) {426            memcpy(kayan_column_row(to*.columns[id]&, to_row),427                kayan_column_row(from*.columns[id]&, from_row), from*.columns[id].size);428        }429    }430    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);431    slot*.table = to_index;432    slot*.row = cast(to_row, u32);433}434 435// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------436// The byte layer, for tools437// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------438 439// e's component `id` as its bytes: an empty slice if e is dead or has no such440// component. The typed layer is for game code, which knows its types; this is441// for tools that work from reflect records instead.442kayan_get_bytes: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> []u8 = {443    none: []u8 = {};444    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || id >= w*.component_count) {445        return none;446    }447    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));448    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);449    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {450        return none;451    }452    c: *kayan_column = t*.columns[id]&;453    row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);454    all: []u8 = c*.data[0..t*.count * c*.size];455    return all[row * c*.size..(row + 1) * c*.size];456}457 458// Give e component `id`, with `value` for its bytes: 2.6's add, by id instead459// of by type, because a command holds its value as bytes.460kayan_add_id: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32, value: []const u8) -> kayan_status = {461    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {462        return kayan_status.dead;463    }464    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;465    if (!kayan_table_has(kayan_table_at(w, from), id)) {466        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, id));467    }468    bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);469    if (value.length != bytes.length) {470        printfmt("kayan: a {}-byte value for a component of {} bytes\n", value.length, bytes.length);471        exit(1);472    }473    memcpy(bytes[0]&, value[0]&, bytes.length);474    return kayan_status.ok;475}476 477kayan_remove_id: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> kayan_status = {478    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {479        return kayan_status.dead;480    }481    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;482    if (!kayan_table_has(kayan_table_at(w, from), id)) {483        return kayan_status.missing;484    }485    kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_without(w, from, id));486    return kayan_status.ok;487}488 489// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------490// The typed layer491// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------492 493// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed494// view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. The pointer is495// good until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.496kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> *T = {497    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {498        return null;499    }500    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));501    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, slot*.table);502    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {503        return null;504    }505    rows: []T = kayan_slice<T>(t);506    return rows[cast(slot*.row, u64)]&;507}508 509kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {510    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;511}512 513// Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does514// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.515kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {516    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {517        return kayan_status.dead;518    }519    p: *T = kayan_get<T>(w, e);520    if (p == null) {521        return kayan_status.missing;522    }523    p* = value;524    return kayan_status.ok;525}526 527// Give e a T, or take its T away: the byte procs, with the type turned into an528// id and the value into its bytes.529kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {530    bytes: ^const u8 = cast(value&, ^const u8);531    return kayan_add_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>(), bytes[0..sizeof(T)]);532}533 534kayan_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {535    return kayan_remove_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>());536}537 538// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose539// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to540// the live count.541kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> u64 = {542    problems: u64 = 0;543    rows: u64 = 0;544    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {545        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));546        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {547            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];548            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {549                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);550                problems += 1;551                continue;552            }553            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots&, cast(e.index, u64));554            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {555                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",556                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);557                problems += 1;558            }559        }560        rows += t*.count;561    }562    if (rows != w*.live) {563        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);564        problems += 1;565    }566    return problems;567}568 569kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {570    printf("{");571    first: b32 = true;572    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {573        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {574            printf(first ? "%s" : " %s", w*.infos[id]*.name);575            first = false;576        }577    }578    printf("}");579}580 581kayan_print_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, ti: u32) -> void = {582    t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);583    printf("    table %u ", ti);584    kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);585    printf(":");586    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {587        printf(" %u:%u", t*.entities[row].index, t*.entities[row].generation);588    }589    printf("\n");590}591 592kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {593    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {594        kayan_print_table(w, ti);595    }596}597 598// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------599// The inspector: reflect records, no component types600// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------601 602kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {603    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {604        printf("    ");605    }606}607 608// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name.609kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {610    if (strcmp(type_name, "f32") == 0) {611        printf("%.2f", cast(cast(at[0]&, *const f32)*, f64));612    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "u32") == 0) {613        printf("%u", cast(at[0]&, *const u32)*);614    } else if (strcmp(type_name, "i32") == 0) {615        printf("%d", cast(at[0]&, *const i32)*);616    } else {617        printf("<%s>", type_name);618    }619}620 621// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented622// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and623// size, both from the reflect record.624kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {625    fields: ^const reflect_field = reflect_fields(type);626    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {627        f: *const reflect_field = fields[i]&;628        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {629            continue;630        }631        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];632        kayan_indent(depth);633        printf("%s:", f*.name);634        info: *const reflect = f*.info;635        if (info != null && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {636            printf("\n");637            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);638        } else {639            printf(" ");640            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);641            printf("\n");642        }643    }644}645 646kayan_inspect: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {647    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {648        printfmt("{}:{} (dead)\n", e.index, e.generation);649        return;650    }651    printf("%u:%u ", e.index, e.generation);652    signature: u64 = kayan_signature(w, e);653    kayan_print_signature(w, signature);654    printf("\n");655    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {656        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {657            info: *const reflect = w*.infos[id];658            printf("    %s\n", info*.name);659            bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);660            kayan_print_fields(info, bytes, 2);661        }662    }663}664 665// Every table: rows in use out of room, and per column its row size and its666// bytes in use out of bytes allocated. The memory a table holds and does not667// use is the cost of doubling on growth.668kayan_print_layout: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {669    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables.length, u32); ti += 1) {670        t: *kayan_table = kayan_table_at(w, ti);671        printf("table %u ", ti);672        kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);673        printf(": %u rows, room for %u\n", cast(t*.count, u32), cast(t*.capacity, u32));674        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {675            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {676                size: u64 = t*.columns[id].size;677                printf("    %-9s %2u bytes a row, %4u of %4u bytes in use\n", w*.infos[id]*.name, cast(size, u32),678                    cast(size * t*.count, u32), cast(size * t*.capacity, u32));679            }680        }681    }682}683 684// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------685// Queries686// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------687 688// The tables a system runs over: every table whose signature has all of `all`689// and none of `none`, kept by index. Tables are only ever added, at the end of690// w.tables, so the query remembers how many it has checked and, brought up to691// date, looks at the new ones only.692kayan_query: struct = {693    all: u64;694    none: u64;695    tables: vec<u32>;696    checked: u64;697}698 699kayan_query_init: proc(all: u64, none: u64) -> kayan_query = {700    q: kayan_query = {};701    q.all = all;702    q.none = none;703    return q;704}705 706kayan_matches: proc(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {707    return (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0;708}709 710// Check the tables made since the query last looked. With none new, this is711// one comparison, so call it before every walk.712kayan_query_update: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {713    for (ti: u64 = q*.checked; ti < w*.tables.length; ti += 1) {714        if (kayan_matches(kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32))*.signature, q*.all, q*.none)) {715            _ = vec<u32>append(w*.arena, q*.tables&, cast(ti, u32));716        }717    }718    q*.checked = w*.tables.length;719}720 721// The query's i-th table. Like any table pointer, good until a table is made.722kayan_query_table: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query, i: u64) -> *kayan_table = {723    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables&, i)*);724}725 726// How many entities the query matches: the rows of its tables.727kayan_query_count: proc(w: *kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> u64 = {728    kayan_query_update(w, q);729    n: u64 = 0;730    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables.length; i += 1) {731        n += kayan_query_table(w, q, i)*.count;732    }733    return n;734}735 736kayan_print_query: proc(w: *kayan_world, name: ^const char, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {737    kayan_query_update(w, q);738    printf("%s: all ", name);739    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.all);740    printf(", none ");741    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.none);742    printfmt("; tables: {}, entities: {}\n", q*.tables.length, kayan_query_count(w, q));743    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables.length; i += 1) {744        kayan_print_table(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables&, i)*);745    }746}747 748// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------749// Commands750// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------751 752// A spawn that has been recorded and not applied. There is no entity yet, so753// this is the spawn command's place in the list; give it components with754// kayan_pending_set.755kayan_pending: struct = {756    command: u32;757}758 759kayan_defer: proc(w: *kayan_world, c: kayan_command) -> u32 = {760    index: u32 = cast(w*.commands.length, u32);761    _ = vec<kayan_command>append(w*.frame&, w*.commands&, c);762    return index;763}764 765// A copy of `value`, as bytes, in the frame arena.766kayan_defer_value: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, value: T) -> []u8 = {767    data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push(w*.frame&, sizeof(T), alignof(T)), ^u8);768    memcpy(data, value&, sizeof(T));769    return data[0..sizeof(T)];770}771 772kayan_defer_spawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, signature: u64) -> kayan_pending = {773    p: kayan_pending = {};774    p.command = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.spawn, .signature = signature });775    return p;776}777 778kayan_pending_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, p: kayan_pending, value: T) -> void = {779    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .spawn = p.command + 1, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),780        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(w, value) });781}782 783kayan_defer_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {784    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.despawn, .entity = e });785}786 787kayan_defer_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> void = {788    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),789        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(w, value) });790}791 792kayan_defer_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {793    _ = kayan_defer(w, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.remove, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>() });794}795 796// One applied command. The components given to a new entity are part of its797// spawn line, so they are not printed on their own.798kayan_print_command: proc(w: *kayan_world, c: *kayan_command, status: kayan_status) -> void = {799    if (c*.spawn != 0 && status == kayan_status.ok) {800        return;801    }802    printfmt("    {} ", c*.kind);803    if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {804        kayan_print_signature(w, c*.signature);805        printf(" -> ");806    } else if (c*.kind != kayan_command_kind.despawn) {807        printf("%s, ", w*.infos[c*.id]*.name);808    }809    printf("%u:%u", c*.entity.index, c*.entity.generation);810    if (status != kayan_status.ok) {811        printfmt(": skipped, {}", status);812    }813    printf("\n");814}815 816// Apply the frame's commands in the order they were recorded, then let them817// all go at once. A command for an entity that died after it was recorded818// (despawned by an earlier command, most likely) does nothing, and is counted.819kayan_flush: proc(w: *kayan_world) -> void = {820    for (i: u64 = 0; i < w*.commands.length; i += 1) {821        c: *kayan_command = vec<kayan_command>at(w*.commands&, i);822        if (c*.spawn != 0) {823            c*.entity = vec<kayan_command>at(w*.commands&, cast(c*.spawn - 1, u64))*.entity;824        }825        status: kayan_status = kayan_status.ok;826        if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {827            c*.entity = kayan_spawn(w, c*.signature);828        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.despawn) {829            status = kayan_despawn(w, c*.entity);830        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.add) {831            status = kayan_add_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id, c*.value);832        } else {833            status = kayan_remove_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id);834        }835        if (status == kayan_status.ok) {836            w*.applied += 1;837        } else {838            w*.skipped += 1;839        }840        if (w*.trace) {841            kayan_print_command(w, c, status);842        }843    }844    w*.commands = {};845    memops_arena_clear(w*.frame&);846}847 848// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------849// Systems850// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------851 852// What a system gets for each table it runs on: the world, the table, and the853// frame's time step. One struct rather than three parameters, so that adding854// to it later changes no system's signature.855kayan_iter: struct = {856    world: *kayan_world;857    table: *kayan_table;858    dt: f32;859    ctx: *void;860}861 862kayan_system_proc: alias = *proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void;863 864// A system: a name, the query that finds its tables, and the proc run on each865// of those tables that has rows. `tables` and `rows` count what it has run866// over. `ctx` is handed to the proc as is: whatever the system needs beyond867// its own tables, such as another query, or the game's state.868kayan_system: struct = {869    name: ^const char;870    query: kayan_query;871    run: kayan_system_proc;872    ctx: *void;873    tables: u64;874    rows: u64;875}876 877kayan_system_init: proc(name: ^const char, all: u64, none: u64, run: kayan_system_proc, ctx: *void) -> kayan_system = {878    s: kayan_system = {};879    s.name = name;880    s.query = kayan_query_init(all, none);881    s.run = run;882    s.ctx = ctx;883    return s;884}885 886// One frame: every system in order, each over every table it matches that has887// rows, then the commands they recorded. A system sees every value the888// systems before it wrote this frame, and no structural change until the889// next.890kayan_progress: proc(w: *kayan_world, systems: []kayan_system, dt: f32) -> void = {891    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems.length; s += 1) {892        sys: *kayan_system = systems[s]&;893        kayan_query_update(w, sys*.query&);894        for (i: u64 = 0; i < sys*.query.tables.length; i += 1) {895            it: kayan_iter = {};896            it.world = w;897            it.table = kayan_query_table(w, sys*.query&, i);898            it.dt = dt;899            it.ctx = sys*.ctx;900            if (it.table*.count > 0) {901                sys*.tables += 1;902                sys*.rows += it.table*.count;903                sys*.run(it&);904            }905        }906    }907    kayan_flush(w);908}909 910kayan_print_schedule: proc(w: *kayan_world, systems: []kayan_system) -> void = {911    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems.length; s += 1) {912        kayan_print_query(w, systems[s].name, systems[s].query&);913    }914}915 916// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------917// The program918// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------919 920// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------921// The game922// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------923 924// What the game's systems share: the drones, for the systems that look for925// them, and the score. Systems get it through their ctx.926game: struct = {927    drones: kayan_query;928    time: f32;929    fired: u32;930    hits: u32;931    fires: u32;932    kills: u32;933    breaches: u32;934    came: u32;935}936 937// Kernels: plain loops over plain slices, as in 3.2.938integrate: proc(ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void = {939    for (i: u64 = 0; The dojo · thirteen building blocks

The dojo

dojo/README.md

An ECS is mostly a few small building blocks put together. None of them is specific to an ECS: a renderer's texture handles are a slot map, a particle system is swap-remove over packed arrays, undo and network replication are command buffers. The course meets each block for the first time in the middle of building something bigger, which is why its chapters can feel dense. The dojo takes the blocks out and gives each one two halves:

  • a playground, to understand it: a small program that runs the block step by step and draws its insides, with one switch at the top that breaks it the way it most often breaks. Step through it in a debugger, flip the switch, watch what goes wrong.
  • a kata, to own it: you write the block yourself, and a harness checks it. Reading and stepping through code feels like learning, but writing it from a blank page, getting it wrong, and doing it again a few days later is what makes it yours.
blockwhat it isin the course
1free list and generationshandles that are safe to keep after what they name is gone1.2, 1.3
2swap-remove and the back-referencevalues packed with no holes, found by id: a sparse set1.4, 2.3, 2.6
3the slot map1 and 2 together: handles into packed values1.4, 2.4
4a type-erased columnan array of any type as bytes, viewed as a typed slice2.2, 2.3, 2.5
5a command bufferstructural changes recorded now and applied later3.3, 3.4
6bitsetsa set of components in a u64: has, all of, none of2.1, 3.1
7an arenapush, push, clear: memory for things that die togetherevery chapter
8index, not pointerlinks that stay right when their storage moves2.2, 2.4, 2.5
9interningfind or make, by key: a hash table that hands out dense ids2.4
10memoized edgesa slow lookup done once, then remembered on the edge2.6
11a reflection walkreading, writing and comparing any value through its type's record2.7
12a watermarklooking only at what was added since last time3.1
13a dispatch tablebehaviour as data: the schedule as a list of functions3.2

Do 1 to 5 in order the first time: 3 is 1 and 2 put together, and 5 applies its commands to something like 3. 6 to 13 come in the order the course meets them and stand on their own, except that 9, 10 and 12 work on 6's signatures. Any of them can come before the course, alongside it, or after it.

Each block

dojo/3.slot_map/
  README.md              the block, its invariant, the levels, the variations
  play_slot_map.rin      the playground
  harness.rin            fixed: a scenario, then a fuzz run against a model
  level1.rin ... 3.rin   where a kata starts
  solution.rin           the reference; don't peek
  kata.rin               yours: made by `start`, ignored by git

The harness doesn't know how your kata works, only what it must do. First it runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random operations from a seed against a simple model of the right answers, and checks after each one. A failure says which operation, which seed, and how to stop just before it in a debugger.

Levels, so the reps get harder:

  1. One function in an otherwise finished file: the one with the idea in it, usually the one people forget.
  2. Every function body, with the fields and signatures given.
  3. A blank page, with only a list of what the harness calls.
  4. Variations: the same harness, different insides, listed in each block's README.

Each README gives a target time for levels 1 to 3.

Watching a playground

python tools/dojo.py play slot_map

A playground runs one scenario, one operation per line of main, and prints what changed after each, so it works without a debugger. In one, put a breakpoint on a line of main and step over the operations. Where the block has slots there are only a few of them, in fixed arrays, so the watch window shows the whole state. From block 6 on, a verify proc runs after every operation, checks the block's invariant, and says what broke; a breakpoint inside its failure branch stops at the first operation that breaks it.

The switch is a global b32, read each time it's used, so besides editing it and running again, you can flip it mid-run: stop where the playground's header says, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue. rin writes C, and the global keeps its name, so in gdb:

(gdb) break handles_free
(gdb) run
(gdb) set var bump_on_free = 0
(gdb) continue

Doing reps

python tools/dojo.py                      the blocks, your reps, and what is due
python tools/dojo.py play slot_map        the playground
python tools/dojo.py start slot_map 2     a fresh kata.rin from level 2; the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py slot_map             build the harness with your kata.rin and run it

A block can be named by its number, its name or the start of its name: 3, slot_map and slot are the same. While the kata fails, fix it and run it again. When it passes, the time since start goes into dojo/log.md, and the block is due again 1, 3, 7, 14 and then 30 days after each pass. python tools/dojo.py with no arguments says what is due. Spacing reps out is what makes them stick, much more than doing many in one day.

start won't overwrite a kata.rin you've changed unless you add --force. Your log is a plain markdown table; commit it or don't.

When a kata fails, the harness says where:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

Run that binary under a debugger with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here. It stops just before the failing operation, with your structure in the state that leads to the failure. If the harness crashes instead, on a vec index past the end say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running. --seed N reruns a different fuzz run, and --sanitize builds with AddressSanitizer and UBSan, which block 4's column of raw bytes is exactly what they're for.

How it's built

Every kata file is a whole program. Yours, the solution and each level import what they use, then the harness, which has main:

import "std/memops.rin"
import "std/vec.rin"
import "std/option.rin"
import "../dojo.rin"
import "harness.rin"

So any of them builds on its own, rin compile dojo/3.slot_map/solution.rin for instance, and rin check or your editor finds every name it uses. Only the harness doesn't build alone: it calls the procs the kata defines. A file imported twice is read once, so the kata and the harness both importing dojo.rin is fine. dojo/dojo.rin holds what every harness shares: dojo_handle and dojo_status, the run's settings, the random number generator, and the reporting. The runner builds kata.rin the way tools/check.py does, rin compile and then the C compiler, with the warnings for unused parameters and locals off, since a kata in progress is full of them.

python tools/check.py dojo keeps the dojo honest: every solution must build on its own, pass its harness and print its harness.expected, level 1 must fail (its gap must be a gap), level 2 must compile, and the playgrounds must print their .expected. The harnesses were also checked against broken solutions, the mistakes each block is about, and catch each one.

The same dojo exists in Rust, in rust-dod. The random number generator is the same, so a seed is the same run in both, and the playgrounds print the same thing, except where block 4's column gets its memory: an arena in rin, a Vec in Rust. The katas differ where the languages do: block 7's arena hands out offsets in Rust and addresses in rin, and in block 8 only rin can keep a pointer across a move, so only rin's switch does; each README says how.

The dojo · block 1

Free list and generations

dojo/1.free_list/play_free_list.rin

Handles name things that come and go: entities, textures, sounds, network connections. A handle is two numbers, index:generation, and two small ideas make it safe to keep:

  • A free list. A freed index is reused before a new one is made, so the arrays an index points into stay as long as the most things ever alive at once, not the most things ever made.
  • A generation per index. Freeing bumps the index's generation, so every handle made for the old life stops matching. A reused index can't be mistaken for whatever had it before.

The invariant: a handle is alive exactly when its generation is the one its index holds now. A free index already holds its next generation, which no handle has yet, so "free" needs no flag of its own. Every index is either alive or on the free list, once. Generations start at 1, so a zeroed handle, {}, is never alive.

In the course: 1.2 builds the free list and meets its bug, 1.3 adds generations, and every later chapter keeps both.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play free_list

It allocates four handles, frees two, reuses one, and draws both arrays after each step:

free b, then d: their generations go up now, before anyone reuses them
    generations  0:1  1:2  2:1  3:2
    free list    [1 3]
alloc e: alloc takes from the end of the free list, so index 3, in its next life
    e 3:2

Step through it: break on handles_alloc and handles_free, and watch generations and free change. Then flip the switch at the top, bump_on_free, to 0 and run it again. The freed b is still alive, the reused index comes back with the old generation so d and e are the same handle, and freeing d again frees e and puts index 3 on the free list twice. That's the bug from 1.2, in four lines of output.

Do reps: the kata

You write handles, an allocator of handles:

handles_alloc: proc(h: *handles) -> dojo_handle = {
handles_free: proc(h: *handles, e: dojo_handle) -> dojo_status = {
handles_alive: proc(h: *handles, e: dojo_handle) -> b32 = {

plus handles_init, handles_live (how many are alive) and handles_slots (how many indices have been handed out). dojo_handle and dojo_status are given, in dojo/dojo.rin, and the arrays are vec<u32>s from the arena handles_init is given.

levelyou writetarget
1handles_free, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given8:00
3the whole file, from a blank page10:00
python tools/dojo.py start free_list 2      kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py free_list              your kata.rin against the harness

The harness first runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random allocs and frees from a seed, against a model that remembers, per index, the last generation handed out and whether the index is free. It checks what your allocator does, not how: a generation is never handed out twice for an index, a freed index is reused before a new one is made, and handles_alive agrees with the model for every handle, live and dead. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the free list inside the dead slots: no free vec, but a next_free field in each slot that is only meaningful while the slot is free, and a first_free in handles. What marks the end of the list?
  • 16-bit generations in the slots, stored as u16, that wrap from 65535 back to 1, never 0. What does wrapping give up?
  • Reuse in first-in, first-out order, so an index rests as long as possible before it comes back. Why might a game want that?

When it fails

FAIL at operation 266 (seed 1): after free, alive() is still true for 43:1
    debug it: build/dojo/free_list/harness --seed 1 --stop 266
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py free_list built that harness with your kata. Run it under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/free_list/harness --seed 1 --stop 266, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

If the harness crashes instead, on an index past the end of a vec say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/1.free_list/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/1.free_list/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 2

Swap-remove and the back-reference

dojo/2.swap_remove/play_swap_remove.rin

Systems loop over values, so values are kept packed: one after another, no holes, nothing to skip. Removing one from the middle would leave a hole, so the last value moves into it instead. That's swap-remove: one copy, however many values there are, at the price of order.

Values move, so an id can't be the position of its value. Two arrays keep track:

  • sparse, by id: rows[id] says which row id's value is in now;
  • packed, by row: ids[row] is the id that owns the row. This is the back-reference: when the last row moves into a hole, it says whose entry in rows to fix.

The whole structure is what EnTT calls a sparse set.

The invariant: the rows are packed, and the two arrays point at each other: for every row, rows[ids[row]] names that row, and an id with no value has no row.

In the course: 1.4 packs entities into rows this way, 2.3 does it for every column of a table, and 2.6 does it when an entity moves between tables.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play swap_remove

It inserts four values, removes one from the middle, and draws both sides after each step:

remove 7, in row 1: the last row, 5's, moves into the hole
    row         0    1    2
    ids         3    5    1
    values     30   50   10
    rows    1->2  3->0  5->1  (id -> row)

Step through it: break on sparse_set_remove, and watch ids and rows as the last row moves. Then flip the switch at the top, fix_back_reference, to 0 and run it again. Id 5's row still says 3, past the end, so get 5 finds nothing. Then insert 9 puts 9's value in row 3, and get 5 returns 90, another id's value, with nothing to say it's wrong. That's the bug every packed array invites, and the reason the back-reference exists.

Do reps: the kata

You write sparse_set. The heart of it is sparse_set_remove:

sparse_set_remove: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32) -> option<u64> = {
    if (sparse_set_get(s, id) == null) {
        return option<u64>none();
    }
    entry: *u32 = vec<u32>at(s*.rows&, cast(id, u64));
    row: u64 = cast(entry* - 1, u64);
    entry* = 0;
    value: u64 = vec<u64>at(s*.values&, row)*;
    last_value: u64 = vec<u64>pop(s*.values&);
    last_id: u32 = vec<u32>pop(s*.ids&);
    if (row < s*.values.length) {
        vec<u64>at(s*.values&, row)* = last_value;
        vec<u32>at(s*.ids&, row)* = last_id;
        vec<u32>at(s*.rows&, cast(last_id, u64))* = cast(row, u32) + 1;
    }
    return option<u64>some(value);
}

That's the reference, so don't read it before level 1 if you'd rather not know. vec has no swap-remove of its own: the last element is popped, and written over the hole unless the hole was the last row. The full API:

sparse_set_insert: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32, value: u64) -> option<u64> = {
sparse_set_get: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32) -> *u64 = {

plus sparse_set_init, sparse_set_len, sparse_set_values (the packed values, in row order) and sparse_set_ids (ids[row] owns values[row]).

levelyou writetarget
1sparse_set_remove, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given8:00
3the whole file, from a blank page10:00
python tools/dojo.py start swap_remove 2
python tools/dojo.py swap_remove

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts and removes over a small range of ids, so the same ids come and go many times, against a plain array from id to value. Every 64 operations it checks the packed rows themselves: as many as the model has, and each row's owner holding exactly that row's value. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Where Rust's kata returns Option<T> and has get_mut, this one uses std's option<u64> for what insert and remove give back (the old value, or none), and one sparse_set_get that returns a pointer to the value, null for none, to read or to change, the way kayan_get<T> does in the course. rows[id] holds the row plus one, so a new entry, 0, means "no row", and growing rows is appending zeros.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Pages: rows split into pages of 64 ids, each page made only when an id in it gets a value: a vec<^u32> of pages, null for a page not made yet. A big id no longer means a big rows. This is what EnTT does.
  • A sentinel: rows[id] holds the row itself, with 0xFFFFFFFF for "no row". What does growing rows cost now?
  • A flag: a second vec<b32>, has_row, beside rows. Compare the memory with the plus-one encoding.

And one that fails on purpose: a remove that keeps order, shifting every later row down and fixing each one's back-reference. The scenario stops it at the first ids line. Why does the harness insist on swap-remove's order, and what does keeping order cost?

When it fails

A forgotten back-reference often shows up as a crash in a sparse_set_get that is right, not in the sparse_set_remove that is wrong: get follows the stale row past the end, and vec<u64>at stops the program.

rin runtime: vec index out of bounds
the harness crashed in the scenario, after the last step printed above

The last step printed is the last that passed, so the bug is in what ran after it. In the fuzz run, the runner runs the harness again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running when it crashed. A failed check gives the operation and the seed:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/2.swap_remove/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/2.swap_remove/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 3

The slot map

dojo/3.slot_map/play_slot_map.rin

Dojos 1 and 2, put together. Values live packed in rows, so a loop over them has no holes (dojo 2). The rest of the program keeps handles, which survive rows moving and say when their value is gone (dojo 1). In between is a slot per index:

handle 1:2  ->  slots[1] { generation 2, row 0 }  ->  values[0]

A lookup is two steps: the handle's generation must be the slot's, and the slot says the row. A remove is both dojos' work: bump the generation and free the index, then swap-remove the row and fix the slot of whoever moved. Game engines keep textures, meshes and sounds this way, and it is the ECS's entity index.

The invariant: dojo 1's and dojo 2's together. A handle is alive exactly when its generation is its slot's; the rows are packed; and for every row, the slot of the row's handle points back at that row.

In the course: 1.4 is a slot map with an entity's components as its value, and every chapter after keeps it, with a table number added to the slot in 2.4.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play slot_map

It keeps three textures, removes one, reuses its index, and draws the slots and the rows after each step:

remove stone: free index 1 in its next life, and water moves into row 1
    slots    0: generation 1, row 0 | 1: generation 2, free | 2: generation 1, row 1
    rows     0:1 grass | 2:1 water

Step through it: break on slot_map_remove, and watch the slot, the free list and the rows change in that order. Then flip the switch at the top, check_generation, to 0 and run it again. The removed stone still finds slot 1, and reads whatever is in slot 1's row now: water, then lava. In a game, that's a sound that plays the wrong sample, or a mesh drawn with another mesh's texture.

Do reps: the kata

You write slot_map. Its two-step lookup:

slot_map_get: proc(m: *slot_map, h: dojo_handle) -> *u64 = {
    if (!slot_map_contains(m, h)) {
        return null;
    }
    row: u32 = vec<slot_map_slot>at(m*.slots&, cast(h.index, u64))*.row;
    return vec<u64>at(m*.values&, cast(row, u64));
}

and the API around it:

slot_map_insert: proc(m: *slot_map, value: u64) -> dojo_handle = {
slot_map_remove: proc(m: *slot_map, h: dojo_handle) -> option<u64> = {

plus slot_map_init, slot_map_contains, slot_map_len, slot_map_values (the packed values, in row order) and slot_map_handles (handles[row] owns values[row]). dojo_handle comes from dojo/dojo.rin, as in dojo 1.

1slot_map_remove, in an otherwise finished file3:00

Level 3 is the one to come back to. Once you can write a slot map from a blank page in fifteen minutes, dojos 1 and 2 are in your hands too.

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts, removes, reads and writes against a model that keeps, per index, the last generation handed out, whether the index is free, and its value. It checks dojo 1's rules for the handles (a generation never handed out twice for an index, a freed index reused before a new one is made, a removed handle never alive again) and dojo 2's for the rows (packed, each row's handle holding that row's value). The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. As in dojo 2, slot_map_remove gives back std's option<u64> and slot_map_get returns a pointer, null for a dead handle, to read or to change the value; Rust's kata has get and get_mut. A zeroed handle, {}, is never alive, since generations start at 1, and the scenario checks that too.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Free list inside the slots: a next_free: u32 in each slot, only meaningful while the slot is free, and a first_free in slot_map. No free vec. What marks the end of the list?
  • One look at the slot: slot_map_remove without slot_map_contains: fetch the slot once, check its generation, and use it. How many times does the reference look the slot up?
  • **slot_map_retain(m, keep)**, with keep a proc(h: dojo_handle, value: u64) -> b32: remove every value it rejects, in one pass, keeping the rows packed. Which way should the loop walk? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 233 (seed 1): remove(33:1) returned 214, the model says 210
    debug it: build/dojo/slot_map/harness --seed 1 --stop 233
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

The wrong value usually means a slot pointing at the wrong row: an earlier remove moved a row and didn't fix its slot. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, then look at the slot of the handle being removed.

If the harness crashes instead, on a row past the end of values say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/3.slot_map/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/3.slot_map/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 4

A type-erased column

dojo/4.column/play_column.rin

A column is one component's rows, kept as bytes. It doesn't know the type it holds, only how many bytes make a row and how they must be aligned. That is enough to grow, to zero a new row, and to move the last row into a hole, which is everything a table does to its columns. The type comes back only at the edge: a typed view turns the bytes into a []T, for a T of the column's size and alignment.

Two things make it work:

  • Aligned storage. The bytes come from the arena aligned to the column's alignment, so every row of the type lands where that type may live.
  • Growing by a factor. A full column doubles, so the copies that growing costs add up to about one per push, however many rows there are.

The invariant: the column holds count rows of size bytes each, packed from the start of a block aligned to align, with room for capacity rows. A typed view is only handed out for a T of exactly size bytes, aligned to exactly align. The type must also be plain data, a struct of numbers with no pointers in it, since a column copies rows as bytes; that part is on you.

In the course: 2.2 builds the column, 2.3 puts columns in a table, and 2.5 is about what happens to a pointer into a column that grows.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play column

It fills a column of vec2s and draws each row's bytes next to the value they are:

push 3 zeroed rows, and write each through the typed view
    capacity 4, 3 rows in use, 32 bytes of storage
    row 0  00 00 80 3f 00 00 00 40   as a vec2 (1, 2)
    row 1  00 00 40 40 00 00 80 40   as a vec2 (3, 4)

Then it grows the column, swap-removes from it, and asks for the rows as two wrong types. Step through it: break on column_grow and watch the rows move to the new block. The old block stays in the arena, unused, so a slice taken before the grow still points somewhere valid, and anything written through it is lost without a word.

The switch at the top, grow_by_doubling, picks how a full column grows. Set it to 0, so the column grows by one row, and run it again. The last line is the point: the same 1000 pushes copy 1,020 rows when the column doubles, and 499,494 when it grows by one.

1000 pushes into a u32 column, growing by doubling
    9 grows, 1020 rows copied to make room

Do reps: the kata

You write column. Its bytes come from the arena, aligned to the column's alignment:

        data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(c*.arena, c*.size * capacity, c*.align), ^u8);

and the typed view is a generic proc that checks the type before it casts:

column_slice: proc<T>(c: *column) -> []T = {

plus column_init(c, arena, size, align), column_len, column_capacity, column_push_zeroed (a zeroed row at the end, and its row number), column_swap_remove(c, row), and column_row(c, row), a row's bytes as a []u8.

levelyou writetarget
1column_slice, the typed view, in an otherwise finished file3:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given15:00
3the whole file, from a blank page20:00
python tools/dojo.py start column 2         kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py column                 your kata.rin against the harness
python tools/dojo.py column --sanitize      the same with AddressSanitizer and UBSan

The harness first runs a short scenario: three vec3s written through column_slice and read back as bytes, a swap-remove, a column aligned to 16, and a column of tags, zero-byte rows. Then it runs 20,000 random pushes, writes and swap-removes, shared between four row types: 3 bytes aligned to 1, a u32, a 12-byte vec3, and a 16-byte vec4 aligned to 16. Each is checked against a vec of that type, through column_slice and through column_row, along with the alignment of every view, and that a full column grows by at least half. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

--sanitize is worth the wait here. A row copied one byte too far, or a memcpy from a block that was never allocated, often works on your machine. AddressSanitizer and UBSan don't let it happen by luck. (They need the C compiler's sanitizer runtime; with clang that may be missing, so try CC=gcc.)

What the harness can't check is a refusal: a column read as the wrong type should stop the program with a message, and so should a row past the rows in use, and a harness that stops can't go on to the next step. Try them by hand in a scratch program: read a vec3 column as a u32, then as a struct of twelve u8s (the right size, aligned to 1), then ask for column_row(c&, 2) of a two-row column. Each should stop with a message that says what was wrong. rust-dod's harness checks these, because Rust can catch a panic.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Grow by 1.5 instead of 2. Count the grows and the rows copied for 1000 pushes. Why do some allocators prefer it?
  • Allocate with **memops_arena_realloc_** instead of a new block and a memcpy. When does it move the rows, and when can it extend the block in place?
  • Shrink: when a swap-remove leaves the column less than a quarter full, move the rows to a block of half the capacity. Why a quarter and not a half? (Push and remove one row, over and over, at the boundary.) In an arena, what does shrinking actually give back?

When it fails

FAIL at operation 11 (seed 1): the column was full at 4 rows and grew to 5; it should grow by at least half
    debug it: build/dojo/column/harness --seed 1 --stop 11
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py column built that harness with your kata. Run it under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/column/harness --seed 1 --stop 11, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

If the harness crashes instead, on a slice index past the end say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

"a slice" : "refused";134}135 136main: proc() -> i32 = {137    arena: memops_arena = {};138    memops_arena_initialize(arena&);139    c: column = {};140    column_init(c&, arena&, sizeof(vec2), alignof(vec2));141    printfmt("a column of vec2: {}-byte rows aligned to {}, kept in blocks from an arena\n", c.size, c.align);142 143    printfmt("push 3 zeroed rows, and write each through the typed view\n");144    for (i: u64 = 0; i < 1000; i += 1) {171        row: u64 = column_push_zeroed(big&);172        values: []u32 = column_slice<u32>(big&);173        values[row] = i;174    }175    if (grow_by_doubling) {176        printfmt("1000 pushes into a u32 column, growing by doubling\n");177    } else {178        printfmt("1000 pushes into a u32 column, growing by one row at a time\n");179    }180    printfmt("    {} grows, {} rows copied to make room\n", big.grows, big.copied);181    sum: u32 = 0;182    values: []u32 = column_slice<u32>(big&);183    for (i: u64 = 0; The dojo · block 5

A command buffer

dojo/5.commands/play_commands.rin

Systems walk tables, and while they walk, they decide to change which things exist: a bullet's time is up, a turret fires, a drone catches fire. Doing it on the spot breaks the walk. A despawn swap-removes, so the last row moves into the hole, behind the loop, and is never looked at. So a system records the change instead, as a command, and the frame applies every command, in order, once nothing is walking anything.

Three details make it work:

  • Pending spawns. A spawn has no handle until it is applied, so recording one hands back a pending number, and later commands in the same buffer can name the spawn by it.
  • Skipping the dead. Two systems may both despawn the same thing, or set a value on something an earlier command removed. Applied in order, the second finds a dead handle and is skipped. Generations make that one comparison.
  • A frame arena. After the buffer is applied its vecs are cleared, and keep their room, so once a game has run a few frames, recording a command allocates nothing.

The invariant: recording changes nothing but the buffer. Applying it has exactly the effect of running every command straight away, in the order it was recorded, with each pending number meaning the handle its spawn made.

In the course: 3.3 builds the buffer and shows the bug it fixes, and 3.4's game runs on it. The Advanced lesson 6 has one too.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play commands

A packed world of five things, and one frame of three systems. The expire system records a despawn for each thing whose life is up, the spawner records a replacement and sets its life through its pending number, and a second system despawns something the first already did. Then the buffer is applied:

apply the buffer, in the order it was recorded
    despawn 0:1: ok, 4:1 moves into 0:1's row
    despawn 2:1: ok, 3:1 moves into 2:1's row
    despawn 3:1: ok, it was the last row
    spawn with life 1: pending 0 is 3:2
    set pending 0 life 5: ok, 3:2 has life 5
    despawn 2:1: skipped, 2:1 is dead

Step through it: break on commands_apply and walk the list. Then flip the switch at the top, defer, to 0, so every system changes the world on the spot, and run it again. The expire system despawns 0:1, 4:1 moves into its row behind the loop, and when the loop ends, 3:1 is still there with no life:

things left with no life: none

becomes things left with no life: 3:1, moved behind the loop and never looked at. That's 3.3's bug.

Do reps: the kata

You write commands. A command names its target either way, a handle or a spawn of this buffer:

target: struct = {
    is_pending: b32;
    handle: dojo_handle;
    spawn: pending;
}

made by target_entity(h) or target_pending(p), so commands_set and commands_despawn take either:

commands_set: proc(c: *commands, t: target, value: u32) -> void = {
commands_apply: proc(c: *commands, w: *world) -> applied = {

plus commands_init, commands_spawn(c, value), which returns a pending, commands_despawn(c, t), and commands_len, the commands waiting. The world is given, in the harness: a generational store of numbers with world_spawn, world_despawn and world_set, where the last two return dojo_status.dead for a dead handle. commands_apply returns applied, the count of commands that changed something and of those that were skipped.

levelyou writetarget
1commands_apply, in an otherwise finished file3:00
2every proc body; the types and signatures are given15:00
3the whole file, from a blank page20:00
python tools/dojo.py start commands 2       kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py commands               your kata.rin against the harness

The harness first runs a short scenario: a set, a despawn, a spawn that reuses the despawned index, a set through the spawn's pending number, and two commands that find their target dead. Then a fuzz run, frame after frame: random commands recorded against live handles, dead handles and the frame's own pending spawns, then applied. A model runs the same commands straight away on a copy of the world from before the frame, and the harness checks the two worlds match, the applied and skipped counts match, and the buffer is empty afterwards. The copies live in a frame arena of the harness's own, cleared after every frame. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the spawned handles in the command list itself, as 3.3 does: a spawn command holds the handle commands_apply gives it, and a pending number finds its spawn through it. No spawned vec.
  • Record the whole buffer as **one vec<u8>**: a kind byte, then the command's fields as bytes. One allocation for any mix of commands, read back in order.
  • Keep the buffer in an arena of its own, and clear the arena after commands_apply instead of clearing the vecs, as lesson 6 does. What must not live in that arena?

When it fails

FAIL at operation 28 (seed 1): commands_apply returned applied 7, skipped 4, the model says applied 9, skipped 2
    debug it: build/dojo/commands/harness --seed 1 --stop 28
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py commands built that harness with your kata. Run it under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/commands/harness --seed 1 --stop 28, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

If the harness crashes instead, on a pending number past the spawns applied so far say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/5.commands/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/5.commands/level1.rin to level3.rin.

    despawn 0:1: ok, 4:1 moves into 0:1's row
    despawn 2:1: ok, 3:1 moves into 2:1's row
    despawn 3:1: ok, it was the last row
    spawn with life 1: pending 0 is 3:2
    set pending 0 life 5: ok, 3:2 has life 5
    despawn 2:1: skipped, 2:1 is dead
the world after the frame
    row 0  4:1  life 2
    row 1  1:1  life 3
    row 2  3:2  life 5
things left with no life: none
commands left in the buffer: 0

The dojo · block 6

Bitsets

dojo/6.bitset/play_bitset.rin

A set of small numbers, 0 to 63, fits in one u64: bit id is set when id is in the set. An ECS keeps what each kind of entity is made of this way, a signature with a bit per component, and a query as two sets: the ids a table must have, and the ids it must not. The questions an ECS asks all day are then one or two instructions each, however many components there are:

with(set, id)            set | (1 shl id)
without(set, id)         set & ~(1 shl id)
has(set, id)             (set & (1 shl id)) != 0
contains_all(set, all)   (set & all) == all
intersects(set, none)    (set & none) != 0

The same trick is a file's permissions, which of 64 workers are idle, and which chunks of a map are loaded.

The invariant: bit id is set exactly when id is in the set. Everything else follows from it: one set contains all of another when masking it with the other leaves the other whole, and two sets share an id when their AND isn't zero.

In the course: 2.1 gives each component a bit and each kind of entity a signature, 2.4 finds a table by its signature, 2.6 moves an entity by setting or clearing one bit, and 3.1 matches queries against tables with contains_all and intersects.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play bitset

It gives five kinds of thing a signature each, draws them as rows of bits, highest id first, and runs queries over them:

query move: all {position velocity}, none {frozen}
    all     00000011
    none    01000000
    player  00011111  matches
    drone   00001111  matches
    turret  00101101  no
    rock    00001001  no
    ghost   01001011  no

Read it by columns: a kind matches when it has a 1 under every 1 of all, and a 0 under every 1 of none. Then the drone is frozen and the ghost thaws, one bit each, and the same query gives a different answer. Each kind keeps its ids twice, as a signature and as a b32 per id, and verify checks the fast answer against the slow one after every step.

Step through it: break on matches, and watch set & wanted in the watch window, in binary. Then flip the switch at the top, all_not_any, to 0 and run it again. contains_all now asks whether the signature has any of the ids. The turret and the rock have a position, so both match the movement query, and the turret and the ghost each have half of what the think query wants:

    verify: turret matches, but it has no velocity

It's the most common bitset bug, and it compiles: the compiler has no idea which question you meant.

Do reps: the kata

You write procs over a u64. The one with the idea in it:

bitset_contains_all: proc(set: u64, wanted: u64) -> b32 = {
    return (set & wanted) == wanted;
}

and a query, built from it:

bitset_matches: proc(set: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {
    return bitset_contains_all(set, all) && !bitset_intersects(set, none);
}

plus bitset_bit (the set of id alone), bitset_with, bitset_without, bitset_has, bitset_intersects, bitset_count and bitset_ids, which writes the ids, smallest first, into a slice with room for 64 and returns how many. Ids are u32s, 0 to 63.

levelyou writetarget
1bitset_contains_all, in an otherwise finished file1:00
2every proc body; the signatures are given5:00
3the whole file, from a blank page6:00
python tools/dojo.py start bitset 2
python tools/dojo.py bitset

The harness runs the playground's kinds and queries as a scenario, then 20,000 random operations on a set: adding and taking away ids, and asking has, contains_all, intersects, matches, count and ids, against a model that keeps a b32 per id and answers one id at a time. The sets it asks about are mostly made from the set itself: part of it, part of it plus one more id, or ids it doesn't have, so the answers aren't nearly always false. Ids go up to 63, so a shift done in 32 bits shows. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. rin binds & tighter than ==, as Rust does, so set & wanted == wanted means what it says; in C it would be set & (wanted == wanted). The reference keeps the parentheses anyway, for anyone reading it with C eyes. And rin gives a bare 1 the type its result is going to, so in a proc that returns a u64, 1 shl id is already a 64-bit shift. The 32-bit bug needs a u32 on the left, one: u32 = 1; one shl id, and --sanitize names it: UBSan reports a shift exponent too large for a 32-bit type.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Count without a loop over 64: set & (set - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Loop until the set is empty, one step per id rather than per bit.
  • **bitset_ids the same way**: low = set & (0 - set) is the lowest set bit alone, its id is the number of bits below it, bitset_count(low - 1), and clearing it moves on.
  • More than 64 components: a struct of two u64s, with id i at bit i % 64 of word i / 64, and the same procs. What does contains_all become? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 2 (seed 1): without({}, 57) gave {57}, it should give {}
    debug it: build/dojo/bitset/harness --seed 1 --stop 2
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one is set ^ bitset_bit(id): an XOR flips the bit, so taking away an id the set doesn't have puts it in. Sets print as their ids, smallest first. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/6.bitset/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/6.bitset/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 7

An arena

dojo/7.arena/play_arena.rin

Most of what a frame allocates dies with the frame: commands, scratch lists, text for the screen. An arena hands all of it out of one buffer and keeps one number, how much of the buffer is used. A push rounds that number up to the alignment asked for, hands out the address there, and moves the number past the new bytes. Nothing is freed on its own. A mark remembers the number, a rewind puts it back, and a clear sets it to 0: everything pushed since goes at once, in one store, with no list of what to free.

push(4, 4) with 1 used:   round 1 up to 4, hand out base + 4, used is now 8

For an align that is a power of two, rounding up is (used + align - 1) & ~(align - 1): adding align - 1 reaches the next multiple unless used is one already, and the mask drops what's past it.

The invariant: every push not yet let go of starts at a multiple of its alignment, ends at or before used, and stops before the next push starts; used never passes the end of the buffer.

In the course: everywhere. Every lesson allocates from a memops_arena, from 2.2's columns on, and never frees anything on its own. 3.3 adds a second arena for one frame's commands, cleared after they're applied, and kayan does the same in 6. This block is that arena, small enough to write in a few minutes.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play arena

It pushes things of different sizes and alignments into a 64-byte buffer, rewinds, fills it to the last byte, and clears it. After each step it draws the buffer, 16 bytes to a group: a letter for each byte of a push, - for padding, . for free.

push b: a u32 count, 4 bytes, align 4
    offset 4, used 8 of 64: 3 bytes of padding first
    a---bbbb........|................|................|................
...
rewind to the mark: e and f are gone at once
    a---bbbbcccccccc|dddddddddddddddd|................|................

Each push is filled with its letter, and verify checks after every step that each push is aligned, inside used, clear of the next, and still holds its letter. Step through it: break on bump_push and watch used. The buffer is a struct[align(16)], so an offset that is a multiple of 16 is an address that is one too.

Then flip the switch at the top, align_offsets, to 0 and run it again. Pushes are handed out at used as it is, packed with no padding, and the u32, the u64 and the 16-byte vector land at offsets 1, 5 and 13:

    verify: b is at offset 1, not a multiple of 4: its address isn't aligned

The playground only ever writes bytes, with memset, so nothing breaks yet. Read a u32 through a *u32 from there, though, and it's undefined behaviour in C, so in rin: on x86 it usually works, slower when it straddles two cache lines; an aligned SIMD load faults; and the optimiser is allowed to assume it never happens. --sanitize reports it, as UBSan's "misaligned address".

Do reps: the kata

You write bump, an arena over bytes it's given. It isn't called arena, since the one every lesson uses already has that name: memops_arena.

bump: struct = {
    base: ^u8;
    capacity: u64;
    // Bytes before `used` are handed out; bytes after it are free.
    used: u64;
}

Its one proc with an idea in it:

bump_push: proc(b: *bump, size: u64, align: u64) -> ^u8 = {

the address of size bytes at an offset from base that is a multiple of align, or null, changing nothing, when they would end past the last byte. Plus bump_init(b, base, capacity), bump_used, bump_capacity, bump_mark, bump_rewind(b, mark) and bump_clear.

python tools/dojo.py start arena 2

python tools/dojo.py arena --sanitize     the same with AddressSanitizer and UBSan

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random pushes, marks, rewinds and clears on a 256-byte buffer, against a model that keeps the used count and every push not yet let go of. Pushes are 1 to 24 bytes at alignments 1 to 16, with some sized to end exactly at the last byte and some one byte past it. Each push is filled with a pattern through the address it gave, and read back later, so a push that lands on another shows. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. bump_push hands out an address, as memops_arena_push does. rust-dod's kata hands out an offset instead, and bytes_mut(offset, len) to write through: a slice from push would borrow the whole arena for as long as it was kept, and the arena couldn't push again until it was gone. rin lets you keep the address, and keep it past a rewind too, which is the arena's one way to go wrong: an address from before a rewind or a clear points at bytes the next push will hand out again.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Align the address, not the offset: round cast(base, usize) + used up, and subtract base again. memops_arena does it this way. The answers are the same for the harness's buffers, which start 16-aligned; what changes for a buffer that doesn't?
  • **bump_push_zero**: the same, with the bytes zeroed. Rewind, push again, and read the bytes before zeroing: what's there? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)
  • Temporary scopes: bump_temp_begin(b) returns a record of the mark and bump_temp_end(t) rewinds to it, like memops_arena_temp_begin and _end. What goes wrong if two scopes end out of order? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: push 4 bytes, align 4: 3 bytes of padding first gave 1, it should give 4

No rounding up at all: the offset is used as it is. The fuzz run is what finds the rest:

FAIL at operation 29 (seed 1): push(12, 2) gave offset 59, which isn't a multiple of 2
    debug it: build/dojo/arena/harness --seed 1 --stop 29
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one rounds every alignment but 2, which the scenario never asks for. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, and step into bump_push.

If the harness crashes instead, on a write through an address outside the buffer say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running. --sanitize stops on the bad write itself.
