The dojo · block 8

Index, not pointer

dojo/8.index/play_index.rin

A linked list whose nodes live side by side in one vec, and link to each other by index: node 1's next is 0, a position in the vec, not an address. When the vec is full and grows, it moves: the nodes are copied to a bigger place, and the old one is let go. Every index is still right after the move, because an index says where a node is in the vec, wherever the vec is. A pointer says where the node is in memory, so it still points at the old place, and nothing tells you.

That's the whole idea, and it's everywhere in data-oriented code: an ECS keeps tables by index because making a table can move the others, a mesh keeps triangles as three vertex indices, a scene graph keeps a parent index. A freed node goes on a free list and is used again before the vec grows, as in dojo 1.

The invariant: walking next from the head visits every live node once and ends at the tail; each node's prev is the node before it; and a node's index names it from the moment it's made until it's removed, however many times the vec moves in between.

In the course: 2.4 keeps tables by index, because making a table can grow the tables vec and move every table. It's why a pointer into 2.2's columns goes stale when a column grows, and why 2.5 says to keep handles and borrow pointers only to use them.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play index

Memory in the playground is an array of 16 cells, small enough to see whole in a debugger, and the list takes 2 cells of it, then 4, then 8. It keeps node b two ways: by its index, and by a pointer to its node. Then the list fills up and moves, and the program writes to b:

push_back 30 as c: the list is full
    the list moves from cells 0..2 to cells 2..6
    c is node 2
...
write 21 into b through its index, 1: cell 3 now
    nodes    0: 10, prev -, next 1 | 1: 21, prev 0, next 2 | 2: 30, prev 1, next -
    list     10 21 30
    memory   0..2 old copy: 10 20 | 2..6 the list: 10 21 30 .

After every step verify walks the links and checks that every node holds what the program last wrote to it. Put a breakpoint on broken, which it calls when something is wrong.

Then break on the line that writes 21 into b, set use_index to 0 in the watch window, and continue. The write goes through the kept pointer, into the old copy, and the list never sees it:

write 21 into b through what was kept, cell 1: where b was before the move
    ...
    memory   0..2 old copy: 10 21 | 2..6 the list: 10 20 30 .
    verify: node 1 holds 20, but the program last wrote 21 to it

Nothing crashes, and AddressSanitizer stays quiet too: the old copy is still memory the program owns, as an arena's old blocks are until the arena is cleared. The write is simply lost.

Do reps: the kata

You write list. The idea is in list_remove: the two neighbours link to each other, past the node, and the node's index goes on the free list:

list_remove: proc(l: *list, node: u32) -> option<u64> = {
    n: *list_node = list_live(l, node);
    if (n == null) {
        return option<u64>none();
    }
    if (n*.prev != list_none) {
        list_at(l, n*.prev)*.next = n*.next;
    } else {
        l*.head = n*.next;
    }
    if (n*.next != list_none) {
        list_at(l, n*.next)*.prev = n*.prev;
    } else {
        l*.tail = n*.prev;
    }

and the kata holds itself to the playground's lesson, in list_insert_after:

// A new node between `node` and the one after it; list_none if `node` isn't
// in the list. Every pointer into the nodes is taken after list_take, which
// can move them.
list_insert_after: proc(l: *list, node: u32, value: u64) -> u32 = {

plus list_init, list_push_back, list_push_front, list_get, list_len, and the links to walk the list by: list_head, list_tail, list_next and list_prev. A link past either end is list_none, the largest u32, which no node ever gets.

levelyou writetarget
1list_remove, in an otherwise finished file3:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given12:00
3the whole file, from a blank page15:00
python tools/dojo.py start index 2
python tools/dojo.py index

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random pushes, inserts, removes, reads and writes against a model that keeps the live nodes in list order. After every operation it walks your list both ways, list_head to the end by list_next, and list_tail back by list_prev, so a link left wrong is caught by the operation that left it. The list grows to about a thousand nodes, moving many times, and every node is checked by the index it was given. A freed index must be handed out again before a new one is made. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Rust's kata has Option<u32> links; here a link is a u32, and list_none stands for none, as UINT32_MAX would in C. list_get returns a pointer, null for a node not in the list, to read or to change the value; Rust's kata has get and get_mut.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • The free list through the nodes: a freed node's next is the next free node, and the list keeps first_free: u32. No free vec.
  • **A pointer kept across list_take**, which fails on purpose: in list_insert_after, take list_live(l, node) once, before list_take, and write through it after. Which operation does the harness stop at, and where did the write go? Then put it back.
  • A list walker: list_each(l, visit), with visit a proc(node: u32, value: u64) -> void, called head to tail. (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 17 (seed 1): walking head to tail, list_next(3) gives 2, but 3 is the last of 3 nodes
    debug it: build/dojo/index/harness --seed 1 --stop 17
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

A link pointing somewhere it shouldn't is usually a node from the free list that kept its old links, or a neighbour that wasn't told about a change: an insert at the tail that didn't move the tail, a remove that fixed next but not prev, or a write through a pointer taken before the nodes moved. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, and look at the nodes the message names.

If the harness crashes instead, on a node past the end of the vec say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

An index alone can't tell a removed node from the new node that took its place: a is node 0, and so is e after it. That's dojo 1's problem, and its answer, a generation beside the index, works here unchanged.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/8.index/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/8.index/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 9

Interning

dojo/9.interning/play_interning.rin

An interner gives each distinct key a small number, an id: the next one, 0, 1, 2, the first time it sees the key, and the same one every time after. Find it, or make it. The ids are dense, so they index plain vecs: the key of id 3 is keys[3], and whatever else belongs to that key can live at index 3 of its own vec.

Behind it is a hash table, written here by hand: a row of slots, each empty or holding an id. A key's hash says which slot to look in first. If that one holds another key, look in the next one, and the next, wrapping round at the end, until the key or an empty slot turns up. This is linear probing. A full table would make those runs long, and an absent key's run endless, so the table doubles before it's more than 3/4 full, and every id is put back where its key's hash says in the bigger table: a different slot, since the hash now picks from twice as many.

The invariant: every id is in exactly one slot, and a walk from its key's hash reaches that slot before it reaches an empty one; the table is never more than 3/4 full; and ids are 0 to len - 1, in the order their keys first came.

In the course: 2.4's kayan_table_for is an interner. Its keys are signatures and its ids are table indices, with std's hashmap doing the lookup, and std's hashmap is this same design: linear probing, a power of two, grown before 3/4. Here you write it. 2.6 then makes the lookup rare, by remembering where each add and remove leads, and dojo 10 practises that.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play interning

It interns the signatures of a few kinds of thing in a game, in a table of 8 slots that grows to 16, and prints every slot it looks at:

intern rock, signature 7
    slots looked at: 4 5 6; new: id 3, in slot 6
    table    1:turret 4:drone 5:player 6:rock, 4 of 8 slots used
...
intern bird, signature 15
    slots looked at: 1 2; not there
    7 ids would fill more than 3/4 of 8 slots: the table grows to 16, and every id
    goes where its key's hash says now
    slots looked at: 9 10; new: id 6, in slot 10
    table    4:rock 5:player 7:chest 8:tank 9:turret 10:bird 12:drone, 7 of 16 slots used

After every step verify checks the invariant; put a breakpoint on broken, which it calls when something is wrong.

Then break on the first interner_intern, set mix_hash to 0 in the watch window, and continue. The hash is now the key itself, so the first slot is the key's lowest bits. Those are the components nearly every kind has, position, sprite and health, since they were made first, so every kind starts at the same slot and the runs pile up:

intern chest, signature 135
    slots looked at: 7 0 1 2 3; new: id 4, in slot 3
...
slots looked at, in all: 41

against 17 with the hash. Nothing is wrong, only slow, so verify stays quiet. Flip it later instead, with ids already in the table, and verify complains straight away: the ids are where the old hash put them, and the new hash looks somewhere else. A table's hash can't change under it.

Do reps: the kata

You write interner, its table included. The idea is in interner_intern:

interner_intern: proc(t: *interner, key: u64) -> u32 = {
    at: u64 = interner_slot_of(t, key);
    if (vec<u32>at(t*.slots&, at)* != 0) {
        return vec<u32>at(t*.slots&, at)* - 1;
    }
    if ((t*.keys.length + 1) * 4 > t*.slots.length * 3) {
        interner_grow(t);
        at = interner_slot_of(t, key);
    }

and the API around it:

interner_find: proc(t: *interner, key: u64) -> option<u32> = {
interner_key: proc(t: *interner, id: u32) -> u64 = {

plus interner_init and interner_len. A slot holds id + 1, so that 0 can mean empty and key 0 is a key like any other.

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random interns and finds against a model, std's hashmap and a vec of the keys in order. The keys are the kinds an ECS's tables meet: small numbers, 0 among them; signatures with a few bits set; keys that differ only in their high bits; and any u64 at all. Ids must be dense, in the order keys were first interned, and never change; interner_find must agree with interner_intern; and interner_key must give the key back. It checks what the interner does, not how fast: an interner with no mixing in its hash passes, and the playground shows what it costs. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • The hash beside the id: two u32s a slot, the id and the low bits of its key's hash, so a run compares hashes and reads keys only when they match, and interner_grow never hashes a key again.
  • Robin Hood: on the way along a run, an id that is closer to its home slot than the new one gives its slot up and moves on instead. The longest run gets much shorter. How does interner_find stop early on an absent key?
  • Grow at 1/2: what happens to the slots looked at in the playground, and to the memory?

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: find turret gave none, it should give 2

A key that was interned and can't be found usually means interner_grow copied the slots across instead of putting each id back by its key's hash: in a table twice the size, a key's run starts somewhere else. A run that steps off the end without wrapping stops the program with rin runtime: vec index out of bounds, and the runner runs it again with --trace 1 to show the operation that was running. If the run stops and never ends, the table filled up: a lookup for a key that isn't there walks round and round, never meeting an empty slot to stop at. Break into it in your debugger and look at slots.

In the fuzz run, a failure says which operation and seed, as in the other blocks; run the harness under your debugger with the --seed and --stop it gives, and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/9.interning/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/9.interning/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 10

Memoized edges

dojo/10.edges/play_edges.rin

In an archetype ECS, an entity that gains a component moves to the table whose signature has one more bit. Finding that table by its signature is a search. But a game moves entities between the same few tables over and over: a drone catches fire, the fire goes out, it catches fire again. So each table remembers where each component leads, once a move has found it:

node 3 {position velocity health}  --+burning-->  node 4
node 4 {position velocity health burning}  --burning-->  node 3

The first move from 3 with burning searches, and writes the answer on both nodes: an add edge one way and a remove edge back. Every move after that, in either direction, follows an edge. Remembering the answer to a slow question is memoizing, and the nodes and their edges are the archetype graph that flecs is built around.

The invariant: every known edge leads to the node one component away, and that node has the edge back. Each move that changes a signature searches at most once; after that, both directions are edges.

In the course: 2.6 adds add_edges and remove_edges to each table, and moves entities along them.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play edges

A drone gains and loses components, eight nodes at most. Each move says where it went and how, and the graph is drawn twice:

catches fire: node 3 -> 4 {position velocity health burning}, by a lookup
the fire goes out: node 4 -> 3 {position velocity health}, by an edge
catches fire again: node 3 -> 4 {position velocity health burning}, by an edge
...
    node 3 {position velocity health}: +burning 4, -velocity 5, -health 2
...
moves that looked up a node by signature: 7; that followed an edge: 4

Step through it: break on with and watch the two edges get written after find_or_make. verify runs after every move and prints any edge that leads to the wrong node or has no edge back. Then flip the switch at the top, memo, to 0 and run it again. The drone goes to the same nodes, but nothing is remembered: eleven moves, eleven lookups, and every node drawn with no edges known. With a few hundred tables and a game moving thousands of entities a frame, that's the difference.

Do reps: the kata

You write graph. The move that adds a component:

graph_with: proc(g: *graph, node: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {
    signature: u64 = graph_signature(g, node);
    if ((signature & graph_bit(id)) != 0) {
        return node;
    }
    edge: u32 = vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes&, cast(node, u64))*.add[id];
    if (edge != 0) {
        g*.hits += 1;
        return edge - 1;
    }
    to: u32 = graph_find_or_make(g, signature | graph_bit(id));
    // graph_find_or_make can make a node, and the vec can move them all to
    // grow, so both pointers are taken after it.
    vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes&, cast(node, u64))*.add[id] = to + 1;
    vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes&, cast(to, u64))*.remove[id] = node + 1;
    return to;
}

and its mirror, graph_without, plus graph_init (node 0 is the empty signature), graph_signature, graph_len, graph_lookups (moves that searched) and graph_hits (moves that followed an edge). The edges are stored as one more than the node, so a zeroed node knows none, 64 each way:

graph_node: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    // add[id] is one more than the node with component id added, once a move
    // has looked it up, so 0 means not known yet; remove[id] is the same, with
    // it removed.
    add: [64]u32;
    remove: [64]u32;
}

The harness runs the playground's moves as a scenario, then 20,000 random moves from random nodes, with ids up to 63, against a model that knows each node's signature and which edges a graph that writes both directions knows by now. After every move it checks the node, its signature, and both counters: a known edge is a hit, any other move that changes the signature is one lookup, and a move that changes nothing (adding what the node has) is neither. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. The comment in graph_with is the one to remember: a pointer into nodes taken before graph_find_or_make can point at memory the vec has moved out of, so the edges are written through fresh pointers after it. That's dojo 8's lesson, and 2.6's tables have the same comment.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • One hash map of edges, hashmap<u64, u32> keyed by node * 128 + id * 2 + adding, instead of two 64-wide arrays per node. Which takes less memory with 300 tables, and which is faster to follow?
  • A hash map for the slow path: graph_find_or_make searches every node. Keep a hashmap<u64, u32> from signature to node, as 2.4 does, or build one in dojo 9.
  • Removing a node. An ECS that deletes empty tables must forget every edge into them. Which nodes have edges into node n? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: lookups and hits gave 5 1, it should give 4 2

Five lookups where the model counts four: the fire going out searched, instead of following the edge back that catching fire should have written. The edge back is the one people forget, or write on the wrong node: the move from 3 to 4 sets node 3's add edge and node 4's remove edge.

The scenario's ids stop at 3. The fuzz run's go up to 63, and a failure there says which operation and seed:

FAIL at operation 9 (seed 1): with(3, 63) gave node 6, which is {2 3 31}; from {2 3} it should be {2 3 63}
    debug it: build/dojo/edges/harness --seed 1 --stop 9
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That's a bit made in 32 bits, 1 shl id on a u32: bit 63 lands on bit 31. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, and step into the move. --sanitize reports the shift itself, as undefined behaviour.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/10.edges/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/10.edges/level1.rin to level3.rin.

1// Dojo 10, the playground: memoized edges.2//3// In an archetype ECS, an entity that gains a component moves to the table4// whose signature has one more bit. Finding that table by its signature is a5// search. But a game moves entities between the same few tables over and6// over, so each table remembers where each component leads: an add edge per7// component, and a remove edge back. The tables and their edges form a graph,8// the archetype graph of the course's 2.6.9//10// Here the nodes are bare signatures, eight at most, over four components. A11// drone gains and loses components, and each move prints the node it went to12// and whether it took a lookup or followed an edge. verify runs after every13// move: every known edge must lead to the node with that one component added14// (or removed) and have its edge back, and the drone's node must have the15// components the drone has. Put a breakpoint inside its failure branch to stop16// where the graph goes wrong.17//18// The switch: set memo to 0 and run it again. Nothing is remembered: the19// drone goes to the same nodes, but every move is a lookup. The dojo · block 11

A reflection walk

dojo/11.reflect/play_reflect.rin

A reflect record lists a struct's fields: each one's name, where its bytes start in the struct, how many there are, and its type, with the type's own record when it's a struct too. rin's compiler writes one for every struct: lamp<> is lamp's. With records, one piece of code can list, read, write and compare the fields of any type it's handed, by name: an inspector, an editor, a save file, a network diff. It never names the type. It walks the bytes by the record:

"at.y" in a lamp:  lamp's field at, offset 8  ->  vec2's field y, offset 4  ->  bytes 12..16

Each offset counts from the start of the field's own struct, so a path adds them up as it goes down. And an offset is the record's to say, not something to work out from the sizes before it: a u8 followed by an f32 leaves 3 bytes of padding, and the f32 starts at 4.

The invariant: the walk reads and writes exactly the bytes the compiler gave each field. Read by path, every field is what the struct holds.

In the course: 2.7 prints any entity field by field from records. The Advanced lesson 5 builds an inspector, and an editor's write by name.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play reflect

It prints a lamp's record, walks the lamp by it, changes fields by path, and diffs the lamp with how it was:

a lamp's record: 20 bytes
    on: offset 0, size 1, u8
    power: offset 4, size 4, f32
    at: offset 8, size 8, a struct
    flicker: offset 16, size 4, f32, hidden
...
set at.x to 5.00: true
diff with the lamp before: power at.x
set flicker to 0.50: true
diff with the lamp before: power at.x

The walk reads the lamp through its bytes. Step through it: break on find and watch offset add up. verify runs after every step and checks every f32 the walk reads against the field read directly, l.power and so on. Then flip the switch at the top, use_record_offsets, to 0 and run it again. The walk adds up the sizes before each field instead, as if nothing had padding: power is read from offset 1, three padding bytes and one byte of the real power, and writing at.x lands on power. The record printed above it still says 4.

Do reps: the kata

You write the walk, over the compiler's records, reflect and reflect_field from std/reflect.rin. First, every field a tool shows, by path, walking into the ones that are structs:

walk_leaves: proc(arena: *memops_arena, type: *const reflect, prefix: ^const char, base: u64,
                  out: *vec<walk_leaf>) -> void = {
    fields: ^const reflect_field = reflect_fields(type);
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < reflect_field_count(type); i += 1) {
        f: *const reflect_field = fields[i]&;
        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {
            continue;
        }
        leaf: walk_leaf = { .offset = base + f*.offset, .size = f*.size };
        path: fmt = fmt_to(leaf.path.text);
        fmt_cstr(path&, prefix);
        fmt_cstr(path&, f*.name);
        if (reflect_is_struct(f*.info)) {
            fmt_char(path&, '.');
            walk_leaves(arena, f*.info, path.data, leaf.offset, out);
        } else {
            _ = vec<walk_leaf>append(arena, out, leaf);
        }
    }
}

and on it and on a walk down one path, walk_find, the procs the harness calls:

walk_paths: proc(arena: *memops_arena, type: *const reflect) -> vec<walk_path> = {
walk_diff: proc(arena: *memops_arena, type: *const reflect, a: []const u8, b: []const u8) -> vec<walk_path> = {
walk_get_f32: proc(type: *const reflect, bytes: []const u8, path: ^const char) -> option<f32> = {
walk_set_f32: proc(type: *const reflect, bytes: []u8, path: ^const char, value: f32) -> b32 = {

A path is a walk_path, 48 characters at most, ending in a zero. A hidden field is left out of walk_paths and walk_diff, with everything inside it, but a path still reaches it: hiding is for tools that list, not for code that asks by name. walk_get_f32 and walk_set_f32 refuse a path that names a struct, a u8, or nothing.

levelyou writetarget
1walk_leaves, the walk, in an otherwise finished file4:00
2every proc body; the types and signatures are given15:00
3the whole file, from a blank page18:00
python tools/dojo.py start reflect 2
python tools/dojo.py reflect

The harness's test types have the traps in them: lamp has padding after on: u8, room has a lamp inside it (paths three deep, offsets added twice), and a hidden draft: vec2. It runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random reads, writes and diffs of a room by path, each checked against the same fields reached directly, r.light.at.x and so on. The paths include ones that name a struct, a u8, or nothing: light.atx.x, corner.x.y, light.. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. rin's compiler writes the records; Rust's kata gets them from a macro in its harness, the way 2.7 makes them, and has paths return Vec<String> where this one fills a vec<walk_path> from the arena it's given. The harness gives each fuzz operation a temporary arena mark, so what a walk allocates is gone after it. A field's bytes are cut out with a slice, bytes[at..at + 4], so a wrong offset past the end stops a Debug build instead of reading past the value.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • **walk_find by recursion**: find the field the first name names, and recurse into its record with the rest of the path.
  • Paths without a vec of leaves: walk with a callback, a proc(path: ^const char, offset: u64, f: *const reflect_field) -> void, and let walk_paths and walk_diff each pass their own.
  • A tiny text format: write a value as path = value lines and read it back. That's a save file and a network message. (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 4 (seed 1): set_f32("light.", -50.25) returns true, it should return false
    debug it: build/dojo/reflect/harness --seed 1 --stop 4
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

The name after the dot is empty, and it matched a field anyway: a name compare that stops at the end of the shorter of the two finds range for nothing, and at for atx. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step through walk_find, watching each name and offset. If it crashes instead, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/11.reflect/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/11.reflect/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 12

A watermark

dojo/12.watermark/play_watermark.rin

A query keeps the list of tables it matches, so a system doesn't search for them every frame. Tables are only ever added, at the end, and never removed. So the query remembers how many tables it has looked at, its watermark, and an update looks only at the tables past it:

tables   0 P   1 PV   2 PVH  |  3 PVHB   4 H
                             ^ movers has checked 3: an update looks at 3 and 4

A frame with no new tables costs one comparison, and each query looks at each table once, ever. It works for anything that only grows at the end: a log read by several readers, a list of events, the lines of a file being written.

The invariant: a query lists exactly the tables below its watermark that match, each once, in order, and it has looked at each of them once.

In the course: 3.1 builds the query and its checked count, and 3.2 updates every system's query at the start of every frame, which is what makes the watermark matter.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play watermark

It makes tables a few at a time, and updates two queries: movers, all {Position Velocity}, and healthy, all {Health}, none {Burning}. After each step it draws the tables, and under them what each query has looked at, with a | at its watermark:

update movers: it looks at tables 3 and 4 only
    table     0    1    2    3    4
    has       P    PV   PVH  PVHB H
    movers    -    yes  yes  yes  -    |    checked 5, scanned 5, tables 1 2 3
    healthy   |                             checked 0, scanned 0, tables none

scanned counts every table an update has looked at. With the watermark it always equals checked. Then verify checks both queries against the tables and prints what's wrong; break inside its if to stop when it fires.

Step through it: break on query_update and watch from, checked and found. Then flip the switch at the top, use_watermark, to 0, and run it again. Every update starts from table 0, and the second update of movers, with nothing new, finds tables 1 and 2 again:

movers    -    yes  yes  |    checked 3, scanned 6, tables 1 2 1 2
verify: movers lists tables 1 2 1 2; it should list 1 2
verify: movers has looked at 6 tables to check 3; each should be looked at once

A system walking that list would run twice over the same entities, and the work grows with every frame. The switch is a global, read on every update, so a debugger can flip it mid-run too: stop on query_update, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.

Do reps: the kata

You write query:

query: struct = {
    arena: *memops_arena;
    all: u64;
    none: u64;
    // The tables that match, by index, in the order they were found.
    tables: vec<u32>;
    // The watermark: tables 0 to checked - 1 have been looked at.
    checked: u64;
    // How many tables query_update has looked at, ever. With the watermark,
    // each table once.
    scanned: u64;
}

and its update, which is given the world's tables as their signatures:

query_update: proc(q: *query, signatures: []u64) -> void = {

plus query_init(q, arena, all, none), query_tables (the matching tables, in increasing order), query_checked and query_scanned. A table matches when its signature has every bit of all and no bit of none.

levelyou writetarget
1query_update, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given5:00
3the whole file, from a blank page7:00
python tools/dojo.py start watermark 2
python tools/dojo.py watermark

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random operations: tables made with random signatures, four queries with random masks updated at random, and now and then one replaced by a new query, which must start from nothing. A model keeps, for each query, the tables that match among the ones it has been updated over. After every update the query must have checked the whole list, list exactly the model's tables, and have scanned each table once. Some none masks have two bits, so "none of these" and "not all of these" give different answers. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • **A while loop, and scanned added once**: scanned grows by the number of new tables, which is known before the loop starts.
  • Push, don't poll: flecs does the reverse. When the world makes a table, it tells every query, and query_update has nothing left to do. What does the world have to keep, and what happens to a query made after the table? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)
  • A table that can go away: the list keeps a tombstone where a removed table was, a signature no query matches. What must a query do with a table it already lists? (Not checked by the harness.)

When it fails

The scenario catches the common mistakes first:

FAIL in the scenario: make tables 3 and 4, update movers: tables gave 1 2 0, it should give 1 2 3

That's a count of the new tables pushed as if it were the table's index: a loop that counts from 0 over the tables past the watermark has to add checked back. A failure in the fuzz run says where:

FAIL at operation 27 (seed 1): after query_update, query 1 (all {0 5}, none {0 6}): it lists 1, the model 0; the first difference is at position 0: table 1, where the model has nothing
    debug it: build/dojo/watermark/harness --seed 1 --stop 27
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one tested none the way it tested all, (signature & none) != none, which is "not every bit of none" rather than "no bit of it". It only differs when none has more than one bit. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step into query_update and look at the table it lists.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/12.watermark/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/12.watermark/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 13

A dispatch table

dojo/13.dispatch/play_dispatch.rin

A frame is a list of systems run in order, and the list is data: a name and a pointer to a proc for each, in an array the program changes as it runs. Adding, removing, reordering or switching off a system is an edit to the array, not to the code that calls them:

schedule  0 move   1 shoot   2 damage   3 die
a frame   for each enabled system, in order: entry.run(world)

The order is a statement about data: a system that reads what another writes runs after it. damage writes health and die reads it, so damage goes before die, and a drone dies in the frame its health runs out. The same table drives an interpreter's opcodes, a menu's actions, a network protocol's message handlers: a number or a name picks a proc.

The invariant: a run calls every enabled system once, in the list's order, and nothing else. Edits keep the order of everything they don't touch.

In the course: 3.2 makes a system a name, a query and a proc pointer, and runs a schedule of them each frame, and 3.4's game has nine, each placed after what it reads.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play dispatch

A drone flies at a turret. Four systems, move, shoot, damage and die, run frame by frame, and between frames the program edits the schedule: shoot is switched off while the turret reloads, back on, and removed at the end. After each step it prints the schedule or the world:

frame 2
    ran       move shoot damage die
    drone     4 from the turret, health 60, alive
switch shoot off: the turret is reloading
    schedule  move (shoot off) damage die
frame 3
    ran       move damage die

Then verify checks that the drone is dead exactly when its health has run out; break inside its if to stop when it fires. Step through it: break on schedule_run and step into each call, through the pointer, into the system.

Then flip the switch at the top, in_order, to 0, and run it again. damage is added at the end of the schedule instead of before die, so die reads the health from before this frame's damage:

frame 5
    ran       move shoot die damage
    drone     0 from the turret, health -20, alive
    verify: the drone has health -20 and is still alive

and it dies in frame 6, a frame late. A frame late is a drone that fires once more after it should be dead, or a death sound one frame after the explosion. The switch is a global, read when damage is added, so a debugger can flip it too: stop on the first line of main, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.

Do reps: the kata

You write schedule. A system is a plain pointer to a proc, which takes the harness's ctx:

system_proc: alias = *proc(c: *ctx) -> void;

schedule_system: struct = {
    name: ^const char;
    run: system_proc;
    enabled: b32;
    // How many times schedule_run has called it.
    calls: u32;
}

and the schedule is a vec of them, in the order they run:

schedule_insert_before: proc(s: *schedule, before: ^const char, name: ^const char, run: system_proc) -> b32 = {
schedule_run: proc(s: *schedule, c: *ctx) -> void = {

plus schedule_init, schedule_add(s, name, run) (at the end), schedule_remove(s, name), schedule_set_enabled(s, name, on), schedule_len and schedule_name(s, i) (every name, enabled or not, in order), and schedule_calls(s, name). schedule_insert_before, schedule_remove and schedule_set_enabled return 0, and change nothing, when there's no system by that name. Names are C strings, compared with strcmp.

levelyou writetarget
1schedule_run, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given10:00
3the whole file, from a blank page15:00
python tools/dojo.py start dispatch 2
python tools/dojo.py dispatch

The harness has twelve systems, input to save, and each one writes its name in the ctx's log when it's called, so after a run the log says what ran, in what order, and through which proc. It runs a short scenario, then 20,000 random adds, inserts, removes, enables, disables and runs against a model that keeps the schedule as a plain list. After every operation the order and every count must match the model, and every run must log exactly the enabled systems, in order. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Rust's kata has order(), which returns the names as a Vec; here schedule_len and schedule_name give them one at a time, so nothing is allocated to read them.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • A fixed array: [16]schedule_system and a count instead of a vec, as the playground has. What happens on the seventeenth add?
  • Struct of arrays: the names, the procs, the flags and the counts in four vecs, one place per system. schedule_insert_before and schedule_remove must move all four the same way.
  • Reads and writes: each system declares bitmasks of what it reads and writes, and schedule_insert_before refuses a place where a system would read something a later one writes. Then: which neighbours could run at the same time, on two threads? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

A system with data of its own is one more pointer beside the proc pointer, handed back on every call: 3.4's kayan_system has a ctx: *void for that, which is what a closure is, written out.

When it fails

The scenario catches the common mistakes first:

FAIL in the scenario: run: what ran gave move, it should give move damage die

That run stopped at the first disabled system, collide: a break where a skip was meant. A failure in the fuzz run says where:

FAIL at operation 110 (seed 1): after schedule_remove(die), schedule_calls(damage) is 0; the model counts 2 since it was added
    debug it: build/dojo/dispatch/harness --seed 1 --stop 110
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That kata kept the counts in a vec of their own, the struct of arrays above, and schedule_remove popped the last count rather than the removed system's, so the counts after it shifted one place. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step into schedule_remove and watch both vecs.

If the harness crashes instead, on a proc pointer that was never set, say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/13.dispatch/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/13.dispatch/level1.rin to level3.rin.

Advanced · seven lessons

Layout and SIMD

docs/README.md

Seven lessons for after Build an ECS. The course builds the ECS. These go underneath it, to the memory and the machine code:

  • Lesson 1, aos vs soa. The same particles in three layouts: what a loop fetches per cache line, what noalias promises the compiler, which loops it vectorizes, and how to check that in the assembly.
  • Lessons 2 to 6 build an archetype ECS again, compressed into five steps, and end with a small game. They came first and move fast. After the course, read them as a recap, or as a second take on the same design. Lesson 4 builds the world in includes/kayan.rin, and lessons 5 and 6 import it unchanged.
  • Lesson 7, layout follows access. Four layouts under streams and under random lookups, timed, and how an ECS decides where each component lives.
  • Lesson 0, from kayan, reviews the original C kayan: what these lessons kept from it, what they changed, and why.
lessonabout
0from kayanwhat was kept from the C kayan, what changed, and why
1aos vs soathe same particles in three layouts, what a loop fetches, and what SIMD needs
2archetype tableone table: columns, rows, spawn, swap-remove, systems over slices
3many archetypesone table type for every archetype: ids, signatures, queries
4entity handlesgenerational handles, slots, moving between archetypes
5inspectorprinting and editing any entity from reflection records
6kayana small game, and deferring structural changes to a command buffer
7access patternsfour layouts under streams and lookups, and how an ECS decides

How to read them

Read each lesson's .rin file from the top. It opens with the problem it solves, and the code follows in the order it runs. Then run it and read the output against the code: every lesson prints what it does, step by step. The guides here give the background that doesn't fit in a file header, and end with exercises.

Timings only mean something in a Release build. Debug checks every slice index. Lesson 1's guide shows how to build one, and what to look for in the disassembly.

Advanced · lesson 0 · review

From kayan

docs/0_from_kayan.md

kayan is a sketch of an archetype entity component system in C, about 200 lines in src/kayan.h, with haikal generating its containers. These lessons start from its idea and rebuild the rest. This page says what was kept, what was changed, and why, so the lessons can be read as a review of it as much as a rewrite.

What kayan does

Components are bits in an enum, positions = 1 << 0, velocities = 1 << 1 and so on. Each archetype is a C struct written by hand (A, B, C, D) that starts with an ArchetypeHeader and then holds one haikal Array_T per component. The header has a u64 signature and a Map_u64 from column name to the column's byte offset in the struct.

A query walks an array of void * pointing at the archetypes, reads each header, and tests (signature & want) == want. For a match it looks up "positions" and "velocities" in the offset map, adds the offsets to the struct's address, and runs the loop over the two columns.

Kept

  • An archetype is a struct of arrays. Each component is a contiguous column and every entity in the table has every column. That is the whole point, and kayan had it right from the start.
  • A signature is a u64 of component bits, and a query is the test (signature & all) == all. Lesson 3 adds a none mask beside it.
  • Arenas for all of it. Nothing in these lessons is freed one at a time.

Changed

  • One table type for every archetype (lesson 3). kayan needs a new C struct, a new signature line and new offset-map lines for every archetype. Here an archetype is data: a signature, and the world makes its table the first time something needs it (lesson 4).
  • Columns by component id, not by name (lesson 3). kayan hashes the strings "positions" and "velocities" on every query. Here a table's columns are an array indexed by component id, so finding one is an index. Names are kept for tools, through reflection (lesson 5).
  • The signature comes from the columns (lesson 3). In kayan they are written separately and can disagree. In D they do: it has positions and velocities columns, but its signature is health | damage | alive, so the movement query never visits it.
  • A row is added and removed in one place (lesson 2). kayan appends to each column at the call site, and keeps entity_count apart from the columns. For B and D it increments a's count instead of their own (kayan.h lines 142, 145, 168, 174), so A reports seven entities and the others report none. Nothing breaks only because the query loop happens to use the column's own length.
  • Entities have handles (lesson 4). kayan's entity id is the value of an archetype's entity_count before it is bumped: meant per table, in practice A's, as above. Nothing records where an entity lives, so there is no way to refer to one entity from elsewhere, to remove it, or to move it to another archetype. The lessons use an {index, generation} handle and a slot list that tracks each entity's table and row.
  • Entities move between archetypes (lesson 4). Adding or removing a component moves the entity to the matching table, copying the components both tables share.
  • Structural changes wait for the end of the frame (lesson 6), through a command buffer in a frame arena. kayan never changes structure while a query runs, but only because it never changes structure at all.
  • Reflection replaces hand-written tables (lessons 3 to 5). A component's size and alignment come from T<>, and so do the names a tool prints. The offset map goes away entirely.

Not carried over

  • **vec4s for positions.** kayan pads 3D vectors to 16 bytes, which suits SIMD loads. The lessons use vec2 and vec3 and plain loops, and leave vectorizing to the C compiler. noalias on the kernels' parameters, in lessons 1, 2, 3 and 6, lets it do that without run-time overlap checks. Lesson 1 adds a third layout, one f32 array per coordinate, which is the one SIMD runs cleanly over, and its exercises come back to vec4. Lesson 7 weighs that layout against lookups, which it is bad at.
  • cglm and the haikal containers. rin's generics and std (vec<T>, hashmap<K, V>, slices) cover what they did.

Small things in kayan.h

  • The query's inner loop declares i32 i, shadowing the outer i (line 201).
  • Each lookup on lines 199 and 200 hashes and compares a string, once per column per archetype per query. That is cheap next to a large loop, but it is work that an array index does for nothing.

Advanced · lesson 1

AoS vs SoA

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rin

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rin

The same 262,144 particles, stored three times: as an array of 68-byte particle structs (AoS), as seven arrays, one per field (SoA), and with position and velocity split one step further into six arrays of f32, one per coordinate (split). Sixty steps of movement run over each, and the program checks that all three end with the same positions.

What the loop fetches

Memory reaches the CPU in 64-byte cache lines. A loop that reads 24 bytes of each 68-byte particle still pulls every byte of every line those particles sit in, so about two thirds of what movement fetches in the AoS loop is tint, age, lifetime, size and name. In the SoA loop the two arrays it reads are the only thing it fetches, and the hardware prefetcher sees two simple streams. The split loop fetches the same 24 bytes per particle as SoA, as six streams.

The program prints that arithmetic:

bytes fetched per step: 17825792     (AoS: 68 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (SoA: 24 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (split: 6 x 4 bytes x 262144)

What the CPU does with each layout

SSE registers hold four floats, AVX registers eight. One instruction adds four (or eight) pairs of floats at once, but only if they arrive side by side. Here is what clang-cl /O2 makes of each loop for Windows x64, read from the object file:

loopparticles per passinstructions per passper particleshuffles
move_aos116161
move_soa477about 1930
move_split42050
move_split, /arch:AVX2814under 20
  • AoS goes one particle at a time: each particle's fields are 68 bytes from the next particle's, so there is nothing to load four of.
  • SoA is vectorized, four particles per pass, but each vec3 keeps x, y and z side by side. To get four x's into one register the compiler loads them one float at a time and stitches them together, then takes them apart again to store. About a tenth of the loop is arithmetic, and per particle it costs about what AoS does.
  • Split is what SIMD wants. Each line of move_split becomes one load of four consecutive floats, one multiply, one add, one store:
  movups (%r11,%rdi,4), %xmm4     four vx
  movups (%rcx,%rdi,4), %xmm5     four px
  mulps  %xmm1, %xmm4             vx * dt
  addps  %xmm5, %xmm4             px + vx * dt
  movups %xmm4, (%rcx,%rdi,4)     four px back

A layout is right for SIMD when its vector loop is mostly full-width loads, math and stores. When it is mostly movss, unpcklps and shufps, the data is fighting the registers.

Split is right for this loop, which runs over every particle in order. It is wrong for a loop that reaches particles by index, where x, y and z in three arrays are three trips to memory instead of one. Lesson 7 measures both kinds of loop over four layouts.

Timings

--time prints how long each layout took. Release builds, best of five runs, on the 2.8 GHz Xeon these lessons were checked on, ms:

buildAoSSoAsplit
clang -O249.626.916.5
clang -O347.526.715.9
clang -O2 -mavx2 -mfma47.918.613.0
gcc -O334.213.714.2
gcc -O246.121.344.3

The same loops with 8,192 particles, so everything stays in L2, and 1,920 steps so the work is the same:

buildAoSSoAsplit
clang -O224.125.611.9
clang -O2 -mavx2 -mfma28.617.86.5
gcc -O312.712.08.9
  • In cache, split is the only layout SIMD helps much. SoA and AoS come out about even in L2 on clang, as the instruction counts say they should.
  • From the 6 MB case, SoA's smaller footprint shows. That machine has 33 MB of L3, so the data stays in cache between steps, but SoA and split still move a third of the bytes AoS does.
  • **gcc -O2 does not vectorize across particles at all,** so split, with six streams and nothing gained for them, is its slowest layout. gcc users want -O3. clang-cl, rin's default, is the clang rows.

The machine is shared; expect about 20 percent noise between runs. Debug numbers are not worth comparing: every positions[i] is bounds checked there.

For a Release build, set build_type to "Release" in build.rin and run rin build again. Release defines NDEBUG, which compiles the bounds checks out. Or compile the C that tools/check.py leaves in build/check/aos_vs_soa/ with -O2 -DNDEBUG.

The parameter list is the data

move_aos(ps: noalias []particle, ...) says it needs particles. move_soa(positions: noalias []vec3, velocities: noalias []vec3, ...) and move_split(px, py, pz, vx, vy, vz, ...) say exactly which data they read and write. In lessons 2 and 3 every system is written that way. In lesson 6 each system runs its own query, then works only on the columns it named.

Naming the columns is what lets a scheduler see that two systems touch different data, and it is what makes a system easy to test: hand it two small arrays.

noalias

As far as the C compiler can tell, two []vec3 slices could overlap. So before it works on several particles at once, it checks at run time that the two are apart, and keeps a one-at-a-time copy of the loop for when they are not. noalias on a parameter promises that, for the call, nothing else reaches the memory behind it. The check and the second copy go away.

The SoA loop without and with it, Release, ms:

buildwithout noaliaswith noalias
gcc -O331.713.4
gcc -O220.521.3
clang -O226.326.5
  • **gcc -O3** is where it shows. Without the promise, its checked vector loop was slower than not vectorizing at all (21 ms with -fno-tree-loop-vectorize), and the SoA loop lost to the AoS one.
  • clang vectorized the loop either way. Its check runs once per call, so removing it saves nothing that shows here.

On Windows, one slice needs it too. move_aos has a single slice, which cannot overlap another, and it still takes noalias. Windows passes a slice to a proc by reference, as a pointer to a copy, and clang-cl does not use C's type rules to decide what can overlap (it matches MSVC). So, without the promise, a float written through ps might be the slice's own pointer or length, and the loop reads both again after every particle:

mov   r8,qword ptr [rcx]                   ps.data, every particle
movss xmm2,dword ptr [gravity]             gravity, every particle
...
cmp   rdx,qword ptr [rcx+8]                ps.length, every particle

With noalias the compiler gets the pointer and the length once, in registers, and the loop is 16 instructions instead of 19.

**And gravity is static.** A global that other files could reach is, to gcc, something a write through a slice might change, even through a noalias one, so gcc -O3 put a run-time check in front of move_split's vector loop. gravity: static f32 keeps it to this file, nothing takes its address, and the check goes away. Passing it as a parameter would do the same.

The promise is checked in Debug. Pass soa.positions as both arguments to move_soa and the Debug build stops before the loop runs:

aos_vs_soa.rin:138: noalias parameters 'positions' and 'velocities' overlap

A Release build does not check. It runs on, and the lesson prints same result: no.

Fused multiply-add

With -mfma, -march=native or clang-cl's /arch:AVX2, clang fuses p + v * dt into one instruction that rounds once instead of twice. All three layouts are fused the same way and still agree, but the checksum's last digits move, from 38572460.505 to 38572460.519, and the byte-for-byte check against aos_vs_soa.expected fails. tools/check.py builds without those flags.

When AoS is right

When the code that touches a record touches most of its fields, AoS fetches nothing wasted, and keeping a record together is simpler. Data-oriented design does not mean SoA everywhere. It means choosing the layout from the loops that run over it. An entity component system is the case where many small loops each touch a few fields.

Try

  1. Run with --time in Release. Then remove tint, age, lifetime and name from particle and run again. The AoS loop should close most of the gap, because the struct shrinks toward what the loop reads.
  2. Add /arch:AVX2 to build_c_flags and compare --time. Then read move_split in the disassembly: eight floats per register, and vfmadd.
  3. kayan stored positions as 16-byte vec4s. Change vec3 to four floats and see what it does to the bytes-per-step line, to move_soa's disassembly and to the timing.
  4. Store the split columns in blocks of eight, { x: [8]f32; y: [8]f32; ... }, and write the loop over blocks. Each block is a whole AVX register per coordinate, and a particle's coordinates stay near each other.
  5. Remove noalias from move_soa and build Release with gcc -O3. Compare --time, then compile with -fopt-info-vec and find "loop versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing".
  6. Remove static from gravity, build with gcc -O3 -fopt-info-vec, and find the same message for move_split.
  7. Pass soa.positions as both arguments to move_soa. Run it in Debug, then in Release.

Advanced · lesson 2

One archetype table

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 4. a type-erased column, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Eight sparks in one table with three component columns, positions, velocities and lives, plus a numbers column that exists only so the output can say which spark is which. Each frame they move, they age, and the ones that ran out are removed.

Two rules

Columns never disagree. spark_spawn and spark_despawn are the only places rows come and go, and each touches every column. A new component means a new column, one line in each of those two procs, and one more argument to spark_spawn. A call site cannot add a row to some columns and forget the others.

Rows are packed. Systems loop over 0..count and never test whether a row is alive. Removing a row moves the last row into the hole:

spark 0 in row 0 expired; spark 7 moved from row 7 into it

That one copy per column is the whole cost of a despawn, whatever the table's size. The price is that a row number is not a name for a spark. After that line, "row 0" means spark 7. Lesson 4 adds names that do not move.

Removing while iterating

expire_system walks the rows backwards. When it removes row i, the row that moves in comes from the end, and the end has already been tested. A forward loop would have to stay on i after a removal, and it is easy to get wrong. Lesson 6 removes the question entirely by not removing anything during a loop.

Systems take slices

move_system(positions: noalias []vec2, velocities: []const vec2, dt) gets the rows in use, sparks.positions[0..sparks.count], and knows nothing about tables. []const says it only reads velocities. Each positions[i] is bounds checked in Debug, against the count rather than the capacity, so a system that runs past the live rows stops with a message instead of reading stale data.

noalias says that for the call, nothing else reaches the memory positions covers. Only the column the system writes needs it: a promise on the written column already rules out a write landing in the column being read. Without it, clang -O2 and gcc -O3 both vectorized this loop behind a run-time check that the two columns are apart. With it, neither checks. A Debug build checks the promise instead, once per call.

age_system(lives: noalias []f32, dt) has one slice, and still takes it. Windows passes a slice by reference, as a pointer to a copy, and clang-cl does not use C's type rules to decide what can overlap. So without the promise, a float written through lives might be the slice's own pointer or length. clang-cl then reads both again after every element and does one float at a time. With it, the loop is eight floats per pass:

movups (%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm2         four lives
movups 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm3     four more
subps  %xmm0, %xmm2                minus dt
subps  %xmm0, %xmm3
movups %xmm2, (%rcx,%r8,4)
movups %xmm3, 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4)

The rule that holds on every compiler: noalias on every slice a loop writes, even when it is the only one.

lives is the one column here that is a plain run of floats. positions and velocities are vec2, x and y side by side, so move_system's vector loop spends some of its instructions pulling the x's and the y's apart. Lesson 1 measures what that costs.

Status codes

spark_spawn returns spawn_status, an enum[must_use]: calling it and ignoring the result is a compile error. That is rin's convention for a proc that can fail: a status, with the result through an out-parameter. The ninth spark shows the full case.

Try

  1. Rewrite expire_system to walk forwards with a plain for. The output does not change, because no frame here expires a spark together with the one in the last row. Change two lives so that one does, and find the spark that outlives its life by a frame. Then fix the loop.
  2. Delete the line in spark_despawn that copies lives. What does the output show, and how long did it take to notice?
  3. Call spark_spawn without using its result and read the compiler's error. Then discard it on purpose with _ = spark_spawn(...).
  4. Make the table grow instead of reporting full: allocate double the capacity from the arena and copy every column across. Lesson 4's kayan_table_grow is one answer.
1// 2. One archetype table2//3// An archetype is one combination of components. Its table holds every entity4// that has exactly that combination: one column per component, one row per5// entity. Spawn appends to every column in8// one place and despawn removes from every column in one place. kayan appended9// to each column at the call site, and three appends that must happen together10// are three chances to forget one.11//12// Rows are packed. Despawn moves the last row into the hole it leaves (a13// swap-remove), so a system loops over 0..count with no gaps and no "alive"14// flag to test. The price is that a row is not a stable name for an entity: the15// last entity changes rows every time something before it dies. Advanced · lesson 3

Many archetypes

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, 6. bitsets, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Four archetypes (rock, ship, bullet, turret) and four components (position, velocity, health, damage). One table type holds all four archetypes, and two queries decide which tables each system visits.

A table without a type

Lesson 2's table had one typed field per column. That cannot work for every archetype at once, so the columns become bytes:

table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    columns: [component<>.count]^u8;
}

columns[id] is null when the table has no such component. Its element size is component_info[id]*.size, where component_info holds each component's reflect record, position<>& and so on. table_add_row and lesson 4's moves work only from sizes, so they never need to know a component's type.

Types come back at the edges. column<T>(t) asks component_of<T>() for T's id, casts that column to ^T, and returns it as a []T of the rows in use. component_of is one specialisation per component, one line each. Systems take []position, []velocity and so on, exactly as in lesson 2.

Sized by reflection

component has no count member at the end. component<>.count is the number of members, from the enum's reflect record, and it sizes both columns and component_info. With a hand-added count member the reflected count is one more than the number of components. That is how the bounds check found a bug while this lesson was being written.

components_check compares each enum member's name with the name in component_info. Swap two entries in component_info and the program stops before anything runs:

component 2 is health in the enum but damage in component_info

Different types, fewer checks

move_system takes noalias []position, as lesson 2's takes noalias []vec2, and for the same reason. regen_system takes noalias []health, its only slice, for the reason lesson 2 gives for age_system.

One difference showed before either had noalias: clang on Linux vectorized this move_system without a run-time overlap check, and lesson 2's only with one. Here the two columns are different struct types, position and velocity, and clang reads C's type rules as saying they cannot share memory; built with -fno-strict-aliasing, it checks here too. In lesson 2 both are vec2. gcc checked in both. clang-cl, rin's default compiler, does not use those rules at all, to match MSVC, so on Windows both lessons were checked. noalias makes the answer the same everywhere, whatever the column types are.

Queries

moving: query = { .all = bit(component.position) | bit(component.velocity) };
healing: query = { .all = bit(component.health), .none = bit(component.damage) };

A table matches when it has every bit in all and none in none. moving visits ships and bullets. healing visits ships but not turrets, which have health but also deal damage. The output prints each visit.

The signature cannot lie

table_create builds the signature from the component list it allocates columns for. kayan wrote them separately, and archetype D's signature left out two of its columns (see 0_from_kayan.md).

Try

  1. Add an armor component, give it to turrets, and make a query that visits only tables with both health and armor.
  2. Ask a rock for column<velocity>. Read the message, then find where it comes from.
  3. Change columns to [4]^u8. Then add a fifth component and see what happens, and where.
  4. Write table_remove_row with the swap-remove from lesson 2, working only from component_info sizes and memcpy.
1// 3. Many archetypes2//3// A game has more than one combination of components. Rocks only have a4// position. Ships move and can be hurt. Bullets move and hurt. Turrets stand5// still, can be hurt and hurt back. Each combination is a table of its own, and6// a system has to visit every table that has the columns it needs.7//8// kayan wrote a C struct per archetype, gave each a hand-set signature, and at9// query time looked each column up by name in a string map. Here one table type10// serves every archetype:11//12//   * A component is a member of the `component` enum, so its id is a small13//     integer, and a set of components fits in a u64 mask, one bit each.14//   * A table's columns are `[component<>.count]^u8`, indexed by component id15//     and null where the table has no such column. Finding a column is an array16//     index, not a string lookup.17//   * A column's element size comes from reflection: `component_info[id]` is the18//     component type's reflect record, `position<>&` and so on.19//   * A table's signature is computed from the components it is created with,20//     so the signature cannot disagree with the columns. In kayan it could, and21//     it did: archetype D held positions and velocities, its signature left them22//     out, and the movement query skipped it.23//24// A query is two masks: a table matches when it has every component in `all`25// and none in `none`. Typed access comes back through generics: `column<T>`26// asks `component_of<T>()` which id T has, one line per component type, and27// returns that column as a []T cut to the rows in use.28 29import "std/print.rin"30import "std/memops.rin"31 32vec2: struct = {33    x: f32;34    y: f32;35}36 37// The components. Advanced · lesson 4

Entity handles

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin, includes/kayan.rin

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, 3. the slot map, 9. interning, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world: tables made on demand, entity handles that survive row moves, despawning with index reuse, and moving an entity between archetypes when a component is added or removed. The code is includes/kayan.rin. The lesson program calls each part and prints what happened.

Handles, slots, rows

kayan_entity: struct = { index: u32; generation: u32; }
kayan_slot:   struct = { generation: u32; table: u32; row: u32; }

A handle is what the rest of a program keeps. Its index picks a slot, and the slot says where the entity lives now. Rows move all the time: every despawn and every archetype change swap-removes. When one does, the table's entities column says which entity owned the moved row, and that entity's slot gets the new row number. Handles never change.

generation is what makes a handle safe to keep after its entity dies. Despawning bumps the slot's generation and frees the index, and the next spawn reuses the index with the new generation:

spawn d: it reuses a's index with the next generation
    d = 0:2 in table 0 row 2 {position velocity} at (4.0, 0.0)
    a = 0:1 is dead

kayan_alive is one comparison: the handle's generation against the slot's. A free slot already holds its next generation, which no handle carries yet, so no separate "alive" flag is needed. a cannot reach d's data, kayan_get returns null for it, and despawning it again returns kayan_status.dead and changes nothing.

Generations start at 1. A zeroed handle, {}, is 0:0, which never matches a slot, so it can stand for "no entity" without a separate flag.

Statuses

kayan_despawn, kayan_add, kayan_remove and kayan_move return kayan_status, an enum[must_use]: ok, or dead when the handle no longer names a live entity. Ignoring one is a compile error. The lesson discards them on purpose with _ = kayan_add<health>(...) where the handle is known to be alive.

Tables on demand

kayan_table_for(w, signature) looks the signature up in a hashmap<u64, u32> and makes the table if it is new. Nobody declares archetypes; they appear when an entity first needs that combination. Tables live in a vec<kayan_table> and are referred to by index, because adding one can move the whole list.

Tables start with room for 16 rows and double when full. The old columns stay in the arena unused, which is a waste these lessons accept. The last part of the program spawns 40 entities so the first table grows twice, despawns every other one, and checks the result two ways.

Checking the world

Reading back each survivor's position is a weak check. Swap-remove copies rows, so a stale row often still holds the right numbers. kayan_verify checks the invariant instead: every row of every table belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows add up to the live count. It prints each problem it finds and returns how many there were. The lesson prints kayan_verify: 0 problems and fails if that is not so.

kayan_get also checks the slot's row against the rows in use, so in Debug a slot that points past the end of its table stops the program at the first lookup.

Moving between archetypes

give b health: b moves to a new table and keeps its position

kayan_add<health> computes signature | bit(health), finds or makes that table, appends a row, copies every component the two tables share, then swap-removes the old row. kayan_remove is the same move with the bit cleared. A move costs two row copies, one into the new table and one to fill the hole in the old, so components that come and go every frame are better as a field than as a component. A burning flag in health, say, instead of a burning component.

Try

  1. Despawn b and keep using its handle. Which calls notice, and which would not if kayan_alive did not check the generation?
  2. Remove the line in kayan_table_remove_row that updates the moved entity's slot. In Debug the program stops at the first kayan_get through a stale row. Build it with -DNDEBUG and run it again: the position check still says all 20 are fine, and kayan_verify lists every broken slot.
  3. At the end of the lesson, table 0 has 22 rows and room for 64. Hold a []position from kayan_column, spawn at least 43 more so the table grows, then write through the old slice and read the position back through kayan_get. The write is lost, and nothing reports it. That stale slice is why lesson 6 defers spawns.
  4. Add kayan_has<T>(w, e) -> b32 without moving anything.

Imports the world from includes/kayan.rin.

    table 0 {position velocity}: 2:1 0:2
    table 1 {position velocity health}:
    table 2 {position health}: 1:1
spawn 40 more

Advanced · lesson 5

The inspector

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

In the dojo: 11. a reflection walk, on its own, to watch and to practise.

A soldier and a crate, printed field by field by code that names no component type, then edited by component and field name, then a table layout report. Everything comes from the reflect records the world already holds for sizes.

What a reflect record has

T<> is a reflect record: name, size, align, kind, count, and for a struct, count fields. Each field has its name, offset, size, type ("f32" for a builtin, "array_16_c8" for a [16]c8), elem_type and array_count for arrays, and info, the record of the field's own type when it has one. A nested struct or an enum field has info; a builtin like f32 does not.

print_fields walks that. It takes the component's bytes as a []const u8, from kayan_get_bytes, and cuts each field's bytes out of it by offset and size, so a record that disagreed with the data would stop the program in Debug. Struct fields recurse through info, enum fields print their member name through reflect_name_from_value_or, a [16]c8 prints as text, and builtins print by type name. Because components are structs, even a single float like health.points has a name to print.

Tags

health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; regen_timer: f32 @ "hidden"; }

@ "hidden" is a string attached to the field, read with reflect_field_has_attr. The inspector skips it. The component decides what a tool shows, and the tool does not need to know the component.

Names belong in tools

set_f32_by_name(w, e, "health", "points", 55.0) finds the component by name, the field by name, checks the field is an f32, and writes it. It refuses weapon.ammo, a u32, and the crate's health, which it does not have. That is the flexibility an editor or a console needs. It is also the string comparison kayan did in every query, once per archetype. Here it runs once per edit, and systems keep using ids.

Layout

print_layout lists each table's columns with size and alignment, and each column's bytes in use out of the bytes allocated for the table's capacity. It is the kind of report that shows when a component has grown padding, when a table has far more room than rows, or when a table carries a column most of its systems never read.

Try

  1. Add a bool-like b32 field to weapon and teach print_builtin to print it as yes or no.
  2. Give position a @ "readonly" tag and make set_f32_by_name refuse fields that carry it.
  3. Write set_by_name for u32 and i32 as well, picking the write from field.type.
  4. Print a whole table as rows and columns: one line per entity, one column per field.

Advanced · lesson 6

kayan

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

In the dojo: 5. a command buffer, 7. an arena, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

A turret at the centre, five wings of three drones, 140 frames. Seven systems run each frame, and every structural change they want goes through a command buffer applied at the end of the frame.

The frame

spawner    wings of drones enter                    records spawns
turret     shoot at the nearest drone               records spawns
movement   position += velocity * dt                writes
lifetime   bullets expire                           records despawns
collision  live bullets against drones              writes health, records despawn and add
burning    burning drones lose health               writes
outcome    destroy dead drones, catch leaks         records despawns
  blast    a destroyed drone hurts its neighbours   writes health, records adds
apply      every recorded change, in order

Writes to components happen in place, during queries. Changes to which table an entity is in are recorded, and applied once nothing is iterating.

Lifetime runs before collision, and collision skips bullets whose lifetime is used up. Those bullets are only still in their table because nothing structural happens until the end of the frame. Without the skip, a bullet that hit on its last frame would be despawned twice and counted as both a hit and a miss.

Systems and kernels

movement_system and burning_system are each a query and a kernel:

integrate: proc(ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void
burn: proc(hs: noalias []health, bs: []const burning, dt: f32) -> void

The system walks the tables and calls the kernel once for each table that matches. The kernel sees two columns, so the compiler sees a straight loop over two arrays. noalias qualifies parameters, so the loop needs a proc of its own to carry it; that is the only reason these two are split out. The output does not change.

Before the split, gcc -O3 vectorized both loops behind a run-time check that the columns were apart. After it, without the check. clang on Linux had no check either way, for the reason lesson 3 gives: the columns are different types. clang-cl, which does not use C's type rules, needs noalias here too.

burn is the cleanest loop in the game. health and burning are each one f32, so their columns are plain runs of floats, and the kernel is eight floats per pass with nothing to rearrange: loads, mulps, subps, stores. integrate works on vec2s and spends some of each pass separating x from y; lesson 1 shows what the fully split layout looks like.

integrate and burn are streams: every row of every matching table, in order. collision_system and blast_system are closer to lookups: for each bullet or each blast, they visit drones that could be anywhere. Lesson 7 measures what each layout costs for both kinds of loop, and why the components here stay small structs.

lifetime_system stays one proc. Its loop records a despawn for each expired bullet, and a loop that calls something per row is not vectorized whatever its parameters say. The other systems branch, search or record in their loops too.

Why not change tables during a query

Each of these would be a real bug with the world from lesson 4:

  • Despawn. The swap-remove moves the last row into the hole, behind the loop, so that entity is not processed this frame. Meanwhile the slice the system cut before the despawn still reaches the old last row, a stale copy, and anything written to it is lost.
  • Spawn. A table that is full grows, and its columns move to new memory. A system holding a []position from before the spawn keeps writing to the old copy. Nothing crashes; the writes are just lost.
  • Add or remove. The entity moves to another table, which the same query may reach later. That entity is processed twice this frame.

The buffer

command: struct = { kind; entity; pending; signature; id; payload; }

Spawned entities have no handle until the buffer runs, so commands_spawn returns a pending number, and commands_set_spawned<T> writes a component into "the entity that pending spawn will create". T has to be in the spawn's signature, and applying the buffer stops the program with a message if it is not. Payloads are copies of the component value, kept as a []u8 in the buffer's frame arena next to the commands. commands_apply runs everything in order, then clears the arena. One memops_arena_clear frees the whole frame's commands.

Skipped commands

Frame 113 is the interesting one. A bullet destroys one drone, and its blast takes two burning neighbours below zero in the same loop. Each of them is destroyed in turn, and each blast reaches back to drones already recorded as destroyed:

bullet 8:9 hits drone 6:1, health -13.2
drone 6:1 is destroyed
drone 7:1 is caught in the blast, health -14.4
drone 4:2 is caught in the blast, health -4.8
drone 7:1 is destroyed
drone 6:1 is caught in the blast, health -54.0
...

The blast cannot know 6:1 is doomed: its despawn is only recorded, and it is still in its table. So it records an add<burning> against it. When the buffer is applied the despawn comes first, and kayan_move reports kayan_status.dead for the add, so the command is skipped. The summary counts three.

Try

  1. Call kayan_despawn directly in outcome_system instead of recording it. The first difference is at frame 56: the program reports drone 3:1 destroyed, but the drone it removed was 1:1. Explain why, from the swap-remove and the slices the loop is holding.
  2. Make blast_system skip neighbours whose health is already at or below zero. The skip count drops to zero. Is the buffer's check still needed?
  3. Give the turret a health component and let leaking drones damage it. When it reaches zero, despawn it through the buffer and end the game.
  4. Print the buffer before applying it, as a log of every structural change the frame made.
  5. Inline integrate back into movement_system, build with gcc -O3 -fopt-info-vec, and find the loop it now versions for aliasing.
  6. Run with --sanitize after each change. A stale slice into a grown table is exactly what AddressSanitizer does not catch, because the old memory is still valid arena memory. Think about what would.
